3. **Small mistakes count more on small boxes.** YOLO's training treats a given error the same whether the box is large or small. But a small error in a small box has a much greater effect on IoU [S1]. Being off by a few pixels barely matters for a box around a bus, yet it can ruin the box around a sparrow. Training therefore doesn't push hard enough for precise small boxes.

These issues fit the authors' own finding that YOLO's main source of error is incorrect localization, meaning boxes in the wrong place or of the wrong size [S1].

How do YOLO's mistakes differ from Fast R-CNN's? Does one just make more errors, or are they different kinds of errors?

answer:
They make different kinds of errors. YOLO mostly puts its boxes in slightly the wrong place, while Fast R-CNN more often "sees" objects where there aren't any.

**Intersection over Union (IoU)**, written "IOU" in the paper, is the standard way to score how well a predicted box matches a real object. You take the area where the two boxes overlap and divide it by the total area they cover together. Two boxes that line up perfectly score 1, boxes that don't touch at all score 0, and a box that is in roughly the right spot but too big or shifted scores somewhere in between.

A **false positive** is a detection that shouldn't exist: the model claims "there's a dog here," but nothing is there.

Fast R-CNN works in two steps. First it proposes a set of "regions" that might contain objects, and then it judges each region separately. Because each region is judged on its own, without much view of the rest of the image, it is easier to be fooled by a patch of background that looks object-like. This is general background about how such detectors work; the passages here don't describe it.

To compare the two systems, the authors sort each wrong detection into a category using IOU and whether the class label is correct [S1]. The passage shown only spells out two of these categories. "Other" means the class is wrong but the box overlaps an object somewhat (IOU above 0.1). "Background" means the box overlaps no object at all (IOU below 0.1) [S1]. The exact definition of a localization error isn't included in this excerpt. Roughly, it means the right kind of object, but a poorly placed box.

The pattern is very different for the two systems:

- **YOLO** struggles mainly with localization. Its localization errors outnumber all its other error types combined [S1].
- **Fast R-CNN** makes far fewer localization errors but many more background errors. 13.6% of its top detections are false positives containing no object, which makes it almost 3 times as likely as YOLO to predict background as an object [S1].

As an analogy, YOLO is like someone who correctly notices "there's a cat on the couch" but points a bit off to the side. Fast R-CNN points precisely but sometimes points at a cushion and calls it a cat.

These numbers compare the types of error, not the overall totals. For each category, the authors look only at the top N detections, where N is the number of real objects of that kind, and chart what share of those fall into each error type [S1].

The difference matters in practice. Because YOLO rarely mistakes background for objects, the authors use it to double-check Fast R-CNN's boxes, boosting the ones YOLO agrees with [S2]. This raised Fast R-CNN's mAP (an overall accuracy score) from 71.8% to 75.0%. Combining Fast R-CNN with other versions of itself added only 0.3 to 0.6% [S2]. The authors credit the gain to YOLO making different kinds of mistakes [S2].

<question>
How do YOLO's mistakes differ from Fast R-CNN's? Does one just make more errors, or are they different kinds of errors?
</question>

answer:
They make different kinds of errors. YOLO's weakness is placing boxes precisely, while Fast R-CNN's weakness is firing on regions that contain no object at all.

Some general background first, since the error categories depend on it. **Intersection over Union (IoU)** measures how well a predicted box matches a ground-truth box: the area of their overlap divided by the area of their union, so it runs from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (a perfect match). A **false positive** is a detection that does not correspond to a real object, or does not match one well enough. Fast R-CNN works from **region proposals**: it first generates many candidate boxes that might contain objects, then classifies each one. YOLO instead predicts boxes directly from the whole image in one pass.

The analysis sorts each wrong detection into a category using IoU thresholds and whether the class is correct. The excerpt only spells out two of these: "Other" means the class is wrong and IoU > .1, and "Background" means IoU < .1 for any object, so the detection sits on empty background [S1]. The definition of the localization category isn't in these passages. In this kind of analysis it usually means the class is right but the box overlaps the object only partly.

Measured this way, the two detectors fail differently:

- **YOLO:** localization errors account for more of its errors than all other sources combined [S1].
- **Fast R-CNN:** it makes much fewer localization errors but far more background errors. 13.6% of its top detections are false positives containing no object, which makes it almost 3x more likely than YOLO to predict a background detection [S1].

Because the mistakes don't overlap much, the two models complement each other. The authors use YOLO to rescore Fast R-CNN's boxes, and this raises mAP from 71.8% to 75.0%. Combining Fast R-CNN with other versions of itself gains only .3 to .6% [S2]. The authors attribute the gain to YOLO making different kinds of mistakes, not to ensembling in general [S2].

The charts count errors among the top N detections per category, where N is the number of objects in that category [S1]. So they compare how each model's errors are distributed across types, not which model makes more errors in total.

Many research efforts in object detection focus on making standard detection pipelines fast. [5] [38] [31] [14] [17] [28] However, only Sadeghi et al. actually produce a detection system that runs in real-time (30 frames per second or better) [31]. We compare YOLO to their GPU implementation of DPM which runs either at 30Hz or 100Hz. While the other efforts don’t reach the real-time milestone we also compare their relative mAP and speed to examine the accuracy-performance tradeoffs available in object detection systems.

Fast YOLO is the fastest object detection method on PASCAL; as far as we know, it is the fastest extant object detector. With 52.7% mAP, it is more than twice as accurate as prior work on real-time detection. YOLO pushes mAP to 63.4% while still maintaining real-time performance.

We also train YOLO using VGG-16. This model is more accurate but also significantly slower than YOLO. It is useful for comparison to other detection systems that rely on VGG-16 but since it is slower than real-time the rest of the paper focuses on our faster models.

Fastest DPM effectively speeds up DPM without sacrificing much mAP but it still misses real-time performance by a factor of 2 [38]. It also is limited by DPM’s relatively low accuracy on detection compared to neural network approaches.

R-CNN minus R replaces Selective Search with static bounding box proposals [20]. While it is much faster than R-CNN, it still falls short of real-time and takes a significant accuracy hit from not having good proposals.

<source label="S2" section="§4.1 Comparison to Other Real-Time Systems" pages="6">

The recent Faster R-CNN replaces selective search with a neural network to propose bounding boxes, similar to Szegedy et al. [8] In our tests, their most accurate model achieves 7 fps while a smaller, less accurate one runs at 18 fps. The VGG-16 version of Faster R-CNN is 10 mAP higher but is also 6 times slower than YOLO. The Zeiler-Fergus Faster R-CNN is only 2.5 times slower than YOLO but is also less accurate.

<question>
If the VGG-16 version of YOLO is more accurate, why does the paper mostly stick with the regular YOLO and Fast YOLO models?
</question>

answer:
The VGG-16 version is more accurate, but it is too slow to count as "real-time," and real-time speed is the whole point of the paper. A few ideas make the tradeoff clear.

**mAP (mean Average Precision)** is the score used to grade object detectors. It works like a percentage grade: it rewards finding the objects that are really in the picture, drawing the boxes in the right places, and not "seeing" objects that aren't there. Higher is better. (This is general background; the paper takes mAP as known.)

**VGG-16** is also general background, since these passages don't describe it. It is a well-known, large image-recognition network that many detectors use as their "eyes," the part that looks at the picture and pulls out useful patterns. It is bigger than YOLO's own network, so it can notice more detail, but it does more work for every image.

**Frames per second (fps)** counts how many images a system can process each second. The paper treats 30 fps or better as "real-time" [S1]. That is roughly the speed of normal video, so a real-time detector can keep up with a live camera.

With those ideas, the numbers tell the story [S2]:

- **YOLO VGG-16:** 66.4% mAP at 21 fps, below the real-time line.
- **YOLO:** 63.4% mAP at 45 fps, comfortably real-time.
- **Fast YOLO:** 52.7% mAP at 155 fps.

Swapping in VGG-16 buys 3 extra points of accuracy but cuts the speed by more than half. A useful analogy is a chef who cooks slightly better meals but can't serve them before customers leave. The authors say the VGG-16 model "is more accurate but also significantly slower than YOLO," and that because it "is slower than real-time the rest of the paper focuses on our faster models" [S1].

They still report the VGG-16 version for a fair comparison. Several competing detectors, such as one version of Faster R-CNN, are built on VGG-16, so testing YOLO with the same "eyes" shows how the two approaches compare when that part is held equal [S1][S2].

Meanwhile, the faster models are where YOLO stands out. The authors call Fast YOLO the fastest object detector they know of, and it is more than twice as accurate as earlier real-time detectors. Regular YOLO raises accuracy to 63.4% while staying real-time [S1].

answer:

| Model | mAP | FPS |

| Fast YOLO | 52.7 | 155 |

<question>
Why is Fast R-CNN so slow if it already sped up R-CNN? And how does Faster R-CNN stack up against YOLO on speed vs accuracy?
</question>

answer:
Fast R-CNN made only one part of the old pipeline faster. The slow part, finding where objects might be, was left as it was. A few ideas make this clearer.

**Region proposals** are candidate boxes that might contain an object, produced before anything decides what the object is. Fast R-CNN gets them from a method called selective search, which can take around 2 seconds per image just to produce these boxes [S1].

The comparison uses **mAP** (mean average precision), a score from 0 to 100 for how well a detector finds and labels objects. Higher is better. This is general background; the passages above don't define it.

Also general background: detectors like R-CNN are often called "two-stage." First they propose boxes, then a second step classifies each box. YOLO is "one-stage": one network looks at the image once and outputs boxes and labels together. Think of checking every drawer in a room one at a time versus taking one look around the whole room.

**Why Fast R-CNN is still slow.** It sped up the classification stage, but it still waits about 2 seconds per image for selective search [S1]. It is like upgrading a factory's packing machine while the delivery truck that brings the parts stays slow. The result is high accuracy, 70.0 mAP, at only 0.5 frames per second (fps), which is far from real time [S1].

**Faster R-CNN** removes that bottleneck by replacing selective search with a neural network that learns to propose boxes itself [S1]. It comes in two sizes, compared here with YOLO's 63.4 mAP at 45 fps [S1]:

- **VGG-16 version:** 73.2 mAP at 7 fps. That is about 10 points more accurate than YOLO, but 6 times slower [S1].
- **ZF (Zeiler-Fergus) version:** 18 fps, only about 2.5 times slower than YOLO, but less accurate at 62.1 mAP [S1].

**The tradeoff.** The paper's table counts detectors at 30 fps or faster as "real-time," and both Faster R-CNN versions fall short of that line [S1]. The big Faster R-CNN buys extra accuracy at a large cost in speed. The small one gives up both speed and accuracy compared with YOLO. YOLO sits above the line at 45 fps with accuracy close to the best [S1].

answer:
Fast R-CNN's speedup only covered half the pipeline. Before any classification happens, a separate step has to propose candidate boxes, and that step was never accelerated.

Three general concepts are needed here, since the paper assumes them:

- **Region proposals**: a detector can first generate a few thousand candidate boxes likely to contain an object, then classify each one. Selective search is a classic hand-designed (non-learned) algorithm for this, built on grouping similar image segments.
- **mAP (mean average precision)**: for each class, average precision summarizes the precision–recall curve of the ranked detections, counting a box as correct when its IoU with the ground truth exceeds a threshold. mAP averages this over classes, so higher is better.
- **Two-stage vs one-stage**: two-stage detectors propose regions first and then classify them. One-stage detectors like YOLO predict boxes and classes directly from the full image in a single network pass.

|---|---|---|---|
| Faster R-CNN VGG-16 | 73.2 | 7 | ~10 mAP higher, 6× slower |
| Faster R-CNN ZF | 62.1 | 18 | less accurate, 2.5× slower |
| YOLO | 63.4 | 45 | — |

In Table 1, the paper's "real-time" group starts at 30 fps. Both Faster R-CNN variants fall in the "less than real-time" group, while YOLO sits well above that line [S1].

<question>
How does YOLO alone stack up against the other methods on the VOC 2012 leaderboard, and which object classes does it do worst on?
</question>

answer:
A few terms first, since the leaderboard is built on them. These are general background rather than the paper's own explanations:

- **PASCAL VOC** is a widely used test set of everyday photos in which people have drawn boxes around objects from 20 categories, such as cats, bottles, sheep and planes. Detectors are ranked by how well they find those objects.
- **Mean average precision (mAP)** is the score used for that ranking. For each category, it rewards a detector for finding the real objects without also raising false alarms, giving a number from 0 to 100. Those per-category numbers are then averaged. Higher is better.
- **Fast R-CNN** is a slower, two-stage detector. It first proposes many candidate regions of the image and then checks each one to decide what, if anything, is in it.

On the VOC 2012 leaderboard, YOLO scores an mAP of 57.9 [S1]. That puts it well behind the top entries, such as MR CNN MORE DATA at 73.9 and Fast R-CNN at 68.4. It sits just below the older R-CNN VGG at 59.2 [S1]. However, YOLO is the only real-time detector on the board [S1]. Every method above it trades speed for accuracy.

The per-category scores show where YOLO struggles [S1]:

- **Weakest:** bottle (22.7), plant (28.9), tv (50.8) and sheep (52.2).
- **Strongest:** cat (81.4), dog (77.2) and aeroplane (77.0).

The gap is clearest on bottles and plants. On those categories, Fast R-CNN scores 38.7 and 35.1, against YOLO's 22.7 and 28.9 [S1]. On sheep the gap is even larger in absolute terms: Fast R-CNN scores 68.3 against YOLO's 52.2 [S1]. The weak categories tend to be objects that are often small or appear in clusters, while YOLO does well on large, distinct animals and planes.

YOLO's real strength shows up when it is combined with Fast R-CNN. YOLO makes far fewer "background" mistakes, which means flagging an object where there is none [S2]. To combine the two, each box Fast R-CNN proposes gets a boost if YOLO predicts a similar box [S2]. On the leaderboard, this Fast R-CNN + YOLO combination reaches 70.7, fourth highest overall and 2.3 points above Fast R-CNN alone [S1]. The authors argue the gain comes from YOLO making *different kinds* of mistakes, not simply from averaging two models. Combining Fast R-CNN with other versions of itself added only 0.3 to 0.6 points [S2].

<question>
How does YOLO alone stack up against the other methods on the VOC 2012 leaderboard, and which object classes does it do worst on?
</question>

answer:
Some general background first, since the table assumes it. **Mean average precision (mAP)** is computed per class: rank all detections of that class by confidence, trace precision against recall (a detection counts as correct if its box overlaps a ground-truth box enough), and take the area under that curve to get the class's average precision (AP). mAP is the mean of the per-class APs. PASCAL VOC is a standard detection benchmark with 20 object classes, and VOC 2012 test results are reported on a public leaderboard. Fast R-CNN is a two-stage detector: it first proposes candidate regions, then classifies and refines each one. That makes it accurate but slower than a single-pass model like YOLO.

On the VOC 2012 leaderboard, YOLO scores 57.9 mAP [S1]. That puts it well below the top entries, such as MR CNN MORE DATA at 73.9 and Fast R-CNN at 68.4, and slightly below R-CNN VGG at 59.2. It is still above Feature Edit (56.3), R-CNN BB (53.3) and SDS (50.7) [S1]. It is also the only real-time detector in the table [S1], so it is the one entry trading accuracy for speed.

Its per-class APs show where the gap comes from [S1]:

- **Weakest:** bottle (22.7), plant (28.9), chair (36.2), boat (38.3), tv (50.8) and sheep (52.2).
- **Compared with Fast R-CNN:** bottle 22.7 vs 38.7, plant 28.9 vs 35.1, and sheep 52.2 vs 68.3.
- **Strongest:** cat (81.4), dog (77.2) and aero (77.0), close to many far more accurate methods.

The weak classes are mostly small or cluttered objects. That fits the paper's own statement that YOLO makes more localization errors than other detectors.

YOLO's errors also differ from Fast R-CNN's: it makes far fewer background false positives [S2]. Using YOLO to rescore Fast R-CNN's boxes gives Fast R-CNN + YOLO a score of 70.7, the fourth highest on the leaderboard and a 2.3% boost over Fast R-CNN alone [S1]. On VOC 2007, ensembling Fast R-CNN with other versions of itself gained only .3 to .6, while adding YOLO gained 3.2 [S2].

answer:
YOLO scores **57.9 mAP** on VOC 2012 test, near the bottom of the comp4 leaderboard [S1]. It trails MR CNN MORE DATA (73.9), Faster R-CNN (70.4), and Fast R-CNN (68.4), and it falls just below R-CNN VGG (59.2) [S1]. It is, however, the only real-time detector in the table [S1]. - **Against Fast R-CNN:** bottle 22.7 vs 38.7, plant 28.9 vs 35.1, sheep 52.2 vs 68.3.
- **Strongest:** cat 81.4, dog 77.2, aero 77.0, train 73.9. These are competitive with R-CNN-family numbers, and cat beats R-CNN VGG's 81.1.

The weak classes are typically small, thin, or clustered objects, while the strong ones tend to be large and centered. The sources shown here don't spell out this explanation. As general background, a coarse grid with few boxes per cell and loose localization would plausibly penalize small and crowded instances most.

YOLO's errors complement Fast R-CNN's. YOLO is used to rescore Fast R-CNN's boxes, boosting those that YOLO also predicts, which suppresses background false positives [S2]. On VOC 2012, Fast R-CNN + YOLO reaches 70.7 mAP, fourth on the board and 2.3 points above Fast R-CNN alone [S1]. Bottle rises to 43.4 and plant to 41.8 [S1]. On VOC 2007 the same combination gains 3.2, compared with only 0.3–0.6 from ensembling other Fast R-CNN variants [S2].

<question>
Why does YOLO hold up so much better than R-CNN when you test it on artwork like Picasso paintings instead of photos?

answer:
The paper's results show *that* YOLO holds up much better on artwork, but these passages don't explain *why*. The numbers first need three ideas.

**Average precision** (AP) is a score for how good a detector is. Imagine the detector pointing at things and saying "that's a person." AP rewards it for finding most of the real people while not pointing at things that aren't people. Higher is better, and here it's shown out of 100.

**Domain shift** means testing a system on a different kind of picture than it learned from. It's like someone who learned to recognize dogs only from photos and is then asked to spot dogs in cartoons. The detectors here learned mostly from ordinary photos and are then tested on paintings.

A **precision-recall curve** is a graph of a trade-off. Precision asks how many of the detector's guesses were right. Recall asks how many of the real objects it found. A detector that guesses more often finds more objects but also makes more wrong guesses, and the curve shows that trade-off at every level of eagerness. The "best F1" score picks the single best balance point on that curve.

Here is what the comparison table shows [S1]:

- **R-CNN** scores 54.2 AP on photos (VOC 2007) but collapses to 10.4 on Picasso paintings. Its best F1 is 0.226, and it scores 26 on the People-Art dataset.
- **YOLO** goes from 59.2 on photos to 53.3 on Picasso, only a small drop. Its best F1 is 0.590, and it scores 45 on People-Art.
- **DPM**, an older detector, also drops much less than R-CNN, from 43.2 to 37.8.

In this work we investigate the effect of the convolutional network depth on its accuracy in the large-scale image recognition setting. In particular, an important role in the advance of deep visual recognition architectures has been played by the ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) (Russakovsky et al., 2014), which has served as a testbed for a few generations of large-scale image classification systems, from high-dimensional shallow feature encodings (Perronnin et al., 2010) (the winner of ILSVRC-2011) to deep ConvNets (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) (the winner of ILSVRC-2012).

With ConvNets becoming more of a commodity in the computer vision field, a number of attempts have been made to improve the original architecture of Krizhevsky et al. (2012) in a bid to achieve better accuracy. For instance, the best-performing submissions to the ILSVRC-2013 (Zeiler & Fergus, 2013; Sermanet et al., 2014) utilised smaller receptive window size and smaller stride of the first convolutional layer. Another line of improvements dealt with training and testing the networks densely over the whole image and over multiple scales (Sermanet et al., 2014; Howard, 2014). In this paper, we address another important aspect of ConvNet architecture design – its depth. To this end, we fix other parameters of the architecture, and steadily increase the depth of the network by adding more convolutional layers, which is feasible due to the use of very small (3 × 3) convolution filters in all layers.

What's the main thing this VGG paper is trying to show, and what did going deeper actually buy them?
</question>

answer:
The paper asks one question: does making an image-recognition network **deeper** (stacking more layers) make it more accurate? The answer is yes. Going to 16–19 layers clearly beat earlier designs [S1]. Three background ideas make this easier to follow.

The first is general background rather than the paper's content. A convolutional neural network ("ConvNet") is a program that learns to recognise pictures by passing an image through a stack of layers. Early layers pick up simple patterns like edges, and later layers combine them into shapes and whole objects. Each layer is a step in this chain, so "depth" means how many steps there are.

The second is also general background. Each layer works by sliding small pattern detectors, called **filters**, across the image, like moving a small magnifying glass over a photo and checking each patch. The filter size is how big that patch is. A 3×3 filter looks at just a 3-by-3 square of pixels at a time, the smallest window that still captures a pattern in every direction.

The third is the contest where results were measured. The ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) is a yearly competition on a huge public photo collection, and it has served as the proving ground for successive generations of image-recognition systems [S2].

The study works like a careful experiment. Earlier work improved networks by changing several things at once, such as the size of the first layer's window or testing at multiple image sizes [S2]. The authors instead hold everything else fixed and change only depth, adding more convolutional layers step by step [S2]. Using tiny 3×3 filters in every layer is what makes this practical: small filters keep each added layer cheap enough that the network can grow very deep [S2].

Going deeper bought them several results:

- **Better accuracy:** pushing depth to 16–19 weight layers gave "a significant improvement on the prior-art configurations" [S1]. "Weight layers" are the layers that contain learned settings.
- **Competition wins:** these networks were the basis of their ImageNet Challenge 2014 entry, which took first place in localisation (finding where the object is in the image) and second place in classification (naming what it is) [S1].
- **Usefulness beyond ImageNet:** what the networks learned carried over to other image datasets, where they achieved state-of-the-art results [S1].
- **A shared tool:** the authors released their two best models publicly so others could build on them [S1]. These released models are the ones people now call VGG-16 and VGG-19.

These findings were the basis of our ImageNet Challenge 2014 submission, where our team secured the first and the second places in the localisation and classification tracks respectively. We also show that our representations generalise well to other datasets, where they achieve state-of-the-art results. Convolutional networks (ConvNets) have recently enjoyed a great success in large-scale image and video recognition (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Zeiler & Fergus, 2013; Sermanet et al., 2014; Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) which has become possible due to the large public image repositories, such as ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009), and high-performance computing systems, such as GPUs or large-scale distributed clusters (Dean et al., 2012). In particular, an important role in the advance of deep visual recognition architectures has been played by the ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) (Russakovsky et al., 2014), which has served as a testbed for a few generations of large-scale image classification systems, from high-dimensional shallow feature encodings (Perronnin et al., 2010) (the winner of ILSVRC-2011) to deep ConvNets (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) (the winner of ILSVRC-2012).

With ConvNets becoming more of a commodity in the computer vision field, a number of attempts have been made to improve the original architecture of Krizhevsky et al. (2012) in a bid to achieve better accuracy. For instance, the best-performing submissions to the ILSVRC-2013 (Zeiler & Fergus, 2013; Sermanet et al., 2014) utilised smaller receptive window size and smaller stride of the first convolutional layer. Another line of improvements dealt with training and testing the networks densely over the whole image and over multiple scales (Sermanet et al., 2014; Howard, 2014). <question>

The paper is a controlled ablation on depth. The authors fix the other architectural parameters and steadily increase depth by adding convolutional layers [S2]. <question>
When they say the nets work on other datasets with a 'simple pipeline', what does that actually mean? Do they retrain the network?
</question>

answer:
No, they don't retrain the network. The "simple pipeline" means the trained network is used as-is to describe images, and a separate, very simple classifier makes the decisions for the new dataset. The authors give the example of "deep features classified by a linear SVM without fine-tuning" [S1].

The paper doesn't define the three ideas behind this. In general:

- **Transfer learning** means taking a model trained on one big task and reusing it on a different one. It is like a trained chef applying knife skills in a new kitchen. Here, the network learned on the huge ImageNet photo collection and is reused on other image datasets.
- **Feature extraction** is the reuse step itself. You feed a new image through the trained network and, instead of reading its final answer ("dog", "car"), you take the long list of numbers it computes just before that. These numbers, called "features", act as a detailed fingerprint of what's in the image.
- A **linear SVM** (support vector machine) is a simple classifier that learns to separate categories by drawing straight dividing lines (or their higher-dimensional equivalent) between groups of fingerprints. It is quick to train because it only has to learn where to put those dividing lines.

In the paper's setup, the network's weights stay frozen. "Without fine-tuning" means they are not adjusted for the new dataset [S1]. Only the small linear SVM learns anything new. This is the opposite of retraining, where the whole network would keep adjusting itself on the new images.

The point of the claim is that the networks still achieve "excellent performance" in this stripped-down setup [S1]. If a frozen network plus a very basic classifier works well on unfamiliar datasets, the fingerprints it learned must capture something broadly useful about images, not just tricks specific to ImageNet.

The authors defer the details of these experiments to Appendix B, which discusses how the "very deep features" generalise to other datasets [S1]. They also released their two best-performing models publicly so others can use them this way [S1].

Since the fully-convolutional network is applied over the whole image, there is no need to sample multiple crops at test time (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), which is less efficient as it requires network re-computation for each crop. At the same time, using a large set of crops, as done by Szegedy et al. (2014), can lead to improved accuracy, as it results in a finer sampling of the input image compared to the fully-convolutional net. Also, multi-crop evaluation is complementary to dense evaluation due to different convolution boundary conditions: when applying a ConvNet to a crop, the convolved feature maps are padded with zeros, while in the case of dense evaluation the padding for the same crop naturally comes from the neighbouring parts of an image (due to both the convolutions and spatial pooling), which substantially increases the overall network receptive field, so more context is captured. While we believe that in practice the increased computation time of multiple crops does not justify the potential gains in accuracy, for reference we also evaluate our networks using 50 crops per scale (5 × 5 regular grid with 2 flips), for a total of 150 crops over 3 scales, which is comparable to 144 crops over 4 scales used by Szegedy et al. (2014).

<source label="S2" section="§3.3 Implementation Details" pages="5">
Our implementation is derived from the publicly available C++ Caffe toolbox (Jia, 2013) (branched out in December 2013), but contains a number of significant modifications, allowing us to perform training and evaluation on multiple GPUs installed in a single system, as well as train and evaluate on full-size (uncropped) images at multiple scales (as described above). Multi-GPU training exploits data parallelism, and is carried out by splitting each batch of training images into several GPU batches, processed in parallel on each GPU. After the GPU batch gradients are computed, they are averaged to obtain the gradient of the full batch. Gradient computation is synchronous across the GPUs, so the result is exactly the same as when training on a single GPU.

While more sophisticated methods of speeding up ConvNet training have been recently proposed (Krizhevsky, 2014), which employ model and data parallelism for different layers of the net, we have found that our conceptually much simpler scheme already provides a speedup of 3.75 times on an off-the-shelf 4-GPU system, as compared to using a single GPU. On a system equipped with four NVIDIA Titan Black GPUs, training a single net took 2–3 weeks depending on the architecture.

<question>
If running the conv net densely over the whole image is more efficient, why would multi-crop testing still add anything on top of it?
</question>

answer:
Dense evaluation and multi-crop testing look at the image in slightly different ways, so each catches things the other misses [S1]. Three ideas make this clear.

In general, a **fully convolutional network** is one built only from small sliding filters, with no part that demands a fixed-size input. Like a magnifying glass slid across a page, it can be run over a picture of any size in one pass and gives an answer for every region at once.

The authors use this to run their network over the whole test image in one go. Because of that, they say there is no need to cut out many smaller crops and run the network separately on each one, which is slower because the network has to be recomputed for every crop [S1].

Multi-crop testing still helps for two reasons the authors give.

First, a large set of crops samples the image more finely than the single dense pass [S1]. Think of photographing a scene from many slightly shifted positions instead of once: some shots may frame the object better.

Second, the two methods treat the edges of a region differently [S1]. Two more general ideas explain why that matters:

- **Zero padding**: when a filter reaches the border of an image, there is nothing beyond the edge, so the network fills that gap with blank (zero) values, like a blank frame around a photo.
- **Receptive field**: the area of the original image that one output "sees". A bigger receptive field means more surrounding context.

When the network runs on a cut-out crop, its edges are padded with zeros. When the same region is processed during the dense pass, the "padding" is the real neighbouring parts of the image. This substantially enlarges the network's receptive field, so more context is captured [S1]. A crop sees its region with a blank frame. The dense pass sees it inside the full scene. Because they differ, the authors call the two approaches complementary [S1].

Even so, the authors believe that in practice the extra computation for many crops isn't worth the possible accuracy gain [S1]. For reference, they still tested it: 50 crops per scale (a 5 × 5 grid of positions, each also flipped left-to-right) across 3 scales, 150 crops in total. This is comparable to the 144 crops over 4 scales used by Szegedy et al. (2014) [S1].

<question>
If running the conv net densely over the whole image is more efficient, why would multi-crop testing still add anything on top of it?
</question>

answer:
In dense evaluation the fully-convolutional network is applied once over the whole image, so there is no need to sample crops; multi-crop testing is less efficient because it re-runs the network for every crop [S1]. The gain from crops comes from two things dense evaluation does differently, so the two methods end up complementary [S1].

Three general ideas help here (background, not from the paper):

1. **Fully convolutional network**: if the fully-connected layers are rewritten as convolutions, the net accepts an image of any size and outputs a spatial map of class scores instead of one vector. Averaging that map gives an image-level prediction from a single forward pass, and neighbouring windows share computation.
2. **Zero padding**: to keep feature maps the same size, a convolution pads the border of its input with zeros. At a crop's edge, those zeros stand in for image content that was cut away.
3. **Receptive field**: the region of the input that can affect a given output unit. It grows with each convolution and pooling layer, so units in deep layers "see" a large patch.

The first reason multi-crop helps is sampling density. A large set of crops, as used by Szegedy et al., samples the input image more finely than the fixed output grid of the fully-convolutional net [S1]. Many shifted and flipped windows give more varied views to average over.

The second reason is boundary conditions. When the ConvNet runs on a crop, its feature maps are padded with zeros at the crop border. In dense evaluation, the "padding" for that same region comes from the real neighbouring parts of the image, through both the convolutions and spatial pooling [S1]. According to the authors, this substantially increases the overall receptive field in the dense case, so more context is captured [S1]. Each approach sees the image a little differently, which is why combining them can help.

The authors still think that in practice the extra computation of multiple crops does not justify the potential accuracy gain [S1]. For reference, they evaluate 50 crops per scale (a 5 × 5 regular grid with 2 flips), 150 crops over 3 scales in total. This is comparable to the 144 crops over 4 scales used by Szegedy et al. [S1].

During training, the input to our ConvNets is a fixed-size 224 × 224 RGB image. The only pre-processing we do is subtracting the mean RGB value, computed on the training set, from each pixel. The image is passed through a stack of convolutional (conv.) layers, where we use filters with a very small receptive field: 3 × 3 (which is the smallest size to capture the notion of left/right, up/down, center). In one of the configurations we also utilise 1 × 1 convolution filters, which can be seen as a linear transformation of the input channels (followed by non-linearity). The convolution stride is fixed to 1 pixel; the spatial padding of conv. layer input is such that the spatial resolution is preserved after convolution, i.e. the padding is 1 pixel for 3 × 3 conv. layers. Spatial pooling is carried out by five max-pooling layers, which follow some of the conv. layers (not all the conv. layers are followed by max-pooling). Max-pooling is performed over a 2 × 2 pixel window, with stride 2. A stack of convolutional layers (which has a different depth in different architectures) is followed by three Fully-Connected (FC) layers: the first two have 4096 channels each, the third performs 1000-way ILSVRC classification and thus contains 1000 channels (one for each class). The final layer is the soft-max layer. The configuration of the fully connected layers is the same in all networks. <question>
Why do they use 3x3 filters specifically instead of something bigger or smaller like 1x1?
</question>

answer:
A **filter** is a small window that slides across the image, looking at a little patch of pixels at a time and asking "is my pattern here?" The authors chose a 3×3 window because it is "the smallest size to capture the notion of left/right, up/down, center" [S1].

Three ideas from general background (not from the paper's text) make that reason clearer:

1. **Receptive field**: the patch of the image a filter can "see" at once. A 3×3 filter sees a pixel plus its eight neighbours. The paper calls 3×3 a "very small receptive field" [S1].
2. **Stride and padding**: stride is how far the window jumps each step. Padding is a thin border of extra pixels added around the image so the window can sit on the edges too. Together they decide whether the image shrinks as it passes through a layer.
3. **1×1 convolution**: a window only one pixel wide. It never looks at neighbours. It only combines the different colour or feature values stored at that single spot.

**Why not smaller (1×1)?** The authors describe a 1×1 filter as "a linear transformation of the input channels (followed by non-linearity)" [S1]. In plain terms, it remixes the information already sitting at one pixel and then applies a simple on/off-style adjustment. It has no sense of what is next to that pixel. Picture reading a word through a pinhole that shows one letter at a time: you can see the letter clearly, but you can't tell what is beside it. A 3×3 window is the smallest one with a centre plus something on every side, so it can notice that something is brighter on the left, or that an edge runs from top to bottom [S1]. The 1×1 filters appear in only one of the configurations [S1].

**Supporting details.** Every 3×3 layer uses a stride of 1 pixel and padding of 1 pixel, so the image keeps the same size after each one [S1]. Shrinking the image is handled separately by five max-pooling layers. Each takes a 2×2 block and keeps only the strongest value, using stride 2 [S1]. This division of labour lets the authors stack many 3×3 layers without the image getting smaller too quickly.

**Why not bigger?** The passages here don't fully spell this out. They do point at the trade-off. Even though the networks are very deep, they don't use more weights than a shallower network built with wider layers and larger receptive fields, which had 144M weights [S2]. Small windows keep each layer cheap, and that makes it practical to stack 16 to 19 weight layers [S2]. The paper's §2.3 Discussion is where the authors make the fuller case for small filters.

[S2].

The standard reasoning, which is general background here, is that $n$ stacked 3×3 convs (stride 1) have an effective receptive field of $(2n+1)\times(2n+1)$. <question>
Why did they train the shallow net A first and copy its layers into the deeper VGG models instead of just randomly initializing everything?
</question>

answer:
The authors were worried that a very deep network started from purely random numbers might not learn at all. Training a smaller network first and reusing its parts gave the deep models a better starting point. Three ideas from general deep learning (not from the paper) explain why.

**Gradients that shrink or blow up.** A network learns by passing a correction signal (the "gradient") backwards from its final answer through every layer, telling each layer how to adjust. In a deep network this signal is multiplied many times on the way back, like a whisper passed down a long line of people. It can fade to almost nothing, so the early layers stop learning, or it can grow wildly, so learning becomes chaotic.

**Weight initialization.** Before training, every layer's internal numbers (its "weights") have to be set to something. These starting values decide whether the correction signal stays a sensible size as it travels through the layers. Poor starting values make the fading or exploding much worse.

**Xavier (Glorot) initialization.** This is a recipe for choosing random starting weights scaled to the size of each layer, so the signal keeps roughly the same strength from layer to layer. It was designed to make deep networks trainable from random numbers alone.

The paper says the same thing in its own words: bad initialization "can stall learning due to the instability of gradient in deep nets" [S1]. To avoid this, the authors first trained configuration A, which is shallow enough to learn from random starting weights [S1]. When they built the deeper networks, they copied A's first four convolutional layers (the image-scanning layers at the start) and its last three fully-connected layers (the decision-making layers at the end) into the new model. The new layers in the middle started randomly [S1]. The analogy is a new employee who joins a team where the first and last stages of the job are already handled by experienced staff.

The copied layers were not frozen. The authors kept their learning rate at its normal value so those layers could keep adjusting to the deeper network [S1]. Wherever random starting values were used, the weights were drawn from a bell curve centred on zero with a small spread (a variance of $10^{-2}$), and the biases (a constant offset each unit adds to its output) started at zero [S1].

The authors also think this head start helped the deep networks reach good accuracy in fewer passes through the data, along with other factors such as depth and small filters [S1]. After submitting the paper, they found the shallow-net step was not actually needed: using the Glorot & Bengio random initialization recipe, they could train the deep models directly without pre-training [S1].

<question>
Why did they train the shallow net A first and copy its layers into the deeper VGG models instead of just randomly initializing everything?
</question>

answer:
Deep networks are fragile at the start of training. A bad initialization can stall learning because gradients become unstable as they pass through many layers [S1]. Net A was shallow enough to train from random weights, so the authors used it as a stable starting point for the deeper models [S1].

The paper does not explain the underlying mechanism, so the next two paragraphs are general background. During backpropagation, the gradient reaching an early layer is a product of per-layer Jacobians. If the typical scale of each factor sits even slightly below 1, the product shrinks toward zero (**vanishing gradients**). If it sits above 1, the product blows up (exploding gradients). Either way, early layers get useless updates, and the deeper the net, the worse the compounding.

Weight initialization controls that per-layer scale at step zero. With a fixed variance, the variance of the activations and gradients is multiplied by roughly $n \cdot \mathrm{Var}(W)$ at each layer, where $n$ is the fan-in. A value that works for 11 layers can drift badly over 19. Xavier (Glorot) initialization instead sets $\mathrm{Var}(W) \approx 2/(n_\text{in}+n_\text{out})$, so the signal and gradient variance stay roughly constant across layers.

Here is how VGG's procedure worked in practice:

- **Random init:** weights were drawn from a zero-mean normal with $10^{-2}$ variance, and biases were set to zero [S1]. This fixed scale ignores layer width, which is exactly what becomes risky with depth.
- **Transfer:** the deeper nets took their first four conv layers and last three FC layers from net A. The intermediate layers were initialized randomly [S1].
- **No freezing:** the copied layers kept the normal learning rate, so they could still adapt to the new architecture [S1].

The authors also credit this pre-initialization, along with implicit regularization from depth and small filters, for the nets converging in fewer epochs than Krizhevsky et al.'s [S1]. After submitting the paper, they found the pre-training step unnecessary: Glorot & Bengio's random initialization lets the deep nets train from scratch [S1].

answer:
The authors' stated reason is optimization stability: "bad initialisation can stall learning due to the instability of gradient in deep nets" [S1]. Their fixed random init draws weights from $\mathcal{N}(0, 10^{-2})$ (variance $10^{-2}$, so std $0.1$) with zero biases [S1]. That scale is set by hand and does not depend on fan-in. Through 16–19 weight layers without batch norm or residual paths, activation and gradient magnitudes can compound layer by layer and vanish or explode.

Configuration A (11 weight layers) is "shallow enough to be trained with random initialisation" [S1], so they trained it first. For the deeper configs, the first four conv layers and the last three FC layers were initialised from net A, and the intermediate layers were initialised randomly [S1]. This places trained filters at both ends of the network. Only the newly inserted middle block starts from scratch, which shortens the stretch of random layers that the signal has to pass through. The transferred layers were not frozen or given a reduced learning rate. They trained at the normal schedule (initial LR $10^{-2}$) and could adapt to the new middle layers [S1].

The authors also point to a second benefit. They conjecture that pre-initialisation of certain layers, together with the implicit regularisation from depth and small filters, is part of why their nets converged in fewer epochs (74) than Krizhevsky et al. despite having more parameters [S1].

The authors also say the staged procedure turned out to be unnecessary. After submission they found that the Glorot & Bengio (2010) random initialisation lets the deep nets train without pre-training [S1].

As general background not covered in the paper: Glorot/Xavier init scales the weight variance by fan-in and fan-out (roughly $2/(n_{in}+n_{out})$). This keeps activation and gradient variance approximately constant across layers, which directly addresses the depth-dependent instability that the A-first scheme worked around. He et al.'s later ReLU-specific variant does the same with variance $2/n_{in}$.

question: Why stack three 3x3 conv layers instead of just using one 7x7 layer if they see the same area of the image?

Close with the regularisation view: the stack acts like a 7x7 filter forced to decompose into 3x3 filters with non-linearities in between.

Our ConvNet configurations are quite different from the ones used in the top-performing entries of the ILSVRC-2012 (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) and ILSVRC-2013 competitions (Zeiler & Fergus, 2013; Sermanet et al., 2014). Rather than using relatively large receptive fields in the first conv. layers (e.g. 11 × 11 with stride 4 in (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), or 7 × 7 with stride 2 in (Zeiler & Fergus, 2013; Sermanet et al., 2014)), we use very small 3 × 3 receptive fields throughout the whole net, which are convolved with the input at every pixel (with stride 1). It is easy to see that a stack of two 3 × 3 conv. layers (without spatial pooling in between) has an effective receptive field of 5 × 5; three such layers have a 7 × 7 effective receptive field. So what have we gained by using, for instance, a stack of three 3×3 conv. layers instead of a single 7×7 layer? <question>
Why stack three 3x3 conv layers instead of just using one 7x7 layer if they see the same area of the image?
</question>

answer:
Covering the same area is the point of the comparison. The authors show the two options see the same area, then argue the stack wins on two other counts. Three ideas make the argument easier to follow.

**Receptive field** is how big a patch of the original image one output spot "looks at." A 3×3 filter is a small window, 3 pixels by 3 pixels, that slides across the image and summarizes each patch it lands on. Stack a second 3×3 layer on top and each of its spots summarizes a 3×3 patch of *summaries*. Each of those already covered a bit of the image, so together they reach further, like reading a summary of summaries.

Following that logic, two stacked 3×3 layers see a 5×5 area of the image, and three see 7×7 [S1]. This holds when each filter moves one pixel at a time and nothing shrinks the image between layers [S1]. So in terms of coverage, three 3×3 layers and one 7×7 layer are equivalent.

The second idea is general background rather than something the paper explains. After each layer, networks apply a simple rule called ReLU: keep positive numbers and turn negatives into zero. This small "bend" lets the network represent complicated patterns instead of only straight-line combinations. Without it, stacking layers would add no extra power.

The third idea, also general background, concerns **parameters**. These are the adjustable numbers a network learns during training. A filter needs one number per pixel in its window, for every pairing of incoming and outgoing feature types (call the number of feature types C). Bigger windows therefore cost more numbers.

With those pieces, the authors give two gains:

1. **More bends, sharper decisions.** Three layers means three ReLUs instead of one, which makes the network's decision-making "more discriminative," better at telling things apart [S1]. Think of drawing a curve with three bends versus one: three let you trace a more detailed shape.
2. **Fewer numbers to learn.** Three 3×3 layers need $3 \times 3^2 \times C^2 = 27C^2$ weights. In words, that is three layers, each with a 9-pixel window, times C² feature pairings. One 7×7 layer needs $7^2 \times C^2 = 49C^2$, which is 81% more [S1].

The authors also offer a deeper way to see this. Using the stack is like taking a 7×7 filter and *forcing* it to be built from smaller 3×3 pieces, with a ReLU between each piece [S1]. That restriction acts as **regularisation**, a constraint that keeps the network from learning overly arbitrary patterns [S1]. An analogy: instead of letting someone paint any picture on a 7×7 canvas, you require them to build it from three rounds of small, simple brushstrokes. They can still produce rich results, but with fewer free choices, so they are less likely to memorise noise.

Then give the two gains: three ReLUs instead of one make the decision function more discriminative, and the parameter count drops from 49C^2 to 27C^2 (the 7x7 needs 81% more). Close with the regularisation view: the stack acts like a 7x7 filter forced to decompose into 3x3 filters with non-linearities in between.

answer:
Coverage is identical: a stack of two 3×3 conv layers with stride 1 and no pooling in between has an effective receptive field of 5×5, and three such layers reach 7×7 [S1]. The authors argue that the stack gives two things the single large filter doesn't [S1].

**1. More non-linearity.** The stack includes three rectification (ReLU) layers instead of one, which the authors say "makes the decision function more discriminative" [S1]. The same reasoning is behind the 1×1 conv layers in configuration C: they add a ReLU without changing the receptive field [S1].

As general background, a 7×7 conv followed by one ReLU is a single linear filter followed by one non-linearity. Three 3×3 convs, each followed by $\max(0,x)$, form a three-step composition that can express functions a single linear filter plus one ReLU cannot.

**2. Fewer parameters.** Assume the stack has $C$ input and $C$ output channels at every layer [S1]. In general, a $k\times k$ conv layer mapping $C$ channels to $C$ channels has $k^2C^2$ weights, ignoring biases. That gives:

$$
\underbrace{3\,(3^2C^2) = 27C^2}_{\text{three }3\times3} \quad\text{vs.}\quad \underbrace{7^2C^2 = 49C^2}_{\text{one }7\times7}
$$

So the single 7×7 layer needs 81% more parameters [S1].

This choice runs through the whole architecture: every conv layer in Table 1 is 3×3, except the 1×1 layers in configuration C [S2].

Dataset. In this section, we present the image classification results achieved by the described ConvNet architectures on the ILSVRC-2012 dataset (which was used for ILSVRC 2012–2014 challenges). The dataset includes images of 1000 classes, and is split into three sets: training (1.3M images), validation (50K images), and testing (100K images with held-out class labels). The classification performance is evaluated using two measures: the top-1 and top-5 error. The former is a multi-class classification error, i.e. the proportion of incorrectly classified images; the latter is the main evaluation criterion used in ILSVRC, and is computed as the proportion of images such that the ground-truth category is outside the top-5 predicted categories.

For the majority of experiments, we used the validation set as the test set. Certain experiments were also carried out on the test set and submitted to the official ILSVRC server as a “VGG” team entry to the ILSVRC-2014 competition (Russakovsky et al., 2014).
</source>
<source label="S2" section="§4.1 Single Scale Evaluation" pages="6">
We begin with evaluating the performance of individual ConvNet models at a single scale with the layer configurations described in Sect. 2.2. The test image size was set as follows: Q = S for fixed S, and Q = 0.5(S_min + S_max) for jittered S ∈[S_min, S_max]. The results of are shown in Table 3. First, we note that using local response normalisation (A-LRN network) does not improve on the model A without any normalisation layers. We thus do not employ normalisation in the deeper architectures (B–E).

Second, we observe that the classification error decreases with the increased ConvNet depth: from 11 layers in A to 19 layers in E. Notably, in spite of the same depth, the configuration C (which contains three 1 × 1 conv. layers), performs worse than the configuration D, which uses 3 × 3 conv. layers throughout the network. This indicates that while the additional non-linearity does help (C is better than B), it is also important to capture spatial context by using conv. filters with non-trivial receptive fields (D is better than C). The error rate of our architecture saturates when the depth reaches 19 layers, but even deeper models might be beneficial for larger datasets. We also compared the net B with a shallow net with five 5 × 5 conv. layers, which was derived from B by replacing each pair of 3 × 3 conv. layers with a single 5 × 5 conv. layer (which has the same receptive field as explained in Sect. 2.3). The top-1 error of the shallow net was measured to be 7% higher than that of B (on a center crop), which confirms that a deep net with small filters outperforms a shallow net with larger filters.

Finally, scale jittering at training time (S ∈[256; 512]) leads to significantly better results than training on images with fixed smallest side (S = 256 or S = 384), even though a single scale is used at test time. <question>
What's the difference between top-1 and top-5 error, and why would ILSVRC care more about top-5?
</question>

answer:
An image classifier doesn't just name one answer. It gives a score to every possible category, so its guesses can be ranked from most to least likely. That ranking is what makes the two kinds of error possible.

In general (the paper takes this as known), the last step of such a network is usually **softmax**, which turns raw scores into probabilities that add up to 100%. For example, a photo might get "Siberian husky 60%, Alaskan malamute 25%, wolf 8%…" and so on down the list.

The images come from the ILSVRC-2012 dataset, the collection used for the ImageNet challenge from 2012 to 2014, which covers 1000 categories [S1]. It is split into a training set of 1.3 million images, a validation set of 50,000 images, and a test set of 100,000 images whose correct labels are kept secret by the organisers [S1]. In general, a validation set is a held-back set of images used to check a model during development, while a test set is reserved for the final, official score.

With those pieces in place, the two measures are:

- **Top-1 error:** the share of images where the network's single highest-ranked guess is wrong [S1]. Only the first guess counts.
- **Top-5 error:** the share of images where the correct category is not anywhere in the network's five highest-ranked guesses [S1]. The network gets five tries.

Top-5 is always the lower number. For the deepest network trained with images at varied sizes, top-1 error is 25.5% and top-5 error is 8.0% [S2].

The paper says only that top-5 is "the main evaluation criterion used in ILSVRC" [S1]. It doesn't explain why. A common reason, offered here as general background, is that 1000 categories include many near-identical ones, such as dozens of dog breeds, and many photos contain several objects. A single strict guess can be marked wrong even when the network saw the picture sensibly. Giving it five guesses is fairer, like grading a quiz where several answers are close.

Most of the numbers in the paper use the validation set as a stand-in test set. Some results were run on the real test set and submitted to the official ILSVRC server under the team name "VGG" [S1].

<question>
Why do the fixed-scale models get tested at only S±32 while the jittered model gets tested at 256, 384, and 512?
</question>

answer:
Each model is tested only at scales it saw during training. A fixed-$S$ model has seen one scale, so it is tested close to it. The jittered model has seen a whole range, so it can be tested across that range.

Three building blocks explain this:

1. **Scale jittering** (training-time augmentation): the network is trained on images whose smallest side $S$ is not fixed but varies within $[S_{min}; S_{max}]$, here $[256; 512]$ [S1]. The network therefore learns to recognise objects at many apparent sizes.
2. **Test-time augmentation**: the model is run on several rescaled versions of the same test image, each with smallest side $Q$, rather than a single one [S1].
3. **Class posterior averaging**: the softmax outputs from those versions are averaged into one prediction [S1]. In general, averaging predictions from several views reduces the effect of any one view being poorly suited to the model.

The authors' reasoning is that "a large discrepancy between training and testing scales leads to a drop in performance" [S1]. A model trained only at $S = 256$ has never seen objects at the size they would appear at $Q = 512$, so test views that far off would add noise to the average rather than help. For this reason the fixed-$S$ models are evaluated only at $Q = \{S-32, S, S+32\}$, which stays near the training scale [S1].

The jittered model has been trained across $[256; 512]$, so every scale in that interval is familiar to it. It is evaluated at the two endpoints and the midpoint, $Q = \{S_{min}, 0.5(S_{min}+S_{max}), S_{max}\} = \{256, 384, 512\}$ [S1]. The wider training range makes the wider test range safe to use.

The results support this. Multi-scale testing beats single-scale testing of the same model, and jittered training beats fixed $S$ [S1]. Configurations D and E trained with $S \in [256; 512]$ and tested at $\{256, 384, 512\}$ both reach 24.8%/7.5% top-1/top-5 validation error. The best fixed-$S$ variants of the same models reach about 26.5–26.7% top-1 [S1]. Adding multi-crop evaluation on top of this setup brings the error down further, to 24.4%/7.1% for E [S2].

<question>
Why do the fixed-scale models get tested at only S±32 while the jittered model gets tested at 256, 384, and 512?
</question>

answer:
The choice of test scales follows from where each model was trained. In multi-scale evaluation, the network runs on several rescaled copies of the test image (different $Q$) and the class posteriors are averaged [S1]. The authors note that a large gap between training and test scale hurts performance, so each model is only tested at scales it can plausibly handle [S1].

- **Fixed-$S$ models** were trained at one scale, so their reliable range is narrow. They are tested at $Q = \{S-32, S, S+32\}$, which perturbs the input slightly without leaving the regime they learned [S1].
- **The jittered model** was trained with $S$ sampled from $[S_{min}; S_{max}] = [256; 512]$. It is therefore tested over that whole interval at its endpoints and midpoint, $Q = \{S_{min}, 0.5(S_{min}+S_{max}), S_{max}\} = \{256, 384, 512\}$ [S1]. Training-time jittering is what makes the wider test range valid [S1].

This makes the comparison slightly asymmetric: the jittered model gets more diverse test views. That diversity is matched to what it was trained on, though, and wider test scales would likely hurt the fixed-$S$ models given the mismatch effect.

Empirically, multi-scale testing beats single-scale testing for every configuration, and jittered training beats fixed $S$ [S1]. For example, D at fixed $S=384$ reaches 26.5%/8.6% top-1/top-5 val error. D and E with jittering both reach 24.8%/7.5%, the best single-network result. E gets 7.3% top-5 on the test set [S1].

<question>
What's the difference between single-class and per-class box regression here, and why is the output layer 4000-dimensional in one case?
</question>

answer:
A box drawn around an object in a photo is called a **bounding box**. Predicting one means the network outputs numbers that describe the box rather than picking a category. The paper describes each box with 4 numbers: the x and y of its center, its width, and its height [S1].

In general (this is background, not something the paper explains), the final stage of a network like this is a "fully connected" layer. It is a set of output slots, and each slot computes one number from everything the network has worked out so far. The number of slots sets how many numbers come out. To train the network to output box coordinates, you need a way to score how wrong a guess is. A "Euclidean" (or L2) loss does this by measuring how far the predicted numbers are from the true ones, much like measuring the straight-line distance between two points, and training pushes that distance down.

For localisation, the authors keep the network they use for classification but change its last fully connected layer so it predicts box location instead of class scores [S1]. They then face a choice about how many boxes that layer should predict [S1]:

- **Single-class regression (SCR):** the network predicts one box and uses it for every possible object type. Asking "where is the dog?" and "where is the cat?" gives the same box. One box needs 4 numbers, so the last layer has 4 outputs [S1].
- **Per-class regression (PCR):** the network predicts a separate box for each object type. The dataset has 1000 classes, and each class gets its own 4 numbers, so the layer has 4 × 1000 = 4000 outputs [S1].

That multiplication is where the 4000 comes from. It is like a form with one address line versus a form with a separate address line for each of 1000 people.

Apart from this last layer, the network is the paper's configuration D, the 16-layer design that performed best on classification [S1]. Training swaps the classification objective for a Euclidean loss that penalises how far the predicted box is from the true box [S1]. The network starts from the already-trained classification model, while the new last layer starts with random values and is trained from scratch [S1].

When testing variants, one protocol reads off only the box for the correct class, so that mistakes in naming the object don't get mixed into the box score [S2].

<question>
What's the difference between single-class and per-class box regression here, and why is the output layer 4000-dimensional in one case?
</question>

answer:
Some general background first, since the paper takes these for granted:

- **Bounding box regression** treats localisation as predicting continuous numbers (the box's coordinates) instead of picking a class.
- A fully connected layer computes $y = Wx + b$. Its output size is just the number of rows of $W$, so the network can be made to output 4 numbers, 1000, or 4000 by choosing that size.
- A Euclidean (L2) loss is the squared distance $\lVert \hat{y} - y \rVert^2$ between the predicted and true vectors. It is the natural loss when the targets are real-valued coordinates.

In the paper's localisation net, the last fully connected layer predicts a bounding box instead of class scores. Each box is a 4-D vector: center coordinates, width and height [S1]. The question is whether one box should serve all classes or each class should get its own [S1]:

- **Single-class regression (SCR):** one box is shared across all classes, so the last layer outputs 4 numbers [S1]. The network says "the object is here" without the box depending on which class it is.
- **Per-class regression (PCR):** the box is class-specific, so the layer outputs one 4-D box for each of the 1000 ImageNet classes. That gives $4 \times 1000 = 4000$ outputs [S1].

With PCR, something must decide which of the 1000 boxes to use. In the paper's validation protocol, only the box for the ground-truth class is considered, which separates localisation errors from classification errors [S2]. In the full test procedure, the predicted boxes are merged and then rated using class scores from the separate classification ConvNet [S2].

Everything except that last layer is architecture D, with 16 weight layers, which was the best classification model [S1]. Training replaces the logistic regression objective with a Euclidean loss on the box parameters [S1]. It starts from the corresponding classification models, with an initial learning rate of $10^{-3}$, while the new last fully connected layer is initialised randomly and trained from scratch [S1].

In this section we first determine the best-performing localisation setting (using the first test protocol), and then evaluate it in a fully-fledged scenario (the second protocol). The localisation error is measured according to the ILSVRC criterion (Russakovsky et al., 2014), i.e. the bounding box prediction is deemed correct if its intersection over union ratio with the ground-truth bounding box is above 0.5.

Settings comparison. As can be seen from Table 8, per-class regression (PCR) outperforms the class-agnostic single-class regression (SCR), which differs from the findings of Sermanet et al. (2014), where PCR was outperformed by SCR. We also note that fine-tuning all layers for the localisation task leads to noticeably better results than fine-tuning only the fully-connected layers (as done in (Sermanet et al., 2014)). In these experiments, the smallest images side was set to S = 384; the results with S = 256 exhibit the same behaviour and are not shown for brevity.

Fully-fledged evaluation. Having determined the best localisation setting (PCR, fine-tuning of all layers), we now apply it in the fully-fledged scenario, where the top-5 class labels are predicted using our best-performing classification system (Sect. 4.5), and multiple densely-computed bounding box predictions are merged using the method of Sermanet et al. (2014). As can be seen from Table 9, application of the localisation ConvNet to the whole image substantially improves the results compared to using a center crop (Table 8), despite using the top-5 predicted class labels instead of the ground truth. Similarly to the classification task (Sect. 4), testing at several scales and combining the predictions of multiple networks further improves the performance.

We envisage that better localisation performance can be achieved if this technique is incorporated into our method. Three ideas help here. The first two are general background, not something the paper explains.

**Bounding box regression** means the network outputs four numbers that describe a rectangle around the object, such as where its edges are. "Regression" just means predicting numbers instead of picking a category. Think of it as the network drawing a frame around the dog in a photo.

**Intersection over union** scores how well a predicted rectangle matches the true one. Take the area where the two rectangles overlap and divide it by the total area they cover together. Two identical boxes score 1, and boxes that don't touch score 0.

The paper counts a predicted box as correct when this overlap score is above 0.5 [S1].

**Fine-tuning** is also general background. It means taking a network already trained for one job, here naming what is in a picture, and training it a little more for a new job, here drawing boxes. You can let all of its layers adjust, or freeze most of them and let only the last few change.

- **Per-class regression (PCR):** a separate box for every possible class, so the network can draw a box shaped for a cat that differs from its box for a car [S1].

PCR won. In their simplified test, the network saw one center crop and was given the correct class [S2]. Under that setup, the single-box version had 36.4% localisation error and the per-class version had 34.3% [S2]. The authors point out that this differs from Sermanet et al. (OverFeat), where the single box came out ahead [S1].

They also found that fine-tuning all layers for box drawing gave noticeably better results than fine-tuning only the last fully-connected layers, which is what OverFeat did [S1]. Per-class boxes with all layers fine-tuned reached 33.1% error [S2]. These comparisons used images resized so the shorter side was 384 pixels. <question>
Why did a 2-model ensemble beat their 7-model ensemble? Wouldn't more networks always help?
</question>

answer:
More networks only help if the extra networks are good. The authors' 7-model ensemble was mostly made of weaker models, while their 2-model ensemble combined their two strongest ones.

**Ensembling** means asking several separately trained networks the same question and combining their answers. Think of a panel of judges instead of one. It helps because different networks tend to make different mistakes, so one network's slip can be outvoted by the others.

The authors combine the networks by **averaging their soft-max class posteriors** [S1]. That phrase means something simple. For each photo, every network gives a list of how likely it thinks each category is, such as "70% dog, 20% wolf, 10% fox." The ensemble averages these lists across networks and picks the category with the highest average. The authors say this works "due to complementarity of the models," meaning they cover each other's errors, and that earlier winning entries used the same trick [S1].

One more idea is needed, and the sources here don't define it, so this is general background. **Multi-scale training** means showing the network training photos at a range of different sizes, not just one. That teaches it to recognise an object whether it fills the frame or appears small.

Now the two ensembles:

- **The 7-network submission (7.3% error):** By the competition deadline, the authors had mostly trained single-scale networks. Their one multi-scale model, configuration D, was only partly adjusted: they fine-tuned just its final layers rather than all of them [S1]. The panel was large, but most of its judges were the weaker kind.
- **The 2-network ensemble (after the deadline):** This combined only the two best multi-scale models, configurations D and E. It reached 7.0% error with one testing method and 6.8% with a combined testing method [S1]. "Dense" and "multi-crop" are two ways of looking at each test photo, and using both together worked best [S1].

The telling detail is that their best *single* network, model E, already scored 7.1% error [S1]. That one network alone beat the entire 7-network ensemble at 7.3%. Averaging in weaker judges pulls the panel's answer toward their less accurate opinions, so adding them can hurt rather than help.

The authors highlight this point. They call it "remarkable" that their best result comes from "combining just two models," far fewer than most competition entries used [S2]. For comparison, the competition winner, GoogLeNet, used 7 networks to get 6.7% [S2].

So the lesson is that the quality of each member mattered more than how many members there were. Adding networks helps when they are strong and make different mistakes, not automatically.

<question>
Why did a 2-model ensemble beat their 7-model ensemble? Wouldn't more networks always help?
</question>

answer:
More networks help only when the extra members are about as strong as the rest. In this paper the 7-net ensemble was mostly weaker models, and two strong ones did better.

In general, **model ensembling** means training several models separately and combining their predictions at test time. It works when the models make *different* mistakes: if one network misclassifies an image, the others may get it right, so the combined vote is more reliable than any single member. The usual way to combine classifiers is to average their softmax outputs. Each network gives a probability distribution $p_m(c \mid x)$ over classes, and the ensemble predicts from

$$\bar p(c \mid x) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} p_m(c \mid x).$$

This is the scheme the paper uses. The authors average the models' soft-max class posteriors and attribute the gain to the **complementarity** of the models [S1].

Some general background on the third ingredient: multi-scale training rescales training images to a range of sizes rather than one fixed size. The network then learns to recognise objects at different scales, which usually makes a single model stronger.

The composition of the two ensembles explains the result. At submission time the authors had trained only single-scale networks, plus one multi-scale model D in which only the fully-connected layers had been fine-tuned rather than all layers [S1]. Combining these 7 networks gave 7.3% test error [S1]. After the submission, they combined only the two best multi-scale models, D and E. That pair reached 7.0% with dense evaluation and 6.8% with dense plus multi-crop evaluation [S1][S2].

The paper doesn't spell out why the larger ensemble lost, but its numbers point to member quality. The best single model, E, already reaches 7.1% error [S1], better than the whole 7-net submission at 7.3% [S2]. Averaging gives every member equal weight, so weaker single-scale nets pull the combined posterior toward their own errors. Adding networks helps only when the new ones are both accurate and complementary. The authors call the 2-model result notable because it uses far fewer models than most ILSVRC submissions [S2].

Why did a 2-model ensemble beat their 7-model ensemble? Wouldn't more networks always help?

answer:
The 2-net ensemble won because its members were much stronger. Fusion here is a plain average of the softmax class posteriors across models, and it helps only to the extent that the models make complementary errors [S1].

The 7-net ILSVRC ensemble was assembled before most multi-scale training was done. It consisted of the single-scale networks plus one multi-scale model D that had been fine-tuned only in its fully-connected layers rather than end to end [S1]. That ensemble reached 7.3% top-5 test error [S1]. It improves the ensemble only if its errors are decorrelated enough from the others to outweigh its lower accuracy. Ensembles of networks with similar architectures and training data have highly correlated errors, so returns diminish quickly. A few strong, diverse members usually beat many mediocre ones.
