<question>
Is the jump from 11.5% to 76.2% on ImageNet over Visual N-Grams actually a fair comparison, or is CLIP just using way more data and compute?
</question>

answer:
No, not as a head-to-head test, and the authors say so themselves. Some background first, because the comparison depends on it.

These are general ideas the passage assumes rather than spells out:

- **Zero-shot transfer** means using a model on a task it was never trained for, with no practice examples. You give it only the names of the categories, like recognizing a new animal from a written description without ever having seen a labelled photo.
- **Contrastive image-text pretraining** is how CLIP learns. It sees huge numbers of internet photos with their captions and practices picking which caption goes with which photo. Matching captions to pictures teaches it what words look like, which is what makes zero-shot use possible later.
- **Top-1 vs top-5 accuracy**: top-1 counts a guess as right only if the model's first choice is correct. Top-5 counts it as right if the correct answer is anywhere in its five best guesses, so top-5 is always the easier, higher number.

The 11.5% vs 76.2% figures are zero-shot top-1 accuracy on ImageNet [S1]. The authors write that the comparison is "meant for contextualizing the performance of CLIP" and "should not be interpreted as a direct methods comparison," because many differences that affect performance were not controlled for [S1].

The uncontrolled differences they list are large [S1]:

- a training dataset 10x larger
- a vision model that needs nearly 100x more compute for each prediction
- likely over 1000x the training compute
- a transformer-based model, a type that did not exist yet when Visual N-Grams was published

So much of the jump could come from scale and newer technology, not only from CLIP's caption-matching idea [S1].

To separate those, the authors ran a closer test. They trained a smaller CLIP (a ResNet-50) on the same dataset Visual N-Grams used, YFCC100M. It matched Visual N-Grams' reported ImageNet result within one V100 GPU day of training [S1]. That is roughly one day on one standard graphics card, a small budget. The CLIP version also started from scratch, while Visual N-Grams began from weights already trained on ImageNet [S1]. This head start makes the test lean in Visual N-Grams' favour. Under roughly equal conditions, CLIP's method still holds its own, even if the full 11.5% to 76.2% gap isn't all due to the method.

Because a single three-dataset comparison can't settle this, the authors widened the evaluation. They went from the 3 datasets Visual N-Grams reported to over 30 datasets and compared against over 50 existing computer vision systems [S1].

<question>
How many labeled examples is CLIP's zero-shot classifier actually worth, and why is the mean (20.8) so different from the median (5.4)?
</question>

answer:
Zero-shot CLIP is worth anywhere from less than 1 to 184 labeled examples per category, depending on the task. On a typical task it is worth about 5 [S1]. To see how the authors measured this, three ideas help first.

**Zero-shot classification** means sorting images into categories without showing the model a single labeled example of those categories. CLIP is only given the category names as text. This is the general meaning of the term; the passages quoted here assume you already know it.

A **linear probe** is a very simple classifier added on top of a model. The model first turns each image into a list of numbers called its features. The probe then learns a straight-line rule that maps those numbers to categories, using labeled examples. In this paper it is a logistic regression [S1].

**Few-shot learning** means training with only a handful of labeled examples per category. "1-shot" means one example of each category, and "16-shot" means sixteen.

The authors trained linear probes on CLIP's own features with 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 examples per category, and also with all available labels [S1]. Training thousands of classifiers would be too costly. So they drew a smooth curve through those few results and read off how many examples a probe needs to match zero-shot accuracy [S1]. The comparison is fair because zero-shot CLIP is itself a linear classifier on the same features [S1]. Think of it as pricing a skill: zero-shot CLIP does as well as a probe that saw N labeled examples per category.

The results vary a lot. On two datasets, Flowers102 and EuroSAT, zero-shot CLIP does worse than a probe trained on just one example per category. On ImageNet it matches a 16-shot probe [S1]. Half the datasets need fewer than 5 examples per category, and the median is 5.4 [S1].

The mean of 20.8 is much higher because about 20% of the datasets need many labeled examples before a probe catches up [S1]. An average is easily pulled up by a few very large values. Picture a room of people earning ordinary salaries when one billionaire walks in. The median is the middle value, so it ignores those extremes and better describes a typical dataset.

There is also a ceiling. A probe trained on all the labels roughly sets the upper bound for what zero-shot can achieve, and zero-shot still trails it by 10% to 25% on most datasets [S1][S2]. It comes close on only 5 datasets, and on all of them both scores are above 90% [S2].

answer:
**Zero-shot classification** in CLIP means building a classifier with no labeled training images. In general terms, each class name is turned into a text prompt and embedded with the text encoder. The resulting text embeddings act as the weight vectors, and an image is assigned to the class whose embedding has the highest cosine similarity with its image embedding.

The paper states the consequence directly: zero-shot CLIP is a linear classifier on CLIP's image features [S1].

As general background, a **linear probe** freezes a pretrained encoder and trains only a linear classifier (here, logistic regression) on its features. **Few-shot learning** means training with only $k$ labeled examples per class ("$k$-shot"). They estimate the shot count that matches zero-shot accuracy by log-linear interpolation instead of training thousands of classifiers [S1]. - ImageNet zero-shot matches a 16-shot linear classifier [S1].
- Half the datasets need fewer than about 5 examples per class, with a median of 5.4 [S1].

A few large values, up to 184, pull the mean far above the typical dataset, while the median ignores how extreme those tail values are.

There is also a ceiling. If the evaluation sets are large enough to estimate a linear classifier's parameters well, the fully supervised linear probe roughly upper-bounds what zero-shot transfer can reach [S1]. How is it possible to improve accuracy by 9.2% on the ImageNet dataset with little to no increase in accuracy under distribution shift? Is the gain primarily from “exploiting spurious correlations”? Is this behavior unique to some combination of CLIP, the ImageNet datatset, and the distribution shifts studied, or a more general phenomena? Does it hold for end-to-end finetuning as well as linear classifiers? We do not have confident answers to these questions at this time. Prior work has also pre-trained models on distributions other than ImageNet, but it is common to study and release models only after they have been fine-tuned to ImageNet. As a step towards understanding whether pre-trained zero-shot models consistently have higher effective robustness than fine-tuned models, we encourage the authors of Mahajan et al. (2018), Kolesnikov et al. (2019), and Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) to, if possible, study these questions on their models as well.

We also investigate another robustness intervention enabled by flexible zero-shot natural-language-based image classifiers. The target classes across the 7 transfer datasets are not always perfectly aligned with those of ImageNet. Two datasets, Youtube-BB and ImageNet-Vid, consist of superclasses of ImageNet. This presents a problem when trying to use the fixed 1000-way classifier of an ImageNet model to make predictions. Taori et al. (2020) handle this by max-pooling predictions across all sub-classes according to the ImageNet class hierarchy. Sometimes this mapping is much less than perfect. For the person class in Youtube-BB, predictions are made by pooling over the ImageNet classes for a baseball player, a bridegroom, and a scuba diver. With CLIP we can instead generate a custom zero-shot classifier for each dataset directly based on its class names. In Figure 14 we see that this improves average effective robustness by 5% but is concentrated in large improvements on only a few datasets. Curiously, accuracy on ObjectNet also increases by 2.3%. Although the dataset was designed to closely overlap with ImageNet classes, using the names provided for each class by ObjectNet’s creators still helps a small amount compared to using ImageNet class names and pooling predictions when necessary.

While zero-shot CLIP improves effective robustness, Figure 14 shows that the benefit is almost entirely gone in a fully supervised setting. To better understand this difference, we investigate how effective robustness changes on the continuum from zero-shot to fully supervised. In Figure 15 we visualize the performance of 0-shot, 1-shot, 2-shot, 4-shot ..., 128-shot, and fully supervised logistic regression classifiers on the best CLIP model’s features. We see that while few-shot models also show higher effective robustness than existing models, this benefit fades as in-distribution performance increases with more training data and is mostly, though not entirely, gone for the fully supervised model. Additionally, zero-shot CLIP is notably more robust than a few-shot model with equivalent ImageNet performance. Across our experiments, high effective robustness seems to result from minimizing the amount of distribution specific training data a model has access to, but this comes at a cost of reducing dataset-specific performance.

Taken together, these results suggest that the recent shift towards large-scale task and dataset agnostic pre-training combined with a reorientation towards zero-shot and few-shot benchmarking on broad evaluation suites (as advocated by Yogatama et al. (2019) and Linzen (2020)) promotes the development of more robust systems and provides a more accurate assessment of performance. We are curious to see if the same results hold for zero-shot models in the field of NLP such as the GPT family. While Hendrycks et al. (2020b) has reported that pre-training improves relative robustness on sentiment analysis, Miller et al. (2020)’s study of the robustness of question answering models under natural distribution shift finds, similar to Taori et al. (2020), little evidence of effective robustness improvements to date.

<question>
Why does CLIP do better on datasets like Youtube-BB when it uses each dataset's own class names instead of mapping from ImageNet's 1000 classes?
</question>

answer:
A few ideas come first, then the answer.

In general, a **zero-shot classifier** sorts pictures into categories it was never specifically trained on. CLIP learned to match pictures with written descriptions, so to make a classifier you just give it the category names as text, and for each picture it picks the name that fits best. Because the categories are only words, you can swap in any list of names you like.

**Distribution shift** means testing a model on pictures that differ in style from what it practised on, for example video frames instead of carefully taken photos. Models usually score lower when this happens. **Effective robustness** measures how much better a model holds up under such a shift than you would expect from its score on the original test. Higher effective robustness means the model drops less when the pictures change. These three ideas are general background; the passages below take them as known.

Two of the shifted test sets, Youtube-BB and ImageNet-Vid, don't use ImageNet's categories. They use broader "parent" categories (superclasses) instead [S1]. A standard ImageNet model can only answer with its fixed list of 1000 categories, so its answers have to be translated. Earlier work did this by taking, for each broad category, the highest score among the ImageNet categories filed under it in ImageNet's family tree of classes [S1].

<question>
Why does CLIP do better on datasets like Youtube-BB when it uses each dataset's own class names instead of mapping from ImageNet's 1000 classes?
</question>

answer:
Youtube-BB's labels don't match ImageNet's, and a fixed ImageNet classifier has to approximate them with a crude mapping. CLIP can instead read the dataset's own label names. Three ideas from the paper's robustness section make the argument easier to follow.

**Zero-shot classification** means classifying images into categories the model was never explicitly trained on. In general (this is background, not this passage's content), CLIP embeds the image and embeds a text prompt for each candidate class name. It then predicts the class whose text embedding has the highest cosine similarity with the image embedding. The class set is therefore just a list of strings you supply.

Effective robustness, in general, is how much better a model does on shifted test data than you would predict from its in-distribution (ImageNet) accuracy. Prior models lie close to a trend line, and points above that line are "effectively robust."

Distribution shift is a change in the data between training and test: different image sources, styles, or, as here, different label sets.

Two of the seven transfer datasets, Youtube-BB and ImageNet-Vid, use *superclasses* of ImageNet categories [S1]. An ImageNet model only outputs 1000 fixed logits. Taori et al. therefore max-pool predictions over all ImageNet subclasses that fall under each target class in the ImageNet hierarchy [S1]:

$$
p(\text{target } c \mid x) \approx \max_{k \in \text{sub}(c)} p_{\text{ImageNet}}(k \mid x)
$$

That mapping can be poor. For Youtube-BB's "person" class, the pooled ImageNet classes are a baseball player, a bridegroom, and a scuba diver [S1]. An ordinary person walking down a street fits none of these well, so the classifier is answering the wrong question.

CLIP avoids the mapping entirely by building a custom zero-shot classifier for each dataset directly from its class names [S1]. The text encoder simply embeds "person," and the classifier then targets the category the dataset actually means.

According to Figure 14, this raises average effective robustness by 5%, although the gain comes mostly from large improvements on only a few datasets [S1]. Accuracy on ObjectNet also rises by 2.3% [S1]. That is notable because ObjectNet was designed to overlap closely with ImageNet classes, yet using its creators' own class names still beats using ImageNet names and pooling when necessary [S1]. Even small mismatches in label wording or granularity cost accuracy.

<question>
Why does CLIP do better on datasets like Youtube-BB when it uses each dataset's own class names instead of mapping from ImageNet's 1000 classes?
</question>

answer:
The issue is label-space mismatch. Youtube-BB and ImageNet-Vid are labelled with *superclasses* of ImageNet, so a fixed 1000-way ImageNet classifier cannot emit their labels directly [S1]. Taori et al. bridge this by max-pooling the logits over all ImageNet subclasses of each target class, following the ImageNet hierarchy [S1]. That mapping can be badly lossy. For Youtube-BB's "person" class, the pooled set is the ImageNet classes for baseball player, bridegroom, and scuba diver [S1]. A generic person who matches none of those three is effectively unrepresentable.

CLIP avoids the mapping entirely. Because its classifier is just the text encoder's embeddings of class names, the authors build a custom zero-shot head per dataset directly from that dataset's own class names [S1]. In Figure 14 this raises average effective robustness by 5%, but the gain is concentrated in large improvements on only a few datasets, presumably those where the hierarchy mapping was worst [S1]. ObjectNet also improves by 2.3%, even though it was designed to closely overlap ImageNet's classes. Using its creators' class names still beats using ImageNet names and pooling where needed [S1].

The paper doesn't analyze the mechanism further. As general background, the plausible reading is that pooling over a hand-picked subset of fine-grained logits leaves large holes in the target class's visual extent. A text embedding of "person" instead points at the concept as it co-occurred with images during contrastive pre-training, which covers the whole category. The gain therefore reflects a better-specified classifier rather than better visual features.

question: Why would CLIP beat an ImageNet-trained EfficientNet so much on traffic sign recognition like GTSRB?
plan: Explain the authors' hypothesis: ImageNet-1K uses a single label for all traffic and street signs, so supervised training can collapse within-class distinctions, hurting fine-grained downstream tasks; cite the 14.7% GTSRB gain. Contrast with CLIP's broader natural-language supervision that doesn't force such collapse. Note this is framed as a possible explanation, and mention related wins (Stanford Cars) plus where EfficientNet still wins (ImageNet, low-res CIFAR, attributed partly to missing scale augmentation).

In 2015, it was announced that a deep learning model exceeded human performance on the ImageNet test set (He et al., 2015). However, research in the subsequent years has repeatedly found that these models still make many simple mistakes (Dodge & Karam, 2017; Geirhos et al., 2018; Alcorn et al., 2019), and new benchmarks testing these systems has often found their performance to be much lower than both their ImageNet accuracy and human accuracy (Recht et al., 2019; Barbu et al., 2019). What explains this discrepancy? Various ideas have been suggested and studied (Ilyas et al., 2019; Geirhos et al., 2020). A common theme of proposed explanations is that deep learning models are exceedingly adept at finding correlations and patterns which hold across their training dataset and thus improve in-distribution performance. However many of these correlations and patterns are actually spurious and do not hold for other distributions and result in large drops in performance on other datasets.

We caution that, to date, most of these studies limit their evaluation to models trained on ImageNet. Recalling the topic of discussion, it may be a mistake to generalize too far from these initial findings. To what degree are these failures attributable to deep learning, ImageNet, or some

<question>
Why would CLIP beat an ImageNet-trained EfficientNet so much on traffic sign recognition like GTSRB?
</question>

answer:
The paper's explanation is that ImageNet's labels are too coarse for traffic signs, so a model trained on them may learn to ignore the very details that tell one sign from another [S1]. Three ideas make that argument easier to follow.

**How the comparison is run.** The authors don't ask either model to read traffic signs directly. They take what each model has learned (its "features," a summary of what it notices in an image) and train a very simple classifier on top of those features for each test dataset [S1]. This is called a **linear probe**. Think of it as checking how well organised someone's notes are: if a simple reader can find the answer in them, the notes captured the right information.

**Fine-grained tasks.** As general background, a "fine-grained" task asks a model to separate things that look very similar, such as different car models or a 30 km/h sign versus a 50 km/h sign. A model can only succeed if its features keep those small differences. Car recognition (Stanford Cars) and traffic sign recognition (GTSRB) are both fine-grained tasks, and CLIP does much better on both [S1].

**How the EfficientNet learned.** Also as general background, an ImageNet-trained model learns by being shown photos alongside one fixed label from a list of 1,000 categories and adjusting itself until it picks the right label. It learns to care about whatever helps choose among those 1,000 labels and nothing more.

That last point is where traffic signs come in. ImageNet-1K has only a single label covering all traffic and street signs [S1]. A stop sign, a speed limit sign and a "no entry" sign all count as the same answer. A model trained this way may learn to treat every sign as "the same kind of thing" and blur away the differences between them, which the authors describe as collapsing "intra-class details" [S1]. When a linear probe later asks those features to tell signs apart, the information may simply not be there. The authors point to CLIP's 14.7% improvement on GTSRB as a sign of this problem [S1].

CLIP learned from captions written in ordinary language rather than a fixed list of labels. A caption can say "speed limit 50" or "yield sign at an intersection," so nothing pushes the model to treat all signs as one blob. The paper describes this as ImageNet's "overly narrow supervision" being the problem [S1].

The authors present this as a possible explanation ("could be indicative," "may reflect"), not a proven cause [S1].

The EfficientNet does not lose everywhere. It still does best relative to CLIP on ImageNet itself, the dataset it was trained on, and slightly better on small, low-resolution images (CIFAR10 and CIFAR100) [S1]. The authors suspect that last gap comes partly from CLIP's training not including scale-based data augmentation, which means not practising on images shown at different sizes [S1]. Overall, CLIP's features beat the EfficientNet's on 21 of the 27 datasets tested [S1].

Contrast with CLIP's broader natural-language supervision that doesn't force such collapse. Note this is framed as a possible explanation, and mention related wins (Stanford Cars) plus where EfficientNet still wins (ImageNet, low-res CIFAR, attributed partly to missing scale augmentation).

<question>
Why would CLIP beat an ImageNet-trained EfficientNet so much on traffic sign recognition like GTSRB?
</question>

answer:
The comparison rests on a few ideas that the paper takes as known. This is general background, not the paper's content:

1. **Linear probe evaluation**: freeze a pretrained network, take its features, and fit only a linear classifier on top for each downstream dataset. A probe scores well only if the features already separate the classes.
2. **Fine-grained classification**: telling apart visually similar subcategories, such as specific car models or specific traffic signs, rather than broad object types.
3. **Supervised pretraining on ImageNet**: training a network with cross-entropy to predict one of 1,000 fixed labels. The features are shaped toward whatever distinctions those labels require, and away from those they don't.

In the paper's linear-probe comparison, CLIP beats the Noisy Student EfficientNet-L2 on 21 of 27 datasets, and it does much better on fine-grained car and traffic sign recognition (Stanford Cars and GTSRB) [S1]. On GTSRB the gain is 14.7% [S1].

The authors' proposed explanation is overly narrow supervision in ImageNet. ImageNet-1K has only a single label for all traffic and street signs [S1]. A classifier trained on it is rewarded for mapping every sign to the same output, and this "could encourage a supervised representation to collapse intra-class details" [S1]. The differences between a stop sign, a speed limit sign and a yield sign are exactly what GTSRB needs. If the features have discarded them, a linear probe cannot recover them.

CLIP is instead trained to match images with free-form captions. Captions can mention "speed limit 30" or "no left turn," so nothing in the objective forces those details to merge. The authors frame this explanation tentatively ("may reflect," "could be indicative") rather than testing it directly [S1].

The advantage is not universal. EfficientNet does best relative to CLIP on ImageNet, the dataset it was trained on, and it slightly wins on low-resolution CIFAR10/100 [S1]. The authors suspect the CIFAR result is partly due to CLIP lacking scale-based data augmentation [S1].

Contrast with CLIP's broader natural-language supervision that doesn't force such collapse. Note this is framed as a possible explanation, and mention related wins (Stanford Cars) plus where EfficientNet still wins (ImageNet, low-res CIFAR, attributed partly to missing scale augmentation).

A concern with pre-training on a very large internet dataset is unintentional overlap with downstream evals. This is important to investigate since, in a worst-case scenario, a complete copy of an evaluation dataset could leak into the pre-training dataset and invalidate the evaluation as a meaningful test of generalization. Using this threshold, we then create two new subsets, Overlap, which contains all examples which have a similarity to a training example above the threshold, and Clean, which est problems for humans. <question>
Why didn't they just deduplicate the training data against the eval sets before training CLIP, and what did they do instead to check for contamination?
</question>

answer:
Imagine studying for an exam and accidentally seeing some of the exact exam questions beforehand. Your score would look better than your real understanding. In machine learning this is called **data contamination**: test examples slip into the training data. The authors worry about exactly this, because CLIP was trained on a huge collection of images and captions from the internet, and in the worst case a full copy of a test dataset could have been included, making the test meaningless [S1].

Two more ideas are general background, not content from these passages. Finding contamination means **near-duplicate detection**: a program that spots images that are the same or almost the same (resized, cropped, slightly edited), not just exact copies. And "zero-shot" means the model is tested on a dataset without any extra training on it. CLIP is simply shown the images and asked to pick the matching label, so any boost from contamination can only come from what it saw during pre-training.

The obvious fix is to remove every test image from the training data before training. The authors agree that this guarantees honest scores, but it only works if you know every test you will ever run ahead of time [S1]. If you later want to try a new benchmark, you would have to either retrain the whole model, which is very expensive, or report a score with an unknown amount of "peeking" baked in [S1]. So instead of preventing overlap, they measure it and measure how much it changes the scores [S1].

Their procedure has these steps [S1]:

1. For each test dataset, run a duplicate detector that finds the most similar training images.
2. A person looks at the matches and picks a similarity cutoff for that dataset. The cutoff is strict, so that flagged items really are duplicates, while still catching as many as possible.
3. Split the dataset into **Overlap** (examples above the cutoff) and **Clean** (examples below it), and keep the full set as **All**.
4. Report the contamination level as the share of the dataset that landed in Overlap.

To see whether overlap actually helped, they measure the zero-shot accuracy of one large CLIP model, RN50x64, on these splits [S1]. Their main number is accuracy on All minus accuracy on Clean. If it is positive, it estimates how much the reported score was inflated by the model having seen some test images [S1].

The effect turned out to be small. Overlap had a median of 2.2%, and overall accuracy rarely moved by more than 0.1% [S2].

answer:
Removing duplicates before training would have given true hold-out numbers, but only for the eval sets known at training time. Every later benchmark would then need an expensive retrain, or its results would carry an overlap benefit nobody had measured [S1].

The setting is general background, not specific to this paper. **Data contamination** means that test examples also show up in the training data, so a high score can come from memorisation instead of generalisation. At internet scale this is a real risk, because benchmark images are often posted online. Near-duplicate detection finds pairs of images that are almost identical, such as crops, resizes or re-encodes, rather than only exact byte-level copies. In practice it means computing similarity scores between examples and applying a threshold. Zero-shot evaluation means testing the pre-trained model on a dataset without training it on that dataset at all, so any overlap can only come from pre-training.

The paper's worst case is a full copy of an eval set leaking into pre-training, which would make it useless as a test of generalization [S1]. The authors chose not to filter in advance. Instead they measured how much overlap exists and how much it changes accuracy [S1]:

3. They measured the zero-shot accuracy of CLIP RN50x64 on all three splits [S1].

The main metric is

$$
\Delta = \text{Acc}(\text{All}) - \text{Acc}(\text{Clean}).
$$

When $\Delta$ is positive, it estimates how much the reported accuracy was inflated by overfitting to overlapping data [S1]. Overlap is usually small, so the authors also ran a one-tailed binomial test with Clean accuracy as the null, plus Clopper-Pearson intervals [S2].

The effect turned out to be minor. Median overlap is 2.2%, and accuracy rarely shifts by more than 0.1%. The largest gain is 0.6%, on Birdsnap [S2].

<question>
Why didn't they just deduplicate the training data against the eval sets before training CLIP, and what did they do instead to check for contamination?
</question>

answer:
Deduplicating before training only gives clean hold-out numbers if you know every eval in advance [S1]. That limits what you can benchmark later: each new evaluation would need an expensive retrain, or you would have to report results with an unquantified boost from overlap [S1]. The authors kept the pre-training set fixed and instead measured how much overlap exists and how much it changes performance [S1].

The procedure, run per eval dataset [S1]:

1. Run a duplicate detector (Appendix C) over the dataset's examples, inspect the nearest neighbours by hand, and set a per-dataset similarity threshold. The threshold is tuned to keep precision high while maximizing recall.
2. Split the dataset at that threshold into **Overlap** (examples with a training example above the threshold) and Clean (everything below it). The unaltered dataset is called All.
3. Report contamination as $|\text{Overlap}| / |\text{All}|$.

The main metric is the zero-shot accuracy of CLIP RN50x64 on All minus its accuracy on Clean [S1]. A positive value estimates how much the reported accuracy was inflated by overfitting to overlapping data [S1]. Because overlaps are usually small, they add a one-tailed binomial test of Overlap accuracy against Clean accuracy as the null, plus 99.5% Clopper–Pearson intervals [S2].

Across 35 datasets, 9 show no detected overlap. Median overlap is 2.2% and mean overlap is 3.2% [S2]. Only 7 datasets shift by more than 0.1%, and only 2 of those are significant after Bonferroni correction. The largest gain is 0.6% on Birdsnap, which has 12.1% overlap [S2]. Country211 has the most overlap at 21.5%, since it is built from YFCC100M, but gains only 0.2%. The likely reason is that the duplicates' captions rarely mention location, which is what that benchmark tests [S2].

question: Why did adding a 'child' label make CLIP stop putting so many young people into the crime and animal categories?

Conclude with the authors' point that class design and wording shape both performance and bias, which matters especially for CLIP since developers can easily define their own classes.

<question>
Why did adding a 'child' label make CLIP stop putting so many young people into the crime and animal categories?
</question>

answer:
CLIP never answers "none of these fit." It always picks whichever label it was given matches the image best. When none of the labels described young people well, their photos landed on whichever bad option seemed least wrong.

The paper takes three ideas as known, so they are explained here as general background:

1. **Zero-shot classification** means sorting images into categories the model was never specifically trained on. Nobody shows it labelled examples of each category first. You just tell it the category names.
2. CLIP turns each category name into a short piece of text and checks how well each one matches the photo, a bit like holding several captions next to a picture and asking which fits best. The list of names you give it acts as the full set of possible answers.
3. A final step, called softmax, turns those match scores into shares that add up to 100%. So the categories compete with each other. If one label fits well, it takes most of the share. If none fit, the share still has to go somewhere.

In the bias probes, people aged 0-20 were the group most often put into the non-human labels ('animal', 'chimpanzee', 'gorilla', 'orangutan'), at 14% [S1]. They were also put into crime labels ('thief', 'suspicious person', 'criminal') about 18% of the time, compared with about 12% for people aged 20-60 [S1]. The label list had nothing that described a young person well, so CLIP was effectively forced to choose among poor fits.

The authors then ran the same classification with one extra category, 'child' [S1]. This gave those photos a label that genuinely matched them. In the competition between labels, 'child' won the share that had been spilling into the harmful categories. The result was a drastic drop in under-20s classified as criminals or animals [S1]. The paper reports the details in Table 7, which you can check for exact numbers.

The authors' wider point is that **class design** largely shapes how the model behaves. Class design means which categories you include and how you word them. It affects both how accurate the model is and what harmful biases it shows [S1]. This matters especially for CLIP, because developers can easily write their own category lists, and a poorly chosen list can lead to poor results in real use [S1].

Why did adding a 'child' label make CLIP stop putting so many young people into the crime and animal categories?

answer:
The short answer is that CLIP's zero-shot classifier has to pick from the classes it is given. When none of them fits, the image still lands somewhere. Adding 'child' gave images of young people a label that actually fit.

The sources here come from the bias section and don't restate how CLIP classifies, so the next three points are general background on that mechanism:

- **Zero-shot classification** means classifying into categories the model was never explicitly trained on. You write down a list of candidate classes at test time, and the model chooses among them.
- **Text prompts as classifiers:** CLIP embeds the image, and it embeds a text prompt for each class name (for example, "a photo of a {label}"). It scores each class by the cosine similarity between the image embedding $I$ and each text embedding $T_k$. The text embeddings act as the weights of a linear classifier that you define just by writing labels.
- **Softmax over candidate classes:** these scores go through a softmax, $p_k = \exp(s_k)/\sum_j \exp(s_j)$. Because it normalises only over the classes provided, the probabilities always sum to one. Even a poor match wins if every other option is worse.

In the probes, people aged 0–20 had the highest rate of being classified as non-human ('animal', 'chimpanzee', 'gorilla', 'orangutan'), at 14% [S1]. The authors then re-ran classification with the same classes plus 'child', and this "drastically reduced" how many under-20 images fell into either category (Table 7) [S1].

The paper reports this effect rather than giving a mechanistic account. The softmax framing explains it, though. Once 'child' is available, it presumably matches those image embeddings better than any denigrating label, so it absorbs the probability mass that previously went to whichever bad option was "least wrong."

The authors' broader point is that **class design**, meaning which categories are included and the exact wording used for each, can determine both performance and the biases the model exhibits [S1]. They stress that this matters especially for CLIP, "given how easily developers can design their own classes" [S1]. Related design choices, such as the probability threshold for returning labels, also change which biased labels appear [S2].

Zero-shot CLIP is a closed-set classifier. It scores the image embedding against the text embedding of each candidate label and takes the best match, so every image is forced into one of the classes you supply. In the FairFace probe, images of people aged 0–20 had no label that fit them well. They ended up disproportionately in the non-human classes ('animal', 'chimpanzee', 'gorilla', 'orangutan'), at 14%, and in the crime-related classes ('thief', 'suspicious person', 'criminal'), at about 18%. The probabilities are normalized only over the label set, so adding a label that sits closer in embedding space to young faces moves the argmax and probability mass to it. The denigrating labels were never strong matches. They won by default because the true concept had no slot.

The authors conclude that **class design** shapes both performance and bias. Probe results change with which categories are included and how each one is worded. question: If CLIP is zero-shot, why do the authors say their evaluation isn't really a true zero-shot setup?
plan: Explain that during development they repeatedly checked performance on full validation sets with thousands of labeled examples, which leaks information that a genuine zero-shot user wouldn't have, similar to critiques in semi-supervised learning. Then cover the second issue: the main 27-dataset collection was assembled somewhat haphazardly and co-adapted with CLIP's development, unlike the standardized 12-dataset suite. Close with their proposed fix: a new benchmark designed explicitly for broad zero-shot transfer.

<question>
If CLIP is zero-shot, why do the authors say their evaluation isn't really a true zero-shot setup?
</question>

answer:
The model itself is zero-shot, but the *process of building it* was not. While developing CLIP, the authors kept checking its scores on large sets of labeled examples, and that gave them information a real zero-shot user would never have.

Three ideas, as general background rather than the paper's own text, make this clearer:

- **Zero-shot transfer** means using a model on a new task without giving it any labeled examples of that task. For CLIP, you just describe the categories in words (like "a photo of a dog"), and it picks the best match.
- **Validation set overfitting**: researchers keep a pile of labeled examples aside to check how well their model is doing. If they check it again and again and adjust their choices each time, the model slowly gets tuned to that particular pile. It's like a student who keeps retaking the same practice exam: their score climbs partly because they've learned that exam, not just the subject.
- **Benchmark co-adaptation**: the tests and the model shape each other. If you pick which tests to report while you're building the model, you may lean, even without meaning to, toward tests your model happens to be good at.

The authors admit to the first problem directly. They say that "despite our focus on zero-shot transfer, we repeatedly queried performance on full validation sets to guide the development of CLIP" [S1]. Those validation sets "often have thousands of examples," which they call "unrealistic for true zero-shot scenarios" [S1]. Someone truly facing a brand-new task wouldn't have thousands of labeled examples to steer by. They note that researchers in semi-supervised learning, a related area that also works with very little labeled data, have raised the same concern [S1].

The second problem is how the test datasets were chosen. The authors did report results on a standard 12-dataset collection from earlier work [S1]. But their main results use "a somewhat haphazardly assembled collection of 27 datasets" that they say is "undeniably co-adapted with the development and capabilities of CLIP" [S1]. Their proposed fix is a new benchmark built specifically to test broad zero-shot ability, instead of reusing existing datasets that were originally made for ordinary training with labels [S1]. A test designed in advance, and not tuned to during development, would give a fairer picture of how CLIP does on tasks it has truly never seen.

We found that the model had 59.2% top-1 accuracy out of 100 possible classes for ‘in the wild’ 8k celebrity images. However, what makes these results noteworthy is that this analysis was done using only zero-shot identification capabilities based on names inferred from pre-training data - we didn’t use any additional task-specific dataset, and so the (relatively) strong results further indicate that before deploying multimodal models, people will need to carefully study them for behaviors in a given context and domain.

CLIP offers significant benefit for tasks that have relatively little data given its zero-shot capabilities. However, large datasets and high performing supervised models exist for many in-demand surveillance tasks such as facial recognition. As a result, CLIP’s comparative appeal for such uses is low. Additionally, CLIP is not designed for common surveillance-relevant tasks like object detection and semantic segmentation. This means it has limited use for certain surveillance tasks when models that are designed with these uses in mind such as Detectron2 (Wu et al., 2019) are widely available.

However, CLIP does unlock a certain aspect of usability given how it removes the need for training data. Thus, CLIP and similar models could enable bespoke, niche surveillance use cases for which no well-tailored models or datasets exist, and could lower the skill requirements to build such applications. As our experiments show, ZS CLIP displays non-trivial, but not exceptional, performance on a few surveillance relevant tasks today.

<question>
If CLIP is worse than dedicated face recognition systems, why are the authors still worried about it being used for surveillance?
</question>

answer:
CLIP's face results are modest. The worry is not how well it recognizes people today but how little effort it takes to point it at a new target. Three ideas from the rest of the paper make this clearer.

In general terms, CLIP learns by matching pictures with the captions that came with them online. During training it sees many image-and-caption pairs and learns which caption belongs with which picture. This is called **contrastive language-image pretraining**. As a side effect, it picks up many names and words linked to what appears in images.

That matching skill allows **zero-shot classification**: sorting images into categories the model was never specifically trained on. You give it a list of labels in plain words, such as a list of names, and it picks the label whose text best matches the picture. No new examples or extra training are needed.

Top-1 accuracy is how often the model's single best guess is correct. If it is right on 59 out of every 100 images, its top-1 accuracy is about 59%.

For celebrity faces, CLIP's best guess was right 59.2% of the time when choosing among 100 names. That fell to 43.3% with 1,000 names [S1]. The authors say this is "not competitive" with production systems like Google's Celebrity Recognition [S1].

What concerns them is how CLIP reached even that level. It used only names it had absorbed during pretraining, and "we didn't use any additional task-specific dataset" [S1]. A model that was never taught to recognize faces can still identify many people fairly well, just from reading the internet. That is why the authors say such models need careful study before they are deployed [S1].

For common surveillance jobs, the risk is lower. Face recognition already has large datasets and strong specialized models. CLIP is also not built for tasks like object detection (finding and outlining objects in an image), where purpose-built tools such as Detectron2 are widely available [S1]. So for mainstream uses, CLIP has little extra appeal [S1].

The real risk lies in unusual cases. Because CLIP removes the need for training data, it could enable "bespoke, niche surveillance use cases for which no well-tailored models or datasets exist" [S1]. It could also lower the skill needed to build such tools [S1]. Picture someone who wants to track something oddly specific that no company has built a system for. Normally they would need to collect and label thousands of examples and train a model. With CLIP, they might only need to type a list of descriptions.

The authors sum it up as "non-trivial, but not exceptional" performance today [S1]. That is enough to raise concern without being state of the art.

<question>
If CLIP is worse than dedicated face recognition systems, why are the authors still worried about it being used for surveillance?
</question>

answer:
The worry is about **who** can build a surveillance tool and **for what**, not about beating the best face recognizers. Three ideas make the argument clear.

The scaffold below is general background on CLIP rather than this section's content. CLIP is trained by **contrastive language-image pretraining**: an image encoder and a text encoder are trained so that the embedding of an image has high cosine similarity with the embedding of its own caption and low similarity with the other captions in the batch. This lets the model learn names and concepts from captions scraped from the web. **Zero-shot classification** builds on this. To classify an image, you embed a text prompt for each candidate label, such as a person's name, and pick the label whose embedding is closest to the image's. No labeled training examples for the task are needed. **Top-1 accuracy** is the fraction of images where that single highest-scoring label is correct.

On celebrity identification, zero-shot CLIP reaches 59.2% top-1 accuracy when choosing among 100 names. This drops to 43.3% with 1k names. Google's production Celebrity Recognition system does better [S1]. What concerns the authors is how CLIP got there. It used only names it had picked up from pre-training data, with no task-specific dataset [S1]. They argue that this relatively strong result means multimodal models need careful study before they are deployed in a given context [S1].

For mainstream surveillance tasks, CLIP has little to offer. Large datasets and strong supervised models already exist for facial recognition, so CLIP's comparative appeal there is low [S1]. CLIP also isn't designed for object detection or semantic segmentation, where purpose-built tools like Detectron2 are widely available [S1].

The real risk comes from removing the need for training data. CLIP could enable bespoke, niche surveillance uses for which no tailored models or datasets exist. It also lowers the skill needed to build such applications [S1]. Someone who wants to recognize a specific, unusual category doesn't have to collect labeled data or train anything; writing the right text prompts is enough. The authors call current zero-shot performance on surveillance-relevant tasks "non-trivial, but not exceptional" [S1]. They present this as a reason for the community to map out where models like CLIP work well and which sensitive applications may call for policy intervention [S2].

question: Isn't CLIP basically just webly supervised learning? What actually makes it different from training on image search results?

A related idea to CLIP is webly supervised learning. This line of work queries image search engines to build image datasets by querying for terms and uses the queries as the labels for the returned images (Fergus et al., 2005). Classifiers trained on these large but noisily labeled datasets can be competitive with those trained on smaller carefully labeled datasets. These image-query pairs are also often used to improve performance on standard datasets as additional training data (Chen & Gupta, 2015). CLIP also uses search queries as part of its dataset creation process. However CLIP only uses full text sequences co-occuring with images as supervision rather than just the queries, which are often only a single word or short n-gram. We also restrict this step in CLIP to text only querying for sub-string matches while most webly supervised work uses standard image search engines which have their own complex retrieval and filtering pipelines that often involve computer vision systems. Of this line of work, Learning Everything about Anything: Webly-Supervised Visual Concept Learning (Divvala et al., 2014) has a notably similar ambition and goal as CLIP.

Finally, CLIP is related to a recent burst of activity on learning joint models of vision and language (Lu et al., 2019; Tan & Bansal, 2019; Chen et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020b; Yu et al., 2020). This line of work focuses on richly connecting vision and language in order to solve complex downstream tasks such as visual question answering, visual commonsense reasoning, or multimodal entailment. These approaches leverage impressively engineered models which combine 3 (or more) pre-trained subsystems, typically an image feature model, a region proposal / object detection model, and a pre-trained masked language model such as BERT. These systems are then jointly fine-tuned via various training objectives on image-text pairs and applied to the aforementioned tasks and achieve impressive results. CLIP is instead focused on learning visual models from scratch via natural language supervision and does not densely connect the two domains with a joint attention model. The only interaction in a CLIP model between the image and text domain is a single dot product in a learned joint embedding space. We are excited to see CLIP hybridized with this line of work.

We have investigated whether it is possible to transfer the success of task-agnostic web-scale pre-training in NLP to another domain. We find that adopting this formula results in similar behaviors emerging in the field of computer vision and discuss the social implications of this line of research. In order to optimize their training objective, CLIP models learn to perform a wide variety of tasks during pre-training. This task learning can then be leveraged via natural language prompting to enable zero-shot transfer to many existing datasets. At sufficient scale, the performance of this approach can be competitive with task-specific supervised models although there is still room for much improvement.

<question>
Isn't CLIP basically just webly supervised learning? What actually makes it different from training on image search results?
</question>

answer:
The overlap is real: CLIP does borrow part of the webly supervised recipe. The difference lies in *what it learns from* and *how it gathers its data*.

**Webly supervised learning** builds an image collection by typing words into an image search engine and treating each word as the "label" for the pictures that come back [S1]. Search "dog" and every returned image gets tagged "dog." The authors note that CLIP uses search queries in its own dataset-building too [S1], which is why the two look alike at first.

Those tags are often wrong, because search engines return some off-topic pictures. Labels like these, mostly right but with mistakes mixed in, are called **noisy labels**. That idea is general background rather than something the paper defines. The paper does note that classifiers trained on large, noisily labelled collections can compete with ones trained on smaller, carefully checked collections [S1]. In other words, having a lot of data can make up for the mistakes.

**Natural language supervision** means learning from ordinary written text about an image, such as a caption, instead of from a single category name. CLIP is built to learn what things look like "from scratch via natural language supervision" [S1].

With those pieces in place, the authors name two concrete differences:

1. **The teaching signal is richer.** Webly supervised work uses the search query itself as the label, and that query is "often only a single word or short n-gram" (a short run of words). CLIP instead learns from the *full text* that appeared alongside each image online [S1]. Compare a picture tagged only "dog" with one described as "a golden retriever catching a frisbee at the beach." The second tells the model much more.

2. **The data-gathering step is simpler and text-only.** Standard image search engines have "their own complex retrieval and filtering pipelines that often involve computer vision systems" [S1]. That means another vision model has already influenced which pictures you get. CLIP limits its querying to plain text matching, checking whether a search term appears as a sub-string of the text [S1].

The goal itself is not new. The authors single out an earlier webly supervised paper by Divvala et al. (2014) as having "a notably similar ambition and goal as CLIP" [S1]. So CLIP is close to webly supervised learning in spirit. What sets it apart is that it learns from whole sentences instead of one-word tags, and it collects its data without relying on a search engine's vision-based filtering.

<question>
Isn't CLIP basically just webly supervised learning? What actually makes it different from training on image search results?

answer:
Overlap exists, but the authors draw two concrete lines between CLIP and classic webly supervised work.

**Webly supervised learning** builds an image dataset by sending terms to an image search engine and using each query as the label for the images it returns [S1]. Those labels are **noisy**: some returned images don't actually show the query concept. Even so, classifiers trained on these large, noisily labeled datasets can compete with ones trained on smaller, carefully labeled datasets [S1]. The image-query pairs are also often used as extra training data for standard benchmarks [S1].

CLIP instead uses **natural language supervision**: it learns visual models from scratch with text as the training signal, and the image and text sides interact only through a single dot product in a learned joint embedding space [S1]. CLIP's dataset creation does involve search queries too [S1], which is where the resemblance comes from. The differences are in what supervises the model and how the data is gathered:

- **Supervision signal.** CLIP trains only on the full text sequences that co-occur with images, not on the queries themselves, which are often a single word or a short n-gram [S1]. A query like "dog" gives roughly one class label. A full caption can describe the breed, the setting, and the action, so the target is a sentence rather than an index into a fixed vocabulary.
- **Collection pipeline.** CLIP restricts its querying step to text-only sub-string matching [S1]. Most webly supervised work relies on standard image search engines, which run their own complex retrieval and filtering pipelines that often include computer vision systems [S1]. Those pipelines decide which images count as matching a query, so the dataset already reflects some other vision model's judgments.

The authors don't treat this as a difference in purpose. They single out Divvala et al. (2014), *Learning Everything about Anything*, as having a notably similar ambition and goal [S1]. The goal is shared. What changes is that CLIP uses raw co-occurring text as the label and a text-only collection step instead of query labels filtered through a search engine. That full-text supervision is what lets CLIP be prompted with natural language for zero-shot transfer [S2].

This line of work focuses on richly connecting vision and language in order to solve complex downstream tasks such as visual question answering, visual commonsense reasoning, or multimodal entailment. These approaches leverage impressively engineered models which combine 3 (or more) pre-trained subsystems, typically an image feature model, a region proposal / object detection model, and a pre-trained masked language model such as BERT. These systems are then jointly fine-tuned via various training objectives on image-text pairs and applied to the aforementioned tasks and achieve impressive results. CLIP is instead focused on learning visual models from scratch via natural language supervision and does not densely connect the two domains with a joint attention model. The only interaction in a CLIP model between the image and text domain is a single dot product in a learned joint embedding space. We are excited to see CLIP hybridized with this line of work.

We have investigated whether it is possible to transfer the success of task-agnostic web-scale pre-training in NLP to another domain. We find that adopting this formula results in similar behaviors emerging in the field of computer vision and discuss the social implications of this line of research. In order to optimize their training objective, CLIP models learn to perform a wide variety of tasks during pre-training. This task learning can then be leveraged via natural language prompting to enable zero-shot transfer to many existing datasets. At sufficient scale, the performance of this approach can be competitive with task-specific supervised models although there is still room for much improvement.

<question>
Isn't CLIP basically just webly supervised learning? What actually makes it different from training on image search results?
</question>

answer:
The overlap is real, and the authors acknowledge it. Webly supervised learning builds datasets by querying image search engines for terms and using those query terms as labels for the returned images. Classifiers trained on these large, noisily labeled sets can be competitive with ones trained on smaller, carefully labeled datasets, and the image-query pairs are also used as extra training data for standard benchmarks [S1]. CLIP's dataset construction also uses search queries [S1], so the two share a starting point.

The authors draw two distinctions:

- **Supervision signal.** In webly supervised work, the query is the label, and it is often a single word or short n-gram. CLIP uses only the full text sequences that co-occur with images as supervision, not the queries [S1]. The query decides which pairs enter the dataset, but the training target is the free-form text. This turns a fixed-vocabulary classification problem into image-text matching, which is what later allows natural-language prompting for zero-shot transfer [S2].
- **Retrieval pipeline.** CLIP limits the querying step to text-only sub-string matching. Most webly supervised work instead relies on standard image search engines, which have their own complex retrieval and filtering pipelines that often involve computer vision systems [S1]. That makes CLIP's data less dependent on the biases and capabilities of an existing vision model.

The goal is not what separates them. The authors single out Divvala et al. 2014, "Learning Everything about Anything," as having a notably similar ambition and goal to CLIP [S1]. The difference is in the supervision signal and the data pipeline, not in what each approach is trying to achieve.

<question>
When they say CLIP got state of the art on 21 of 27 datasets in linear probes, does that mean it had the single highest score, or something looser?
</question>

answer:
It's something looser. "State of the art" here means CLIP's score was **statistically indistinguishable** from the top score on that dataset, not necessarily the single highest number [S1]. Three ideas explain what that means.

**Linear probe evaluation.** This is how the paper tests what CLIP has learned. The trained model is "frozen," meaning no further changes are made to it. It turns each image into a list of numbers that summarizes what it sees. Then a very simple classifier, essentially a straight-line rule, is trained on top of those numbers to sort images into categories. If even this simple rule works well, the frozen model must have learned useful descriptions of images. The paper compares many pre-trained models this way across 27 datasets [S1].

**Confidence interval.** This is general background, not something the paper explains. A test set is a sample of images, so every score contains some luck. A slightly different set of test images might have shifted it up or down a little. A confidence interval is a range around a score that says "the true value is very likely somewhere in here." Think of two runners whose times differ by a hundredth of a second, when the stopwatch is only accurate to a tenth. Calling one of them faster isn't justified.

**Clopper-Pearson interval.** This is also general background. It is one specific, cautious way to compute that range when the score counts right-versus-wrong answers, such as accuracy. "99.5%" means the range is built to be very wide and safe, so a score has to fall well below it to count as clearly worse.

Now the paper's rule. For each dataset, the authors took the top score from any model and drew a 99.5% Clopper-Pearson interval around it. The best CLIP model counted as state of the art if its score landed inside that interval [S1]. That model uses the ViT-L/14 design and looks at images at 336 by 336 pixels. It met this bar on 21 of the 27 datasets [S1]. Scores falling inside the interval are shown in bold in Table 10, so a dataset can have more than one bold entry [S1].

So on some of those 21 datasets, another model may have scored a bit higher, but the gap was too small to call meaningful. The authors also point out that on many datasets CLIP wins by a large margin, not just a tie [S1]. They read this as evidence that learning from natural-language captions works better than the traditional approach of pre-training on labelled image categories [S1].

<question>
When they say CLIP got state of the art on 21 of 27 datasets in linear probes, does that mean it had the single highest score, or something looser?
</question>

answer:
Looser. "State of the art" here means CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336×336 pixels scored inside a statistical confidence interval around each dataset's top score, not that it had the strictly highest number on all 21 datasets [S1].

In general, a **linear probe** evaluation freezes a pretrained model, extracts its features for each image, and trains only a linear classifier (such as logistic regression) on top. The accuracy of that classifier measures how linearly separable, and so how useful, the frozen representation is. This is general background on the method, not a definition taken from the paper.

Also general background: a test-set accuracy is an estimate from a finite sample, so it carries uncertainty. A confidence interval gives the range of true accuracies consistent with the observed score. A 99.5% interval is wide enough that a score inside it can't be confidently separated from the top score. The Clopper-Pearson interval is an exact interval for a binomial proportion, such as the fraction of test images classified correctly. It is computed from the binomial distribution itself rather than from a normal approximation, so it stays valid for small test sets and for accuracies near 0% or 100%.

The authors draw a Clopper-Pearson 99.5% interval around each dataset's best score. If CLIP's score falls inside it, CLIP counts as state of the art for that dataset [S1]. These scores are the ones printed in bold in Table 10 [S1]. CLIP can therefore be slightly below the best number and still count. In Table 10, for example, the L/14-336px row has 97.9 in its second column while the L/14 row has 98.0 [S2]. Test-set size also matters: the test sets range from 500 images (CLEVR Counts, Hateful Memes) to 50,000 (ImageNet) [S1]. On small test sets the interval is wide, so a fairly large gap can still fall inside it.

The authors still read the results as a strong win. On many datasets CLIP performs significantly better than the other models, which they take as evidence that natural language supervision beats pre-training on image classification [S1]. Section 3.2 discusses the linear probe results further [S1].

<question>
When they say CLIP got state of the art on 21 of 27 datasets in linear probes, does that mean it had the single highest score, or something looser?
</question>

answer:
Something looser. "State of the art" here means CLIP ViT-L/14@336px scored inside the Clopper-Pearson 99.5% confidence interval around each dataset's top score [S1]. So on some of those 21 datasets another model may have the single highest number, and CLIP still counts because its score is statistically indistinguishable from it at that confidence level.

You can see this in the raw rows. On CIFAR-10, for example, L/14 at 224px has 98.0 and L/14-336px has 97.9 [S2]. A strict "highest score" criterion would not credit the 336px model there, but the interval criterion does.

The protocol is the standard **linear probe**: the pre-trained encoder is frozen, and a linear classifier is trained on its features for each of the 27 datasets [S1]. It measures how linearly separable the representation is, not how well the full network performs after fine-tuning.

In Table 10, the scores that fall inside each dataset's 99.5% interval are shown in bold [S1]. A dataset can therefore have several bolded entries, and the "21 of 27" counts the datasets where the best CLIP model is among them.

The authors also point out that on many datasets CLIP's margin is large, not just a tie within the interval. They read this as evidence that natural language supervision beats traditional pre-training based on image classification [S1].

The paper doesn't spell out how the Clopper-Pearson interval is computed for metrics that aren't simple proportions, such as 11-point mAP, mean-per-class accuracy, or ROC AUC. The interval is naturally defined for binomial accuracy, so for those metrics the "within CI" call is presumably an approximation.

<question>
Why did they test CLIP on images of rendered SST-2 sentences, and is 80.5% actually a good result?
</question>

answer:
The authors wanted to know whether CLIP can do more than recognize letters in a picture. Can it actually understand what a sentence written in an image *means*? To test this, they took SST-2, a dataset of sentences used in language research, and turned each sentence into an image of text [S1]. Their stated goal was to check whether CLIP can turn "low level OCR capability into a higher level representation" [S1].

Three ideas help make sense of the test and the result. These explanations are general background rather than the paper's own content:

1. **Optical character recognition (OCR)** means reading the letters and words out of an image, like a scanner turning a photo of a page into typed text. Reading the characters is not the same as understanding the sentence they form.
2. A **linear probe** is a simple way to check what a model has learned. The model stays frozen. A very basic classifier, which can only draw a straight dividing line, is trained on top of the model's internal summary of each input. If that simple classifier does well, the useful information must already be in the summary.
3. A **bag-of-words baseline with GloVe** represents a sentence by averaging pre-learned "meaning vectors" for each word. It ignores word order completely, like judging a recipe by its ingredient list. It is a classic, simple benchmark for language tasks.

Also as general background, SST-2 sentences come from movie reviews, and the task is to label each one as positive or negative.

On the results: a linear probe on CLIP's view of the rendered sentences reaches 80.5% accuracy [S1]. That roughly matches the 80% of a bag-of-words baseline using GloVe word vectors [S1]. It is well below the best existing result of 97.5% [S1], and the authors acknowledge that the bag-of-words method is "a simple NLP baseline by today's standard" [S1].

So 80.5% is not good compared with dedicated language models. It is impressive given the handicap: CLIP sees only pixels, while the text-based methods are given the actual typed sentences [S1]. CLIP has to read the words and grasp their combined meaning, and it still lands at the level of a reasonable text method. The authors call it "encouraging" that CLIP builds "a non-trivial sentence level representation" from an image [S1].

A second result points the same way. On Hateful Memes, a task of detecting hateful image-and-text memes, fully supervised CLIP is only 0.7 points behind the best single model. The competing methods there also get the true text, which CLIP does not [S1].

<question>
Why did they test CLIP on images of rendered SST-2 sentences, and is 80.5% actually a good result?
</question>

answer:
SST-2 is a sentence-level sentiment dataset that the authors rendered into images, so CLIP has to classify a picture of a sentence rather than the sentence itself [S1]. Three concepts help interpret the result.

As general background, a **linear probe** freezes a pretrained model, extracts its feature vector for each input, and trains only a linear classifier (e.g. logistic regression) on top. High probe accuracy means the information is already linearly accessible in the representation, rather than learned by the probe.

Also as general background, optical character recognition (OCR) is reading characters and words from pixels. That is a low-level skill: a model can transcribe "not bad" without representing that it expresses positive sentiment.

A continuous bag-of-words (CBoW) baseline with GloVe, in general terms, averages pretrained word vectors for every word in a sentence and classifies the average. It ignores word order, so it is a simple text baseline.

**Why test on rendered SST-2.** The authors wanted to check whether CLIP can "convert low level OCR capability into a higher level representation" [S1]. Sentiment depends on the meaning of the whole sentence, so a linear probe can only succeed if CLIP's image embedding encodes something like sentence semantics, not just which glyphs are present.

**Is 80.5% good?** It depends on the comparison:

- It is on par with the 80% of a CBoW baseline using GloVe vectors pre-trained on 840 billion tokens [S1].

<question>
Why did they test CLIP on images of rendered SST-2 sentences, and is 80.5% actually a good result?
</question>

answer:
The SST-2 test checks whether CLIP's OCR ability is more than reading characters. SST-2 is a sentence-level sentiment dataset, and the authors render each sentence as an image. That tests whether CLIP turns low-level OCR into a higher-level, sentence-level representation [S1]. Recognising glyphs is not enough here. A linear probe can only classify sentiment if the frozen image embedding already encodes something like the meaning of the sentence.

Whether 80.5% is good depends on the baseline. A linear classifier on CLIP features of the rendered sentences reaches 80.5% [S1].

- It matches a continuous bag-of-words baseline on GloVe vectors pre-trained on 840B tokens, which scores 80% [S1].
- It is far below the 97.5% SOTA, and the authors call CBoW "a simple NLP baseline by today's standard" [S1].
- The other 56 models in the evaluation suite top out at 59.0% on SST-2 under linear probing (the "ES Best" row of Table 14) [S2].

So CLIP is weak by NLP standards but strong among vision representations. The comparison is also uneven against CLIP. The text baselines get the ground-truth text, while CLIP sees only pixels and must solve OCR and sentence encoding together, with no text-side training for this task [S1].

The Hateful Memes result points the same way. A fully supervised CLIP probe there is only 0.7 points behind the single-model SOTA, and several points above the best baseline from the original paper. Those competing results also use ground-truth text that CLIP does not get [S1].

The authors read all this as evidence that CLIP turns rendered text into a "non-trivial sentence level representation." They also note that zero-shot CLIP beats the fully supervised linear probes of every other model in their suite on these OCR tasks [S1].

<question>
Does making CLIP bigger always improve zero-shot accuracy, or are there datasets where larger models actually do worse?
</question>

answer:
Making CLIP bigger usually helps, but not always. In the paper's full results table, a few datasets have larger models scoring the same or even worse than smaller ones [S1].

**Zero-shot classification** means the model sorts images into categories it was never specifically trained on. You give it the category names as text (like "a photo of a dog"), and it picks the description that best matches the image. The scores below measure how often it picks correctly, as a percentage, without any extra training on that dataset.

CLIP comes in two families of image-reading "engines." One is based on ResNet, an older, widely used design for processing images. The other is the **Vision Transformer** (ViT), which chops an image into small square patches and processes them somewhat like words in a sentence. In the table, the ResNet versions are named RN50 through RN50x64, and the ViT versions are B/32, B/16, L/14 and L/14-336px [S1].

Model scaling means making a model larger, with more internal parts and more computation, which usually lets it learn more. Within each family, the names roughly run from smaller to larger: RN50 up to RN50x64, and B/32 up to L/14-336px. The "336px" version also looks at higher-resolution images.

The table lists every model's zero-shot accuracy on 27 datasets [S1]. The passage gives the numbers but not the dataset names, so the columns below are identified by position:

- **The usual pattern:** in the first column, accuracy climbs fairly steadily with size, from 81.1 for RN50 to 93.8 for L/14-336px [S1]. Many columns behave like this.
- **Column 19, a clear reversal:** the smallest ResNet, RN50, scores 42.2, but the two largest ViT models score only 23.1 (L/14) and 21.9 (L/14-336px) [S1]. Even among ResNets, RN50x4 drops to 26.0 [S1].
- **Column 24, a bumpy pattern:** RN50 scores 20.3, RN101 rises to 28.1, then RN50x4 falls to 17.0 and RN50x16 to 17.6 before RN50x64 recovers to 27.5 [S1]. The biggest ViT only reaches 24.8 [S1].
- **Smaller dips elsewhere:** in column 21, B/16 scores 48.1, below the smaller B/32's 58.4 [S1]. In column 13, RN101 (59.3) is below RN50 (66.6) [S1].

The answer is no. Bigger is a strong general trend, but on some datasets it stalls or reverses. The table itself doesn't explain why. One plausible general reason is that some tasks are unusual or very specialized, so they don't benefit from the broad knowledge that larger models gain.

<question>
Does making CLIP bigger always improve zero-shot accuracy, or are there datasets where larger models actually do worse?
</question>

answer:
Mostly yes, but not always. Across the 27 datasets in Table 11, larger CLIP models usually score higher, but several columns break the trend [S1].

Three terms help in reading the table. The cited passage is only the table, so these definitions are general background, not text from the passage.

- **Zero-shot classification** means CLIP is not trained on the target dataset. Each class name is turned into a text prompt and embedded. The image is assigned to the class whose text embedding has the highest cosine similarity with the image embedding.
- A Vision Transformer (ViT) splits an image into patches and processes them as a sequence of tokens. "B/32" means a Base-size model with 32×32-pixel patches, and "L/14" means a Large model with 14×14 patches. Smaller patches give more tokens and more compute.
- Model scaling increases width, depth and input resolution together. RN50x4, x16 and x64 are ResNet-50s scaled to roughly that multiple of compute. "336px" means the model runs on higher-resolution inputs.

The table lists nine backbones: RN50, RN101, RN50x4, RN50x16 and RN50x64, then ViT B/32, B/16, L/14 and L/14-336px [S1]. The general trend is clear in the first column, which rises from 81.1 for RN50 to 93.8 for L/14-336px [S1]. The passage doesn't say which dataset each column is, so the columns below are counted by position from the left.

Clear exceptions:

- **Column 19:** RN50 scores 42.2 and B/16 scores 44.0. The largest ViTs drop to 23.1 (L/14) and 21.9 (L/14-336px), and RN50x4 falls to 26.0 [S1]. The biggest models are roughly half as accurate as the smallest one here.
- **Column 24:** RN50 scores 20.3 and RN101 scores 28.1. RN50x4 then drops to 17.0 and RN50x16 to 17.6, and no ViT goes above 24.8 [S1]. The scores move up and down with no consistent pattern.
- **Column 21:** B/16 scores 48.1, well below B/32 at 58.4 [S1].
- **Columns 13 and 16:** RN101 scores below RN50, with 59.3 vs 66.6 and 33.1 vs 41.1 [S1].
- **Column 2:** L/14-336px scores slightly below L/14, at 95.7 vs 96.2 [S1].

Most of these columns have low absolute accuracy. That suggests tasks where zero-shot CLIP is weak overall, so scores may be noisy or near chance. On those tasks, extra capacity does not reliably help. The general background on how zero-shot prompts work suggests prompt or label mismatch as one plausible cause, but the cited passage does not explain the drops.

answer:
No. Table 11 shows a strong overall scaling trend, but it is not monotone on every dataset [S1]. The extracted passage does not give the dataset names for the columns, so the columns below are identified by position (1 to 27).

**General trend.** Within each family, accuracy usually rises with scale [S1]:

- **Column 13**: RN101 (59.3) is below RN50 (66.6).

question: What actually makes SimCLR work better than earlier contrastive methods if it doesn't use a memory bank or special architecture?
plan: Start by noting SimCLR deliberately drops specialized architectures and memory banks, so its gains come from other design choices. Then walk through the three findings in order: composing multiple data augmentations defines a harder, more useful prediction task; a learnable nonlinear projection head between the representation and the contrastive loss improves representation quality; and larger batches plus longer training help contrastive learning more than supervised learning. Close with the headline results (76.5% linear-eval top-1, matching supervised ResNet-50; 85.8% top-5 with 1% labels) as evidence these choices pay off.
