<source label="S1" section="Abstract" pages="1">
This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations.

We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50. When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100× fewer labels.^1

1 Google Research, Brain Team. Correspondence to: Ting Chen <iamtingchen@google.com>.

Proceedings of the 37 th International Conference on Machine Learning, Vienna, Austria, PMLR 119, 2020. Copyright 2020 by the author(s).

1 Code available at https://github.com/google-research/simclr.
</source>
<source label="S2" section="§1 Introduction" pages="1">
Learning effective visual representations without human supervision is a long-standing problem. Most mainstream approaches fall into one of two classes: generative or discriminative. Generative approaches learn to generate or otherwise model pixels in the input space (Hinton et al., 2006; Kingma & Welling, 2013; Goodfellow et al., 2014). on representations learned with different self-supervised methods (pretrained on ImageNet). Gray cross indicates supervised ResNet-50. Our method, SimCLR, is shown in bold.

However, pixel-level generation is computationally expensive and may not be necessary for representation learning. Discriminative approaches learn representations using objective functions similar to those used for supervised learning, but train networks to perform pretext tasks where both the inputs and labels are derived from an unlabeled dataset. Many such approaches have relied on heuristics to design pretext tasks (Doersch et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Noroozi & Favaro, 2016; Gidaris et al., 2018), which could limit the generality of the learned representations. Discriminative approaches based on contrastive learning in the latent space have recently shown great promise, achieving state-of-the-art results (Hadsell et al., 2006; Dosovitskiy et al., 2014; Oord et al., 2018; Bachman et al., 2019).

In this work, we introduce a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations, which we call SimCLR. Not only does SimCLR outperform previous work (Figure 1), but it is also simpler, requiring neither specialized architectures (Bachman et al., 2019; Hénaff et al., 2019) nor a memory bank (Wu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2019; He et al., 2019; Misra & van der Maaten, 2019).

<question>
What actually makes SimCLR work better than earlier contrastive methods if it doesn't use a memory bank or special architecture?
</question>

answer:
SimCLR's gains come from how it sets up the learning task, not from extra machinery. The authors say it needs neither specialized architectures nor a memory bank (a stored collection of past results that some earlier methods kept for comparison) [S2]. To see what replaces them, three ideas help.

**Contrastive learning** is a general approach, not something specific to this paper. A network learns by comparison: it is shown two pictures and has to tell whether they come from the same original image or from different ones. Think of a "spot the same photo" game played over millions of images. To win, the network has to summarise each picture in a way that captures what is in it. That summary is called a **representation**.

**Data augmentation** is also general background. It means making altered copies of a picture, for example by cropping it, changing its colours or blurring it. In contrastive learning, two altered copies of the same photo count as a "match", so the choice of alterations decides what the network has to learn to ignore and what it has to notice.

The **linear evaluation protocol** is the paper's way of grading the result. A very simple classifier, which can only draw straight-line boundaries, is trained on top of the representations [S1]. If even this simple tool can sort images into categories, the representations must already contain the useful information.

With that in place, the authors point to three findings [S1]:

<question>
How does contrastive learning differ from regular supervised training in what it needs, like augmentation strength, batch size, and training length?
</question>

answer:
In **contrastive learning**, the model learns without labels. Each image is randomly altered twice, and the model is trained to recognize that the two altered copies came from the same original while telling them apart from the other images [S2]. The two copies are called a "positive pair," and the task is to pick out an image's partner from a group of other images [S2].

Those random alterations are **data augmentation**. In this paper they are cropping a random piece of the image and resizing it back, randomly distorting its colors, and randomly blurring it [S2]. The authors find that combining several of these operations is crucial for defining a task that teaches the model something useful, and that cropping together with color distortion matters most [S1][S2].

One more idea is general background, not something these passages define. A **batch** is the group of examples the model looks at together in one training step, and batch size is how many images that group holds. Supervised training, by contrast, means learning from images that come with human-provided labels like "cat" or "dog."

With those pieces, the paper reports three differences in what contrastive learning needs compared with supervised training:

1. **Stronger augmentation.** Contrastive learning benefits from more aggressive alterations to the images than supervised learning does [S1]. This matters especially here because the augmentations *are* the task. They decide what "two versions of the same image" means, so their strength shapes what the model has to learn [S1][S2].
2. **Larger batches.** Contrastive learning gains more from bigger batches than its supervised counterpart [S1].
3. **Longer training.** It also benefits more from more training steps [S1].

They share one trait. Like supervised learning, contrastive learning improves with deeper and wider networks, meaning neural networks with more layers and more units per layer [S1].

A useful way to picture the difference is that a supervised model gets an answer key, while a contrastive model has to invent its own puzzle from the images and their altered copies. The passages report *that* this puzzle needs stronger alterations, bigger batches and longer training. They don't explain *why* bigger batches or longer training help. Later sections of the paper (§3.2 and §5.2) test these findings in detail.

• Composition of multiple data augmentation operations is crucial in defining the contrastive prediction tasks that yield effective representations. In addition, unsupervised contrastive learning benefits from stronger data augmentation than supervised learning.

How does contrastive learning differ from regular supervised training in what it needs, like augmentation strength, batch size, and training length?

answer:
The authors report three ways contrastive learning's requirements differ from the supervised regime, and one way they match [S1]:

Two augmentations $t, t' \sim \mathcal{T}$ applied to the same example give a positive pair $(\tilde{x}_i, \tilde{x}_j)$. The task is to identify $\tilde{x}_j$ among $\{\tilde{x}_k\}_{k \neq i}$ given $\tilde{x}_i$ [S2]. Batch size and training length both shape this same task. The other examples in the set $\{\tilde{x}_k\}$ are the distractors the positive must be picked out from [S2]. <question>
Why does per-device batch norm cause a problem for contrastive learning, and how does SimCLR fix it?
</question>

answer:
To see the problem, three ideas come first.

**Batch normalization** (BN) is a layer inside the network that tidies up the numbers flowing through it. It looks at a whole group of images processed together (a "batch"), computes their average and spread, and rescales everything with those two numbers. Each image's output therefore depends a little on which other images happen to share its batch.

Training on many chips at once usually means **data parallelism**: the big batch is split into smaller chunks, and each chip (or "device") handles one chunk. This is general background. SimCLR trains this way on 32 to 128 Cloud TPU cores [S1].

In contrastive learning, the model takes one photo, makes two altered copies of it (cropped, recoloured and so on), and must recognise that the two copies came from the same photo. Those two copies are a **positive pair**. Every other image in the batch is a "negative" that it should treat as different [S1].

Ordinarily, BN computes its average and spread separately on each device [S1]. SimCLR computes positive pairs on the same device, so both copies of a photo always share the same local batch [S1]. The authors say this lets the model "exploit the local information leakage to improve prediction accuracy without improving representations" [S1]. In other words, the model finds a shortcut for matching pairs instead of learning what the images actually show.

The paper doesn't spell out how the shortcut works. As general background, the usual intuition is this: the average and spread are slightly different on every device, so every image on one device carries the same faint "device fingerprint" after normalization. The model can use that fingerprint to narrow down which images might be partners. It is like solving a matching puzzle by noticing which pieces came out of the same box rather than by looking at the pictures.

SimCLR's fix is **global BN**. During training, the average and spread are combined across all devices, so every image is normalized with the same statistics [S1]. That removes the per-device fingerprint. The paper also mentions two other approaches used elsewhere [S1]:

- shuffling images across devices, so the two copies of a photo don't share local statistics;
- replacing batch normalization with layer norm, which normalizes each image on its own and so never mixes information between images.

<question>
Why does per-device batch norm cause a problem for contrastive learning, and how does SimCLR fix it?
</question>

answer:
SimCLR trains with large batches spread across many devices, and in that setup the usual per-device batch norm gives the model a shortcut for spotting which two images belong together [S1]. Three pieces of background make the problem clear.

**Batch normalization** is a general technique that normalizes each activation channel using the mean and variance computed over the current batch:

$$\hat{x} = \frac{x - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2 + \epsilon}}$$

So each example's output depends slightly on the other examples in its batch. In data-parallel training, the batch is split into shards across devices. Each device computes gradients on its own shard, and only the gradients are averaged. In the paper's setup, the model trains on 32 to 128 TPU cores [S1]. A contrastive task gives each image two augmented views, a **positive pair**, and the model must pick out each view's partner among the other examples in the batch [S1].

The paper notes that the BN mean and variance are usually computed locally on each device. Because both views of an image are processed on the same device, the model can "exploit the local information leakage to improve prediction accuracy without improving representations" [S1]. In other words, the contrastive loss goes down for the wrong reason.

The paper doesn't spell out exactly how the leak works. The usual explanation is that every example on a device is normalized with that device's statistics, which gives the shard a shared signature. Both views of an image carry the same signature, while many negatives come from other devices with different statistics. That signature becomes a cheap cue for matching positives, and the model can use it instead of image content.

SimCLR's fix is **global BN**. The BN mean and variance are aggregated over all devices during training, so every example is normalized with the same statistics and the device-specific cue disappears [S1]. The authors mention two alternatives from other work [S1]:

- Shuffling examples across devices, as in MoCo [S1].
- Replacing BN with layer norm, which normalizes within each example and so shares no statistics across the batch [S1].

answer:
Some general background first, since the paper builds on these ideas:

- **Contrastive learning** teaches a model by showing it two versions of the same picture and asking it to recognise that they belong together, while telling them apart from versions of other pictures. - **Data augmentation** is how those two versions are made: random edits such as cropping, changing colours or blurring. Which edits are used decides how hard the matching game is and what the model ends up learning.
- A **two-branch setup** sends each version of the image down its own path through the network. The two outputs are then compared.

To find out which edits matter, the authors test edits one at a time and in pairs [S1]. Some edits change the shape or layout of the picture, such as cropping, rotation or cutting out a patch. Others change its look, such as colour distortion, blur or edge filtering [S1].

The other branch is left unchanged, which the paper calls the identity, written $t(x_i) = x_i$ ("t of x equals x", meaning no change) [S1]. The unedited branch works as a reference point, so the comparison shows the effect of the tested edit itself.

This makes a fair grid of experiments possible. Each square on the diagonal of Figure 5 is one edit on its own. Each square off the diagonal is two edits applied one after the other [S1]. With the grid, they found that no single edit is enough on its own. Pairing random cropping with colour distortion stands out as the best combination [S2].

The authors admit this lopsided setup lowers overall performance. They argue it should not substantially change how the edits compare with one another, and that comparison is what the experiment is for [S2].

answer:
The two-branch setup is general background on how SimCLR-style methods work, which the paper describes in its §2 framework:

- **Contrastive learning** trains an encoder so that two views of the same image map to nearby representations, while views of different images are pushed apart. The model is effectively solving "which other view in the batch came from my image?"
- **Data augmentation** is what creates those views: random transforms such as crops, color changes and blur. The choice of transforms defines what the network must become invariant to, which is why the ablation studies them.
- The framework is a **siamese two-branch network**. Each image $x_i$ is passed through two augmentation pipelines, $t$ and $t'$, then through a shared encoder. The positive pair is the two outputs.

Cropping is always applied because ImageNet images come in different sizes, so they must be cropped and resized to a common resolution before batching [S1]. This creates a confound. Every run already contains a crop, so you can't measure what color distortion or blur does on its own without cropping mixed in [S1].

The asymmetric setup removes that confound. Every image is first randomly cropped and resized to the same resolution [S1]. The targeted transform(s) are then applied to only one branch, while the other branch is left as the identity, $t(x_i) = x_i$ [S1].

The crop is the shared base for both branches, so the difference between the two views comes only from the transform under test. This lets the authors compare single augmentations (the diagonal of Figure 5) fairly against sequential pairs of two augmentations (the off-diagonals) [S1].

The authors acknowledge the cost. This asymmetric augmentation lowers absolute performance, but they argue it should not substantively change the relative impact of individual augmentations or their compositions [S2].

The result justifies the design. No single transformation is enough to learn good representations, even though the model can almost perfectly identify positive pairs. Composing transforms makes the task harder but improves representations dramatically [S2]. Crop plus color distortion stands out because crops of the same image share similar color histograms, which the network could otherwise use as a shortcut [S2].

<question>
If most of SimCLR's pieces already existed in earlier papers, what do the authors say actually makes it work better? And is it really about mutual information?
</question>

answer:
The authors credit the combination of pieces, not any single new idea. They write that almost every part of SimCLR had shown up in earlier work, sometimes in a slightly different form, and that its advantage "is not explained by any single design choice, but by their composition" [S1]. On mutual information, they say it is unclear whether that is really the reason these methods work [S1].

Three ideas help make sense of the mutual information debate. The paper doesn't define them in these passages, so the next three paragraphs are general background.

A **contrastive loss** is the scoring rule that trains the network. It shows the model two altered versions of the same photo, such as one cropped and one recolored, alongside versions of other photos. The model is rewarded when the two versions of the same photo end up with similar descriptions and different photos end up with different ones. It works like a "spot the matching pair" game.

Mutual information measures how much knowing one thing tells you about another. If the description of a cropped photo lets you guess the description of the recolored version, the two descriptions share a lot of mutual information.

InfoNCE is a popular contrastive loss built like a multiple-choice quiz: pick the true match out of many decoys. It is often described as pushing up a lower bound on mutual information. That link is why many researchers explained contrastive learning in terms of mutual information.

Several earlier papers did exactly that, attributing their success to maximizing mutual information between the learned representations [S1]. The authors point to Tschannen et al., who questioned this. The gains might come from mutual information, or they might come from the particular shape of the contrastive loss itself [S1]. In plain terms, the "matching pairs" game might work for reasons other than the theory used to justify it. The authors don't settle the question; they flag it as open.

The authors also say that SimCLR differs from ordinary supervised ImageNet training in only three ways [S2]:

- the choice of data augmentation, meaning how the photos are altered
- an extra small nonlinear "head" added at the end of the network
- the loss function

Their point is that careful choices and combinations of these familiar parts are enough to beat previous methods. They take this as a sign that self-supervised learning "remains undervalued" [S2]. For a side-by-side comparison of each SimCLR design choice against earlier methods, Appendix C has the details [S1].

If most of SimCLR's pieces already existed in earlier papers, what do the authors say actually makes it work better? And is it really about mutual information?
</question>

answer:
The authors say no single new ingredient explains SimCLR's advantage. Almost every individual component of the framework appeared in earlier work, sometimes in a different form, and its superiority "is not explained by any single design choice, but by their composition" [S1]. By studying each component and combining the findings, they improve over earlier self-supervised, semi-supervised and transfer-learning results [S2].

- A **contrastive loss** treats two augmented views of the same image as a positive pair and the other images in the batch as negatives. It pulls the embeddings of a positive pair together and pushes negatives apart, usually through a softmax over similarity scores.
- Mutual information $I(X;Y)$ measures how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about another. Here the two variables are the representations of two views of one image.
- InfoNCE is a softmax-style contrastive objective. Minimizing it maximizes a lower bound on $I(X;Y)$, which is why contrastive methods are often described as "maximizing mutual information."

For a side-by-side view of how each of SimCLR's design choices compares with earlier methods, the authors point to Appendix C [S1].

<question>
Why doesn't AutoAugment beat plain crop + color jitter for SimCLR, when it was tuned to be a better augmentation policy?
</question>

answer:
AutoAugment was "tuned to be better" for a different job than the one SimCLR does. It was found using supervised learning [S1], so it is good at helping a model learn from labelled images, not at what SimCLR asks of a model. Three ideas make this clearer.

**Data augmentation** means making altered copies of a training photo: cropping it, flipping it, or shifting its colours. In general background terms, it teaches a model that a cat is still a cat when the picture changes a little. AutoAugment is a recipe for which alterations to apply, found by automatically trying many combinations and keeping the one that worked best.

**Contrastive learning** is the kind of training SimCLR uses, and this paragraph is general background. The model gets no labels. Instead it sees two altered copies of the same photo and must recognise them as a pair among many other photos. Think of it as a "spot the same original" game. The alterations decide how hard and how useful that game is.

The **linear evaluation protocol** is how the paper scores the result. After training, the learned model is frozen, and only a very simple classifier is trained on top of it. If that simple classifier does well, the model must have learned useful descriptions of images on its own.

Now the finding. Turning up the strength of colour changes "substantially improves" linear evaluation of SimCLR's models [S1]. In that setting, AutoAugment "does not work better than simple cropping + (stronger) color distortion" [S1]. So the plain recipe holds its own, as long as the colour changes are strong.

The contrast with supervised learning explains why. When the authors trained ordinary labelled models with the same augmentations, stronger colour changes "does not improve or even hurts their performance" [S1]. Their conclusion is that contrastive learning benefits from stronger augmentation than supervised learning [S1]. They add that augmentation which gives no accuracy benefit for supervised learning "can still help considerably with contrastive learning" [S1].

The paper doesn't test exactly why AutoAugment falls short. The likely reading, which follows from the finding above, is that AutoAugment's search judged recipes by supervised accuracy. That score never rewards very strong colour changes, so the search had no reason to pick them. SimCLR needs those strong colour changes to make its matching game useful. A recipe that is best for one goal is not automatically best for another.

<question>
Why doesn't AutoAugment beat plain crop + color jitter for SimCLR, when it was tuned to be a better augmentation policy?

answer:
The short answer is that AutoAugment was tuned for a different objective. It is "a sophisticated augmentation policy found using supervised learning" [S1]. Its search optimized for supervised accuracy, and that is not what makes a good contrastive task.

Two pieces of general background make the argument concrete:

- **Contrastive learning**, as SimCLR uses it, takes two augmented views of the same image and trains the network to match them against the other images in the batch. The augmentations decide what the network has to ignore. If both crops of an image share the same color statistics, the network can match them on color alone without learning anything about shape or content. Strong color distortion removes that shortcut.
- **Linear evaluation** freezes the learned encoder and trains only a linear classifier on top of its features. The resulting accuracy measures how linearly separable the representation is.

With that framing, the paper's result follows. Raising the strength of color augmentation "substantially improves the linear evaluation of the learned unsupervised models" [S1]. In that setting, AutoAugment "does not work better than simple cropping + (stronger) color distortion" [S1]. The authors also trained supervised models with the same augmentations. There, stronger color augmentation "does not improve or even hurts their performance" [S1]. They conclude that contrastive learning "benefits from stronger (color) data augmentation than supervised learning," and that augmentation which gives no benefit in supervised learning "can still help considerably with contrastive learning" [S1].

So the augmentation that suits each objective is different. A supervised search like AutoAugment's has no reason to favor heavy color distortion, because labels already give the network its learning signal and heavy color changes may destroy useful cues. The contrastive objective, by contrast, depends on augmentation to rule out easy solutions. "Better" for AutoAugment meant better for supervised training, and that ranking does not carry over.

The paper reports this comparison but does not analyze which of AutoAugment's operations fall short. The shortcut explanation above is a common interpretation of contrastive learning in general, not a claim the authors test in this passage.

<question>
Why doesn't AutoAugment beat plain crop + color jitter for SimCLR, when it was tuned to be a better augmentation policy?
</question>

answer:
AutoAugment was tuned for a different objective. The paper describes it as "a sophisticated augmentation policy found using supervised learning" [S1], so its search optimized supervised classification accuracy, not the quality of representations learned under a contrastive loss.

In general (not from this paper), AutoAugment's controller is rewarded by the validation accuracy of a supervised child network. A policy found that way favours transformations that regularize a labelled classifier without destroying label-relevant signal. That is a different criterion from making the instance-discrimination task hard enough to force invariant features.

The paper's evidence is that, for linear evaluation of unsupervised models, AutoAugment "does not work better than simple cropping + (stronger) color distortion" [S1]. Stronger color augmentation substantially improves linear evaluation of the contrastive models [S1]. The same augmentation set has the opposite effect under supervised training: stronger color augmentation "does not improve or even hurts" supervised performance [S1].

The authors conclude that contrastive learning benefits from stronger (color) augmentation than supervised learning, and that augmentation with no accuracy benefit for supervised learning can still help contrastive learning considerably [S1]. So "better" is objective-dependent. A policy at the optimum for supervised accuracy sits at an augmentation strength, particularly for color, below what the contrastive objective wants. It therefore does not transfer as an improvement.

As general background, a common explanation for why color matters so much in contrastive setups is that, without it, two crops of the same image can be matched by low-level color statistics, which lets the model solve the task without learning semantic features.

<question>
How does SimCLR do when you only have 1% or 10% of ImageNet labels, and how do they fine-tune in that case?
</question>

answer:
A few ideas help here, and the paper assumes them, so this is general background rather than the paper's content.

**Self-supervised pretraining** means a model first learns from a huge pile of photos with no labels at all, by practising a made-up task it can check by itself. SimCLR's task is spotting that two edited copies of the same photo belong together. The model comes out with a good general sense of what images look like, even though no one has told it what anything is.

**Fine-tuning** means taking that already-trained model and training it a bit more on a smaller, labelled set of examples, so its general knowledge gets adjusted to a specific job, such as naming the object in a photo. It is like a well-read person cramming for a particular exam.

**Semi-supervised learning** is the situation where you have lots of images but only a few of them come with labels. This is the setting the question is about: pretrain on everything without labels, then fine-tune on the labelled few.

To create this setting, the authors follow an earlier study by Zhai et al. They keep the labels for only 1% or 10% of the ImageNet training set (ILSVRC-12 is the formal name of this dataset of about a thousand object categories) [S1]. The labelled images are picked in a "class-balanced" way, meaning every category gets the same share. That works out to roughly 12.8 labelled images per category at 1% and roughly 128 per category at 10% [S1].

The fine-tuning recipe is deliberately plain. They take the whole pretrained network and keep training all of it on just the labelled images, "without regularization" [S1]. Regularization is the usual set of extra tricks that stop a model from memorizing a small dataset. So there is no special machinery here, only ordinary further training. Full details are in Appendix B.5 [S1].

The results are strong. At both 1% and 10% labels, SimCLR "significantly improves over state-of-the-art" [S1]. This holds even against a supervised baseline from Zhai et al. that the authors describe as strong, because its settings (including the image edits used during training) were searched very thoroughly [S1]. The exact numbers are in the paper's Table 7.

The authors also tried fine-tuning with all of ImageNet's labels. They used their wider ResNet-50 models, at 2× and 4× the usual width. Starting from SimCLR's pretrained network beat training the same model from scratch by up to 2% [S1]. In other words, the unlabelled pretraining still helps even when labels are plentiful.

<question>
How does SimCLR do when you only have 1% or 10% of ImageNet labels, and how do they fine-tune in that case?
</question>

answer:
The setup is **semi-supervised learning**: you have a large pool of images but labels for only a small fraction of them, and the goal is to use the unlabeled part to make the labeled part go further. SimCLR's answer is two-stage. First comes self-supervised pretraining, where the encoder learns representations from all of ImageNet with no labels by pulling augmented views of the same image together under the contrastive loss. Then the pretrained network is adapted to the classification task using only the labeled subset. The first stage is what lets the second stage succeed with so few labels.

**Label subsets.** The authors follow Zhai et al. and sample 1% or 10% of the labeled ILSVRC-12 training set in a class-balanced way. That is about 12.8 and 128 images per class respectively [S1]. The exact subsets are published as a TensorFlow Datasets catalog entry, so other methods can be compared on identical splits [S2]. These experiments use ResNet-50 at width multipliers 1×, 2× and 4×, pretrained for 1000 epochs [S1].

**Fine-tuning procedure.** The procedure is deliberately minimal. The authors fine-tune the whole base network on the labeled data without regularization [S1]. They do not freeze layers, and they do not add consistency losses or pseudo-labeling on the unlabeled images during this stage. Appendix B.5 has the optimizer details [S1].

**Results.** SimCLR significantly improves over the prior state of the art with both 1% and 10% of the labels. The comparison set includes semi-supervised methods such as those of Zhai et al., Xie et al. and Sohn et al., along with other self-supervised approaches [S1]. The authors point out that the supervised baseline from Zhai et al. is strong because it went through an intensive hyperparameter search, including over augmentation, which makes the margin more meaningful [S1]. The per-method numbers are in Table 7, which isn't among the retrieved passages.

The same recipe also helps when all labels are available. Fine-tuning the pretrained ResNet-50 (2×, 4×) on full ImageNet beats training from scratch by up to 2% [S1]. So the self-supervised initialization is useful even when labels aren't scarce.

question: Why does SimCLR's NT-Xent loss beat margin or logistic losses? Is it just better tuning, or something about how the gradient treats negatives?
plan: Explain that the advantage comes from the gradient. With l2 normalization and temperature, cross-entropy automatically weights each negative by its relative hardness, and a well-chosen temperature focuses learning on hard negatives. Contrast this with logistic and margin losses, which don't weight negatives this way and so need semi-hard negative mining; define semi-hard negatives (inside the margin and closest, but farther than the positive). Finish with the fairness controls: the same l2 normalization and tuned hyperparameters for every loss. Mining helps, but those losses still end up clearly worse than NT-Xent.

We compare the NT-Xent loss against other commonly used contrastive loss functions, such as logistic loss (Mikolov et al., 2013), and margin loss (Schroff et al., 2015). Table 2 shows the objective function as well as the gradient to the input of the loss function. Looking at the gradient, we observe 1) l_2 normalization (i.e. cosine similarity) along with temperature effectively weights different examples, and an appropriate temperature can help the model learn from hard negatives; and 2) unlike cross-entropy, other objective functions do not weigh the negatives by their relative hardness. As a result, one must apply semi-hard negative mining (Schroff et al., 2015) for these loss functions: instead of computing the gradient over all loss terms, one can compute the gradient using semi-hard negative terms (i.e., those that are within the loss margin and closest in distance, but farther than positive examples).

To make the comparisons fair, we use the same l_2 normalization for all loss functions, and we tune the hyperparameters, and report their best results.^8 Table 4 shows that, while (semi-hard) negative mining helps, the best result is still much worse than our default NT-Xent loss.

<question>
Why does SimCLR's NT-Xent loss beat margin or logistic losses? Is it just better tuning, or something about how the gradient treats negatives?
</question>

answer:
It isn't just tuning. The paper traces the advantage to how the loss's **gradient** (the signal that tells the model which way to adjust) treats different negatives [S1]. Three ideas, in general terms, make this clear.

In general, a contrastive loss trains a model by comparison. Two edited copies of the same photo form a "positive" pair that should look alike to the model, and every other image in the batch is a "negative" that should look different. The loss is a score of how badly the model is doing at this matching game.

NT-Xent, like many such losses, uses a **temperature**, a single number that controls how sharply the loss reacts to differences in similarity. A low temperature is like a strict judge: the closest look-alikes dominate the score and faint ones barely count. A high temperature treats everything more evenly. This is general background.

Also in general terms, a "hard negative" is a different image the model currently thinks looks a lot like the positive, such as two different dogs on grass. These teach the most. Easy negatives, such as a dog and a car, teach almost nothing. "Hard negative mining" means deliberately picking out the hard ones to train on.

The paper shows that NT-Xent does this picking automatically. It measures similarity with l2 normalization, meaning it compares the direction two images point in the model's internal space and ignores their size. Combined with temperature, this makes the gradient give each negative a weight according to how hard it is compared with the others, and the right temperature focuses learning on the hard negatives [S1]. Logistic and margin losses don't weight negatives by relative hardness [S1].

Because logistic and margin losses lack that built-in focus, they need **semi-hard negative mining**. Instead of learning from every negative, they learn only from "semi-hard" ones: negatives that fall within the loss's safety margin and are the closest, but are still farther away than the true match [S1]. It's a hand-built filter for something NT-Xent does on its own.

To rule out tuning as the explanation, the authors gave every loss the same l2 normalization, tuned each one's settings, and reported its best result [S1]. Mining did help, but the best result was still much worse than NT-Xent [S1]. On linear evaluation accuracy, a standard test of representation quality:

- margin loss: 50.9, or 57.5 with mining [S2]
- logistic loss: 51.6, or 57.9 with mining [S2]
- NT-Xent: 63.9 [S2]

Temperature and normalization matter inside NT-Xent too. Without normalization and a suitable temperature, performance drops significantly [S2]. With normalization, a temperature of 0.1 gave 64.4, while 1 gave 58.0 [S2].

<question>
Why does SimCLR's NT-Xent loss beat margin or logistic losses? Is it just better tuning, or something about how the gradient treats negatives?
</question>

answer:
It's the gradient, not tuning. The authors gave the other losses the same normalization and tuned them too, and NT-Xent still wins clearly [S1].

Some general background first, since the paper takes these ideas as known:

- **Contrastive loss.** Each example (an anchor) has one positive, here another augmented view of the same image, and many negatives, the other images in the batch. Training pulls the anchor toward its positive and pushes it away from the negatives in embedding space.
- **Softmax temperature.** NT-Xent applies a softmax over the similarities $s_k / \tau$. A small $\tau$ sharpens the softmax, so the most similar negatives get most of the probability mass.
- **Hard negative mining.** A hard negative is one the model currently places close to the anchor. Mining means choosing which negatives contribute to the loss, instead of using all of them equally.

As general background on the mechanism: for a softmax cross-entropy, the gradient with respect to a negative's similarity $s_k$ is proportional to that negative's softmax probability:

$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial s_k} \propto \frac{1}{\tau}\,\frac{\exp(s_k/\tau)}{\sum_j \exp(s_j/\tau)}.$$

Each negative is therefore weighted automatically by how hard it is compared with the others.

The paper reads this off the gradients in Table 2. With $\ell_2$ normalization (cosine similarity) and a temperature, NT-Xent weights different examples, and a suitable $\tau$ helps the model learn from hard negatives [S1]. Logistic and margin losses do not weight negatives by their relative hardness, so they need **semi-hard negative mining** [S1]. That means computing the gradient only over negatives that are inside the loss margin and closest to the anchor, but still farther away than the positive [S1].

For fairness, the authors used the same $\ell_2$ normalization for every loss and report each loss's best tuned result [S1]. Mining does help: margin loss rises from 50.9 to 57.5 top-1 and NT-Logistic from 51.6 to 57.9 [S2]. Both still fall well short of NT-Xent's 63.9 [S2].

The weighting depends on normalization and temperature working together. With normalization, $\tau = 0.1$ reaches 64.4 top-1, while $\tau = 1$ drops to 58.0 [S2]. Removing normalization gives around 57 even though accuracy on the contrastive task itself is higher [S2]. NT-Xent's advantage therefore comes from the hardness-weighted gradient, and only when $\ell_2$ normalization and a well-chosen temperature are both in place.

answer:
It's the gradient, not tuning. The authors read it off the gradient of each loss with respect to its input: with $\ell_2$-normalized embeddings (cosine similarity) and a temperature $\tau$, cross-entropy weights each negative by its **relative hardness**, and a suitable $\tau$ concentrates learning on hard negatives [S1]. $$p_k = \frac{\exp(s_k/\tau)}{\sum_j \exp(s_j/\tau)}$$

is a softmax over the similarities to the anchor. Each negative's gradient therefore scales with how it ranks against the others, and lowering $\tau$ sharpens that weighting toward the hardest negatives. A hinge only switches each term on or off, and a sigmoid weights each pair on its own, so in neither case do negatives compete within the batch.

The authors control for tuning. Every loss uses the same $\ell_2$ normalization, and its hyperparameters are tuned to report its best result [S1]. Linear-evaluation top-1 accuracy is [S2]:

- Margin: 50.9, or 57.5 with semi-hard mining

<source label="S1" section="§A Data Augmentation Details" pages="12">
In our default pretraining setting (which is used to train our best models), we utilize random crop (with resize and random flip), random color distortion, and random Gaussian blur as the data augmentations. The details of these three augmentations are provided below.

Random crop and resize to 224x224 We use standard Inception-style random cropping (Szegedy et al., 2015). The crop of random size (uniform from 0.08 to 1.0 in area) of the original size and a random aspect ratio (default: of 3/4 to 4/3) of the original aspect ratio is made. This crop is finally resized to the original size. This has been implemented in Tensorflow as “slim.preprocessing.inception_preprocessing.distorted_bounding_box_crop”, or in Pytorch as “torchvision.transforms.RandomResizedCrop”. Additionally, the random crop (with resize) is always followed by a random horizontal/left-to-right flip with 50% probability. This is helpful but not essential. By removing this from our default augmentation policy, the top-1 linear evaluation drops from 64.5% to 63.4% for our ResNet-50 model trained in 100 epochs.

Color distortion Color distortion is composed by color jittering and color dropping. We find stronger color jittering usually helps, so we set a strength parameter.

A pseudo-code for color distortion using TensorFlow is as follows.

import tensorflow as tf def color_distortion(image, s=1.0):

# image is a tensor with value range in [0, 1].

# s is the strength of color distortion.
</source>
<source label="S2" section="§A Data Augmentation Details" pages="12-13">
def color_jitter(x):

# one can also shuffle the order of following augmentations # each time they are applied.

x = tf.image.random_brightness(x, max_delta=0.8*s) x = tf.image.random_contrast(x, lower=1-0.8*s, upper=1+0.8*s) x = tf.image.random_saturation(x, lower=1-0.8*s, upper=1+0.8*s) x = tf.image.random_hue(x, max_delta=0.2*s) x = tf.clip_by_value(x, 0, 1) return x

def color_drop(x):

image = tf.image.rgb_to_grayscale(image) image = tf.tile(image, [1, 1, 3])

# randomly apply transformation with probability p.

image = random_apply(color_jitter, image, p=0.8) image = random_apply(color_drop, image, p=0.2) return image

A pseudo-code for color distortion using Pytorch is as follows^12.

# s is the strength of color distortion.

color_jitter = transforms.ColorJitter(0.8*s, 0.8*s, 0.8*s, 0.2*s) rnd_color_jitter = transforms.RandomApply([color_jitter], p=0.8) rnd_gray = transforms.RandomGrayscale(p=0.2) color_distort = transforms.Compose([ rnd_color_jitter, rnd_gray]) return color_distort

Gaussian blur This augmentation is in our default policy. We find it helpful, as it improves our ResNet-50 trained for 100 epochs from 63.2% to 64.5%. We blur the image 50% of the time using a Gaussian kernel. We randomly sample σ ∈[0.1, 2.0], and the kernel size is set to be 10% of the image height/width.

<question>
How much does the random horizontal flip actually matter in SimCLR's augmentation pipeline?
</question>

answer:
Very little. Removing the flip costs about one percentage point of accuracy, and the authors call it "helpful but not essential" [S1].

Three ideas help make sense of that number.

**Data augmentation** means making altered copies of a training photo: cropping it, changing its colours, blurring it. In general background terms, SimCLR learns by showing the computer two altered copies of the same photo and teaching it that they still show the same thing. The alterations decide what the model learns to ignore. If the copies are flipped, for example, it learns that a cat facing left is still the same cat as one facing right.

The paper's main score is a **linear evaluation**. This is general background: after the model has learned from unlabelled photos, it is frozen. Then a very simple classifier is trained on top of what it learned, and its accuracy on ImageNet shows how useful those learned features are. "Top-1" means the classifier's first guess was correct.

The flip comes right after a random crop. The authors pick a random piece of the photo, anywhere from 8% to 100% of its area, with a somewhat random shape. They then stretch that piece back to full size [S1]. This is the standard "Inception-style" crop, called `RandomResizedCrop` in PyTorch [S1].

Here is where the flip fits:

- Every time a crop is made, it is mirrored left-to-right with a 50% chance, like a coin toss [S1].
- When the authors removed the flip from their default settings, linear evaluation top-1 accuracy fell from 64.5% to 63.4%. That result is for a ResNet-50 model trained for 100 epochs, meaning 100 passes over the data [S1].

For scale, Gaussian blur, another extra in the same default recipe, is worth a similar amount. Removing it lowers that same 100-epoch ResNet-50 from 64.5% to 63.2% [S2]. The default recipe is built from three main ingredients: random crop, colour distortion and blur [S1]. The flip is a small add-on tucked inside the crop step [S1].

Taken together, the flip gives a modest gain worth keeping, but SimCLR would still work well without it.

<question>
How much does the random horizontal flip actually matter in SimCLR's augmentation pipeline?
</question>

answer:
Not much. The flip gives a gain of about one point in linear evaluation, and the authors call it "helpful but not essential" [S1].

To read that number, two pieces of the setup matter:

- **Linear evaluation**: the pretrained encoder is frozen, and a single linear classifier is trained on its features with ImageNet labels. Top-1 accuracy of that classifier is the measure of representation quality. This is general background on the protocol; the ablation below reports it.
- **Inception-style random resized crop**: SimCLR samples a crop covering a uniformly random 0.08 to 1.0 of the image area, with an aspect ratio between 3/4 and 4/3, then resizes it back to 224×224 [S1]. This is `torchvision.transforms.RandomResizedCrop` in PyTorch [S1].

The flip is not a separate stage of the pipeline. The random crop "is always followed by a random horizontal/left-to-right flip with 50% probability" [S1]. So each view is a random crop that is mirrored half the time.

The appendix gives a single ablation. For a ResNet-50 pretrained for 100 epochs, removing the flip lowers top-1 linear evaluation from 64.5% to 63.4%, a 1.1-point drop [S1]. Gaussian blur, also applied 50% of the time, is in the same range: removing it lowers the same model from 64.5% to 63.2% [S2].

The paper ranks these two as secondary to the main default augmentations, random crop and color distortion. Color distortion combines color jitter, applied with $p=0.8$, and grayscale conversion, applied with $p=0.2$, controlled by a strength parameter $s$ [S1][S2]. Flip and blur each add roughly a point on top of that core.

These passages don't report how the flip interacts with the crop, or whether its effect changes with longer training or larger models. The 1.1-point figure holds only for that one 100-epoch ResNet-50 setting.

<question>
Why do they use the representation before the projection head instead of the output z? Is there evidence h is actually better?
</question>

answer:
SimCLR builds a picture's "summary" in two stages, and the evidence the authors give suggests the first stage, **h**, keeps more useful information than the second stage, **z**. Three ideas make that evidence readable.

In general, a **projection head** is a small extra network attached after the main image-reading network. The main network turns a picture into a long list of numbers (h), and the head transforms that list into another list (z), which is what the training objective actually compares. In the paper's notation, z = g(h), and in the simplest version the head just multiplies h by a grid of numbers W, so z = Wh, where W is 2048 by 2048 [S1].

In general, a **low-rank** matrix is a transformation that squashes information. Imagine taking a 3D object and casting its shadow on a wall: the shadow keeps some directions and flattens others away. A low-rank W does something similar to h, so details that get flattened cannot be recovered from z.

**t-SNE** is a common tool for drawing high-dimensional data as a 2D scatter plot, placing items that are similar close together. If pictures of the same kind (say, all the dogs) form tight, separate clusters, the representation is grouping them well.

The first piece of evidence concerns W. When the authors examined the linear projection matrix, it had only a few large eigenvalues, which they read as a sign that it is approximately low-rank [S1]. Eigenvalues roughly measure how strongly the matrix stretches each direction. A few large ones and many small ones mean most directions get shrunk almost to nothing. So passing h through W likely throws away information that h still holds.

The second piece is the t-SNE plots. The authors took their best ResNet-50 model, which scores 69.3% when a simple classifier is trained on its features [S1]. They plotted h and z for 10 randomly chosen classes from the validation set. Classes are better separated when represented by h than by z [S1].

Together these two results support using h for later tasks: z appears to be a compressed version tuned for the training objective, while h keeps richer detail. Keep in mind that t-SNE pictures are visual impressions, not precise measurements. They support the conclusion, but they do not prove it on their own.

answer:
SimCLR trains with the contrastive loss on $z$, the output of a small head, but keeps the layer before it, $h$, for downstream use. The appendix gives two pieces of evidence that $h$ holds more useful information than $z$ [S1].

**Background (general, not from these passages).** A **projection head** is a small network $g(\cdot)$ placed after the encoder. It maps the representation $h$ to $z = g(h)$, and the loss is computed on $z$. Because the loss acts on $z$, the head is free to drop any feature that does not help the contrastive objective. A matrix is low-rank when only a few directions carry most of its action, so it compresses its input into a lower-dimensional subspace. t-SNE is a method that maps high-dimensional vectors to 2-D while trying to keep nearby points close together, which lets you see cluster structure.

**Evidence 1: the projection is nearly low-rank.** For a linear head $z = Wh$ with $W \in \mathbb{R}^{2048\times 2048}$, the eigenvalue distribution (Figure B.3) has relatively few large eigenvalues. This indicates that $W$ is approximately low-rank [S1]. A natural reading is that $z$ lives in a much smaller effective subspace than $h$. Information about the image that is present in $h$ is therefore squashed out in $z$, probably the information that the loss does not reward.

**Evidence 2: classes separate better in $h$.** Figure B.4 shows t-SNE plots of $h$ and $z = g(h)$ for 10 randomly selected validation classes. The plots come from the authors' best ResNet-50, which reaches 69.3% top-1 under linear evaluation [S1]. Classes are better separated in $h$ than in $z$ [S1]. This means $h$ keeps more of the class-relevant structure that a downstream classifier needs.

Both observations point the same way: the head discards information and $h$ keeps it, so $h$ is the better choice for downstream tasks [S1]. Two caveats apply to this evidence. The eigenvalue analysis is for a linear head, and t-SNE plots are qualitative. They support the choice but do not measure the gap on their own.

**Spectral evidence.** For the linear-head variant $z = Wh$ with $W \in \mathbb{R}^{2048\times 2048}$, the eigenvalue spectrum of $W$ has relatively few large eigenvalues, so $W$ is approximately low-rank [S1]. The contrastive objective is therefore effectively optimized in a low-dimensional subspace of $h$. Directions of $h$ that the projection suppresses still exist in $h$ but are attenuated or removed in $z$.

**Qualitative evidence.** The authors show t-SNE embeddings of $h$ and $z = g(h)$ for 10 randomly selected validation classes, using their best ResNet-50 (69.3% top-1 linear eval). Classes are better separated in $h$ than in $z$ [S1].

Both observations support taking the pre-head representation for downstream use. They have limits:

- **Linear head only.** The low-rank result concerns the linear head. The nonlinear MLP head used in practice is not characterized this way in the passage [S1].
- **t-SNE is qualitative.** Its cluster separation depends on perplexity and initialization, and 10 classes is a small sample.

The passages provided don't include the linear-evaluation numbers comparing $h$ and $z$ directly. Section 4.2 is where the paper makes that quantitative case, so check it for the actual accuracy gap.

The usual explanation, which is general background rather than a claim in these passages, is that the contrastive loss trains $z$ to be invariant to the augmentations. So $z$ discards attributes like color or orientation that may help downstream tasks. The head absorbs that invariance and leaves $h$ richer.

<question>
Why do they report mean per-class accuracy for some datasets like Aircraft and Pets but plain top-1 accuracy for others?
</question>

answer:
The authors didn't pick these metrics themselves. They follow the evaluation rules set out in the papers that first introduced each dataset [S1]. Whatever measure a dataset's creators said to use, SimCLR uses too.

The paper assumes these measures are already familiar, so here they are in general terms first:

- **Top-1 accuracy** is the simplest score. The model makes one best guess per image, and you count the share of all test images it got right.
- **Mean per-class accuracy** works in two steps. First, accuracy is worked out separately for each category (say, each aircraft model or each pet breed). Then those numbers are averaged. Every category counts equally, however many test images it has. With plain top-1, a category with lots of images would weigh more than a rare one.
- **Mean average precision (mAP)** fits tasks where an image can contain several things at once, like a dog *and* a person. For each category, it scores how well the model ranks the images that truly contain that category above the ones that don't. It then averages those scores across categories.

Here is how the paper splits the datasets [S1]:

- **Top-1 accuracy:** Food-101, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Birdsnap, SUN397, Stanford Cars, and DTD (textures).
- **Mean per-class accuracy:** FGVC Aircraft, Oxford-IIIT Pets, Caltech-101, and Oxford 102 Flowers.
- **11-point mAP:** PASCAL VOC 2007, using the exact definition from that dataset's creators.

The paper gives no reason why the original creators chose per-class averaging for Aircraft and Pets. In general, creators pick it when some categories have more test images than others, so a model can't score well just by doing well on the big categories.

Copying each dataset's official rules keeps the numbers comparable with earlier published results. It's like playing each sport by its league's rulebook so scores can be compared across seasons. The same idea guides the authors' other setup choices [S1]:

- **DTD and SUN397:** the creators defined several ways to split the data into training and test images, and the authors report only the first split.
- **Caltech-101:** the dataset has no official split, so the authors picked 30 random images per category for training and tested on the rest. They did this "for fair comparison with previous work."

<question>
Why do they report mean per-class accuracy for some datasets like Aircraft and Pets but plain top-1 accuracy for others?
</question>

answer:
The authors don't choose the metric per dataset themselves: they "follow the evaluation protocols in the papers introducing these datasets" [S1]. Aircraft and Pets get mean per-class accuracy because the papers that introduced those benchmarks defined it that way.

As general background, the three metrics differ as follows:

1. **Top-1 accuracy**: the fraction of all test images whose highest-scoring predicted class is correct. Every *image* counts equally, so classes with many test images dominate the number.
2. **Mean per-class accuracy**: compute top-1 accuracy separately within each class, then average those $C$ values: $\frac{1}{C}\sum_{c} \text{acc}_c$. Every *class* counts equally, so a model can't score well by doing well only on the frequent classes. It equals top-1 when every class has the same number of test images.
3. **Mean average precision (mAP)**: for multi-label tasks, rank test images by score for each class, compute average precision from the precision–recall curve, and average over classes. The "11-point" version averages precision at recall levels $0, 0.1, \dots, 1.0$.

The paper's split is [S1]:

- **Top-1:** Food-101, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Birdsnap, SUN397, Stanford Cars, DTD
- **Mean per-class:** FGVC Aircraft, Oxford-IIIT Pets, Caltech-101, Oxford 102 Flowers
- **11-point mAP:** PASCAL VOC 2007, as defined by its creators

Using each dataset's original protocol keeps the numbers directly comparable with earlier published results. The same reasoning shows up in the other protocol choices. For DTD and SUN397, which have several official train/test splits, they report only the first split. For Caltech-101, which has no defined split, they randomly pick 30 training images per class and test on the rest, "for fair comparison with previous work" [S1].

The paper doesn't say why the original creators preferred per-class averaging for those four datasets. In general, the per-class average is chosen when test sets are imbalanced across classes. Caltech-101 is a clear example: after taking 30 images per class for training, the remaining test counts vary a lot from class to class. VOC 2007 uses mAP because its images can contain several object classes at once, so a single top-1 prediction isn't well defined.

Use Table B.1 to show that the benefit of larger batches shrinks as epochs increase (e.g., at 800 epochs 256 vs 8192 differ by only ~2.5 points vs ~7 at 100 epochs). Note the slash compares linear vs square-root LR scaling and that differences between the two are small, mostly favoring sqrt at small batches/short training.

<question>
Does SimCLR keep improving if you push batch size past 8K, or is it better to just train for more epochs?
</question>

answer:
Going past a batch size of 8192 doesn't seem to help much, while training for more epochs keeps paying off [S1]. Three ideas help in reading the evidence.

**Why batch size matters at all.** This is general background, though the paper relies on it. SimCLR learns by recognising that two edited copies of the same photo belong together. The other photos in the same batch serve as "wrong answers", called **negatives**. A bigger batch means more wrong answers to tell apart, which is why bigger batches help at first.

**Learning rate scaling.** Also general background: the learning rate is the size of each adjustment step during training. When the batch gets bigger, the step size is usually raised too. A "linear" rule raises it in proportion to the batch size. A "square-root" rule raises it more gently.

**Linear evaluation.** This is how the paper scores a model, so the numbers below are this kind of score. The learned features are frozen, and only a very simple classifier is trained on top. Its top-1 accuracy (how often its first guess is right) shows how useful the features are.

**What the paper found.** The authors trained with batches up to 32K and for up to 3200 epochs (an epoch is one full pass over the dataset), using the square-root rule. Performance "seems to saturate with a batch size of 8192, while training longer can still significantly" improve it [S1].

Table B.1 shows the trade-off. Each cell has two numbers separated by a slash, one for each learning-rate rule [S1]. The caption is cut off in the extracted text, so the order is taken from the plan: left is linear, right is square-root.

- **At 100 epochs**, batch 256 scores 57.5 / 62.8 and batch 8192 scores 64.8 / 64.8 [S1]. That is a gap of about 7 points with the linear rule but only 2 with the square-root rule.
- **At 800 epochs**, batch 256 scores 66.6 / 66.5 and batch 8192 scores 69.0 / 69.1 [S1]. Both rules now give a gap of about 2.5 points.

The two rules mostly agree. The square-root rule clearly helps only with small batches and short training, such as 57.5 vs 62.8 at batch 256 and 100 epochs [S1].

The advantage of huge batches shrinks the longer you train. Longer training lets a small batch see many different "wrong answers" over time, which makes up for having fewer at once. So past about 8K, more epochs is the better use of compute [S1].

<question>
Does SimCLR keep improving if you push batch size past 8K, or is it better to just train for more epochs?
</question>

answer:
Pushing past 8K buys little: with square-root learning-rate scaling, accuracy saturates around a batch size of 8192, while training longer (up to 3200 epochs) still gives significant gains [S1]. Three pieces of background explain why.

The following is general background rather than the paper's content:

1. **Negatives come from the batch.** SimCLR's contrastive loss pulls two augmented views of an image together and pushes them away from every other image in the same batch. A batch of $N$ gives each positive pair $2(N-1)$ negatives, so larger batches mean more negatives per step.
2. **Learning rate scales with batch size.** Larger batches give less noisy gradients, so the learning rate is usually raised with them. Linear scaling sets $\text{lr} \propto N$, and square-root scaling sets $\text{lr} \propto \sqrt{N}$, which is gentler at large $N$.
3. **Linear evaluation.** The encoder is frozen and only a linear classifier is trained on its features. The resulting top-1 accuracy measures how good the representation is.

The paper trains with batches up to 32K, but performance stops improving at about 8192 [S1]. Table B.1 shows how this interacts with training length. The two numbers in each cell are the two learning-rate scalings; the plan reads them as linear on the left and square-root on the right, though the caption is cut off in the extracted text [S1].

- **At 100 epochs**, batch 256 reaches 57.5 and batch 8192 reaches 64.8 on the left-hand numbers, a gap of about 7 points [S1].
- **At 800 epochs**, the same comparison is 66.6 vs 69.0, only about 2.5 points [S1].

Longer training therefore closes most of the gap that big batches open. Small-batch models can catch up because they get many more gradient steps over the same number of epochs. The two scalings end up close; the right-hand numbers are clearly higher mainly at small batches and short training (62.8 vs 57.5 at batch 256 and 100 epochs) [S1].

In practice, once you are near 8K, more epochs are the better investment. Very large batches matter mostly when the training budget is short.

<question>
If a SimCLR model does better on the linear probe, does that mean it'll also do better when you fine-tune it? How closely do the two track each other?
</question>

answer:
Mostly yes. As training length changes, the two scores rise and fall together almost in a straight line, so a better linear-probe score generally means a better fine-tuned score. The paper backs this with plots rather than an exact measure of how tight the link is.

SimCLR first trains a network on images with no labels at all, a stage called **self-supervised pretraining**. The network learns by checking whether two altered copies of a photo came from the same original. Linear probing and fine-tuning are then two ways of grading what it learned. This short description is general background rather than a claim from the passages here.

In the paper's two grading settings, the linear probe trains only a simple classifier on top of the frozen learned features. Fine-tuning instead lets every weight in the network keep adjusting [S2]. Because fine-tuning can change so much more, it's reasonable to ask whether the two grades agree.

The authors test this in an appendix section devoted to the question [S1]:

- **Varying training length:** They took a ResNet-50 (a standard image network) and pretrained it with batch size 4096 for anywhere from 50 to 3200 epochs, where an epoch is one full pass over the training images. They then scored each version both ways using top-1 accuracy, which is how often the model's first guess is right [S1]. The finding is that the two scores are "almost linearly correlated" [S1]. Plotted against each other, the points fall close to a straight line, so longer pretraining improves both by a predictable amount.
- **Varying architecture:** A second figure, Figure B.6, compares the two scores across different network designs [S1]. The text only points to the figure and states no conclusion about it, so the passage alone doesn't say how closely they track across architectures.

There is a gap in the text. Right after the "almost linearly correlated" remark, the sentence starts a caveat, "it seems fine-tuning on a small fraction…", and then breaks off [S1]. It presumably concerns fine-tuning with only a small share of the labels, but the passage doesn't say what the caveat is. So for that low-label case, a better linear probe score may not translate as neatly, and the paper's full point there can't be recovered from this excerpt.

<question>
When they compared NT-Xent against margin and logistic loss, how did they make sure the other losses weren't just handicapped by bad hyperparameters?
</question>

answer:
The authors gave the other losses their own tuning instead of reusing the settings that worked for NT-Xent [S1]. Some general background first makes this easier to follow.

In general, a **hyperparameter** is a setting chosen by people before training rather than learned by the model, like the oven temperature in a recipe. The learning rate is the most common one: it controls how big a step the model takes each time it corrects itself. Steps that are too big overshoot, and steps that are too small barely move. **Hyperparameter tuning** means trying several values and keeping whichever works best.

NT-Xent is SimCLR's main loss, the score the model tries to improve during training. It compares how similar two pictures look to the model, and it uses "normalization and temperature to restrict the range of similarity scores" [S2]. Temperature works like a contrast knob that decides how sharply the loss separates close matches from poor ones.

The paper does not explain margin loss in this passage. In general, a triplet margin loss takes three images: an anchor, a matching version of it, and a non-matching one. It pushes the match closer to the anchor than the non-match, by at least a fixed gap called the margin. Logistic loss treats each pair as a yes-or-no question: same image or not?

The fairness problem is this. A learning rate that suits NT-Xent "may not be a good learning rate for other loss functions" [S1]. If the authors had reused NT-Xent's settings, the other losses could look worse simply because they were run in the wrong oven. To avoid that, they took three steps:

1. **Learning rate.** They tried 0.01, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 and 1.0 separately for both margin loss and logistic loss [S1].
2. **Margin loss's own setting.** They tried margins of 0, 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 [S1].
3. **Logistic loss's own setting.** They tried temperatures of 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 1.0 [S1].

There is one more detail. Each training image is turned into two altered copies, called "views." For simplicity, every loss drew its non-matching examples from only one view instead of both [S1]. The authors note that this "slightly impairs performance but ensures fair comparison" [S1]. All three losses carried the same small handicap, so the comparison stayed even.

While we focus on using ImageNet as the main dataset for pretraining our unsupervised model, our method also works with other datasets. We demonstrate it by testing on CIFAR-10 as follows.

Setup As our goal is not to optimize CIFAR-10 performance, but rather to provide further confirmation of our observations on ImageNet, we use the same architecture (ResNet-50) for CIFAR-10 experiments. Because CIFAR-10 images are much smaller than ImageNet images, we replace the first 7x7 Conv of stride 2 with 3x3 Conv of stride 1, and also remove the first max pooling operation. For data augmentation, we use the same Inception crop (flip and resize to 32x32) as ImageNet,^15 and color distortion (strength=0.5), leaving out Gaussian blur. We pretrain with learning rate in {0.5, 1.0, 1.5}, temperature in {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}, and batch size in {256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096}. The rest of the settings (including optimizer, weight decay, etc.) are the same as our ImageNet training.

Our best model trained with batch size 1024 can achieve a linear evaluation accuracy of 94.0%, compared to 95.1% from the supervised baseline using the same architecture and batch size. The best self-supervised model that reports linear evaluation result on CIFAR-10 is AMDIM (Bachman et al., 2019), which achieves 91.2% with a model 25× larger than ours. We note that our model can be improved by incorporating extra data augmentations as well as using a more suitable base network.

<question>
Why does SimCLR lose to supervised pretraining on transfer tasks with a regular ResNet-50 but not with the 4x wider version?
</question>

answer:
Three ideas from general background (not this paper's content) help here.

- **Linear evaluation**: the trained network is frozen, like a camera whose settings are locked, and only a simple final decision layer is trained on top. This tests how useful the network's learned features are on their own.
- **Fine-tuning**: instead of freezing the network, every part of it is allowed to adjust a little on the new task. Weak starting features can be partly repaired this way.
- **Transfer learning**: a network is trained on one big collection of images (here ImageNet) and then reused on different tasks, such as recognizing bird species or car models. The question is how well that "head start" carries over.

The authors compared SimCLR against a supervised network (trained with human labels) on 12 such transfer tasks. With the 4× wider ResNet-50, neither side has a clear advantage [S1]. With the regular, narrower ResNet-50, supervised pretraining wins on all 12 datasets under linear evaluation and on 10 of 12 under fine-tuning [S1].

The authors suggest the explanation lies in how far behind SimCLR already is on ImageNet itself. The regular SimCLR ResNet-50 reaches 69.3% top-1 accuracy, which is 6.8 points worse than its supervised counterpart. The 4× version reaches 76.5%, only 1.8 points worse [S1]. A network that starts with noticeably weaker features carries that weakness into new tasks. The authors present this cautiously: the weaker transfer results "may relate to" that gap [S1].

Fine-tuning shrinks the difference a lot. On Birdsnap, a bird-species dataset, SimCLR scores 37.4 versus supervised 53.7 under linear evaluation, but 75.9 versus 75.8 after fine-tuning [S1]. On Cars, the scores go from 50.3 versus 66.7 to 91.3 versus 92.1 [S1]. When the whole network is allowed to adjust, it can make up for most of what SimCLR's frozen features were missing. When the features are locked, as in linear evaluation, their shortcomings show fully.

<question>
Why does SimCLR lose to supervised pretraining on transfer tasks with a regular ResNet-50 but not with the 4x wider version?
</question>

answer:
**Linear evaluation** freezes the pretrained encoder and trains only a linear classifier on its features, so it measures how good the representation is as-is. **Fine-tuning** starts from the pretrained weights and updates the whole network on the new task, so weaknesses in the initial features can be corrected. **Transfer learning** means pretraining on one dataset (here ImageNet) and then applying the model to different downstream datasets with either protocol. This is general background; the paper uses all three terms without defining them in this section.

With ResNet-50 (4×), neither supervised nor SimCLR pretraining has a clear advantage on transfer [S1]. With the standard ResNet-50, supervised pretraining wins on all 12 datasets under linear evaluation and on 10 of 12 under fine-tuning [S1].

The authors suggest the cause is how far behind SimCLR already is on ImageNet itself [S1]. The self-supervised ResNet-50 reaches 69.3% top-1, which is 6.8% below its supervised counterpart. The self-supervised ResNet-50 (4×) reaches 76.5%, only 1.8% below [S1]. So the transfer gap seems to follow the quality gap on the pretraining task. A narrow model gives up more in self-supervised training, and that shortfall carries over to downstream tasks. The authors only say this "may relate" to the gap, so it is a hypothesis, not a tested explanation [S1].

Fine-tuning closes much of the gap, because the whole network can adapt to the new task [S1]:

| Dataset | Linear (SimCLR / Sup.) | Fine-tuned (SimCLR / Sup.) |
|---|---|---|
| Birdsnap | 37.4 / 53.7 | 75.9 / 75.8 |
| Cars | 50.3 / 66.7 | 91.3 / 92.1 |

Under linear evaluation, the representation's deficits are fully exposed. Under fine-tuning, the two models end up within about a point of each other on most datasets [S1].

Note that fine-tuning narrows the gap considerably compared to linear evaluation, citing a couple of example numbers (e.g., Birdsnap 37.4 vs 53.7 linear but ~75.9 vs 75.8 fine-tuned).

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [17, 16] have demonstrated recognition accuracy better than or comparable to humans in several visual recognition tasks, including recognizing traffic signs [3], faces [30, 28], and handwritten digits [3, 31]. In this work, we present a result that surpasses human-level performance on a more generic and challenging recognition task - the classification task in the 1000-class ImageNet dataset [22].

In the last few years, we have witnessed tremendous improvements in recognition performance, mainly due to advances in two technical directions: building more powerful models, and designing effective strategies against overfitting. On one hand, neural networks are becoming more capable of fitting training data, because of increased complexity (e.g., increased depth [25, 29], enlarged width [33, 24], and the use of smaller strides [33, 24, 2, 25]), new nonlinear activations [21, 20, 34, 19, 27, 9], and sophisticated layer designs [29, 11]. On the other hand, better generalization is achieved by effective regularization techniques [12, 26, 9, 31], aggressive data augmentation [16, 13, 25, 29], and large-scale data [4, 22].

Among these advances, the rectifier neuron [21, 8, 20, 34], e.g., Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU), is one of several keys to the recent success of deep networks [16]. It expedites convergence of the training procedure [16] and leads to better solutions [21, 8, 20, 34] than conventional sigmoid-like units. Despite the prevalence of rectifier networks, recent improvements of models [33, 24, 11, 25, 29] and theoretical guidelines for training them [7, 23] have rarely focused on the properties of the rectifiers.
</source>
<source label="S2" section="§1 Introduction" pages="1-2">
In this paper, we investigate neural networks from two aspects particularly driven by the rectifiers. First, we propose a new generalization of ReLU, which we call Parametric Rectified Linear Unit (PReLU). This activation function adaptively learns the parameters of the rectifiers, and improves accuracy at negligible extra computational cost. Second, we study the difficulty of training rectified models that are very deep. By explicitly modeling the nonlinearity of rectifiers (ReLU/PReLU), we derive a theoretically sound initialization method, which helps with convergence of very deep models (e.g., with 30 weight layers) trained directly from scratch. This gives us more flexibility to explore more powerful network architectures.

On the 1000-class ImageNet 2012 dataset, our PReLU network (PReLU-net) leads to a single-model result of 5.71% top-5 error, which surpasses all existing multi-model results. Further, our multi-model result achieves 4.94% top-5 error on the test set, which is a 26% relative improvement over the ILSVRC 2014 winner (GoogLeNet, 6.66% [29]). To the best of our knowledge, our result surpasses for the first time the reported human-level performance (5.1% in [22]) on this visual recognition challenge.

Figure 1. ReLU vs. PReLU. For PReLU, the coefficient of the negative part is not constant and is adaptively learned.
