<question>
Why do the authors think the FlashAttention trick could carry over to kernel methods like SVMs or Gaussian processes?
</question>

answer:
The authors' argument is that kernel methods have the same structure that FlashAttention exploits: a huge grid of numbers that can be cheaply rebuilt from much smaller inputs. A few background ideas make the parallel clear.

In general, a **kernel matrix** is a big table of similarity scores. With N datapoints, it has N rows and N columns, and each cell says how alike two datapoints are. Methods like support vector machines and Gaussian processes depend on this table. Its size grows with the square of N, so 100,000 datapoints means 10 billion cells.

Also as general background, a GPU has two kinds of memory. A large but relatively slow main memory is called HBM. A tiny but very fast workspace sits right next to the processing units and is called SRAM. Moving data back and forth between them often takes more time than the arithmetic itself. A useful picture is a big warehouse across town and a small workbench in your shop.

**Recomputation** means recalculating something whenever it is needed instead of saving it and fetching it later. This sounds wasteful, but if the calculation is cheap and the fetch is slow, recalculating is faster.

FlashAttention relies on the fact that the large N-by-N attention table is built from two much smaller inputs, called Q and K [S1]. Each of these has only a few numbers per word, far fewer than N [S1]. The algorithm never stores the whole table. It repeatedly loads the small Q and K into fast memory and recomputes just the piece of the table it needs, which greatly cuts trips to the slow HBM [S1].

The authors point out that kernel methods look the same [S1]. Each cell of an N-by-N kernel matrix is computed from just two datapoints, each described by a short list of d numbers, where d is much smaller than N [S1]. So the same strategy should work: keep the small datapoints, rebuild pieces of the similarity table in fast memory on demand, and never write the full table to slow memory.

As evidence that this pays off, the authors cite the KeOps library, which has already shown that reducing memory reads and writes speeds up kernel operations [S1]. Their broader hope is that kernel methods will focus more on reducing memory traffic, not only on counting arithmetic operations [S1].

The paper speaks of "kernel machine learning" in general and doesn't name SVMs or Gaussian processes. Both are standard examples of methods built on a kernel matrix, so the argument applies to them.

A **kernel matrix** is the $N \times N$ matrix $K$ whose entry $K_{ij}$ measures the similarity between datapoints $x_i$ and $x_j$, each a vector of size $d \ll N$ [S1]. SVMs and Gaussian processes are built on this matrix, so their cost grows with $N^2$, just like attention.

The paper's main text explains the GPU memory hierarchy, but in general terms it works like this. A GPU has large but relatively slow off-chip memory (HBM) and a small, fast on-chip memory (SRAM). Many operations are limited by how much data moves between the two, not by arithmetic. Materializing an $N \times N$ matrix in HBM and reading it back is therefore expensive even when the math is cheap.

**Recomputation** means you don't store the large intermediate. You keep only the small inputs and rebuild each piece when you need it. FlashAttention does this by repeatedly loading $Q$ and $K$ and recomputing whichever block of the attention matrix it needs, which greatly reduces HBM access [S1].

The authors say this works because the $N \times N$ attention matrix is a function of the low-rank product $QK^\top$, whose rank is $d \ll N$ [S1]. All the information in that huge matrix comes from inputs of size $N \times d$. Loading those small inputs and redoing the arithmetic in SRAM costs less than writing and reading the full matrix.

They argue that kernel machine learning has the same structure. Each $K_{ij}$ depends only on two $d$-dimensional vectors, so a block of $K$ can be recomputed on the fly from the datapoints instead of being stored [S1]. They point to the KeOps library as evidence that reducing memory reads and writes speeds up kernel operations in practice [S1].

The broader point is about what to optimize. Kernel methods have usually been sped up by cutting FLOPs, and the authors hope to encourage kernel methods that focus on reducing IO as well [S1]. This mirrors the paper's main argument that approximate attention cut compute without delivering wall-clock speedups. The paper presents the extension as a direction for future work and does not test it on SVMs or Gaussian processes [S1].

<source label="S1" section="§D.2 Potential Extensions" pages="25-26">
We discuss here a few potential extensions of the IO-aware approach to speed up deep learning training.

Multi-GPU Attention. Large language models are trained on hundreds or thousands of GPUs, and one typically splits the attention computation between 4-8 GPUs on the same node [77]. This introduces another level of memory hierarchy: beside GPU SRAM and GPU HBM, we also have the HBM of other GPUs. For very long sequences, the different GPUs on the same node can cooperate to compute attention by taking into account the asymmetry of different levels of memory hierarchy.

Sparse MLP layers. Typical dense MLP layers are compute-bound and not memory-bound. To improve their efficiency, MLP layers with sparse weight matrices can be used [17]. However, many sparse MLP layers are instead memory-bound, and their speedup is often not proportional to the sparsity. We believe that an IO-aware implementation can alleviate this issue and realize the benefits of sparsity. We are excited about future work in this direction, to reduce the computational requirement of large models and improve their wall-block runtime.

Kernel machine learning. Our approach in FlashAttention relies on the fact that the N× N attention matrix is a function of a low-rank matrix QK^{⊤}(of rank d≪N). As a result, we can repeatedly load the inputs Q, K and recompute the block of the attention matrix that we need, significantly reducing HBM access. As similar scenario happens in kernel machine learning: each element K_ijof the N× Nkernel matrix K is a function of two vectors of size d≪N, as it measures the similarity between two datapoints x_i and x_j. The KeOps library [8, 26] is a successful example of how reducing memory reads/writes can speed up kernel operations. We hope that this will motivate kernel methods that focus more on reducing IOs instead of just FLOPs.

Why do the authors think the FlashAttention trick could carry over to kernel methods like SVMs or Gaussian processes?

answer:
The argument rests on one structural property. The $N\times N$ attention matrix is a function of the low-rank product $QK^\top$, which has rank $d \ll N$ [S1]. The authors point out that kernel matrices have the same structure. Each entry $K_{ij}$ of an $N\times N$ kernel matrix is a similarity between two datapoints $x_i, x_j$ of dimension $d \ll N$ [S1]. The full Gram matrix is $O(N^2)$ to store, but it is fully determined by $O(Nd)$ inputs. A kernel computation can therefore stream tiles of $X$ into fast memory, recompute the corresponding tiles of $K$ on the fly, and reduce them directly into whatever is needed, such as a kernel–vector product, without writing $K$ to slow memory.

As evidence that this works in practice, they cite the KeOps library, which speeds up kernel operations by reducing memory reads and writes [S1]. They end with a methodological point: kernel methods have largely been optimized for FLOP count, and the authors hope future work will target IO instead [S1]. This mirrors their critique of approximate attention, which reduces FLOPs but often fails to deliver wall-clock speedup.

The paper only sketches this extension; it doesn't analyze specific models. Applying the idea to SVMs or Gaussian processes is therefore an inference from general background. GP inference and SVM training are commonly dominated by kernel-matrix products, for example inside iterative solvers, and those products are exactly the operation this tiling-and-recompute approach would accelerate. Operations that genuinely need the factorized matrix, such as an exact Cholesky decomposition, would not fit the pattern as cleanly.

<question>
Why is FlashAttention slower than Apex FMHA on the backward pass but faster on the forward pass for short sequences?
</question>

answer:
The difference comes from one choice: Apex FMHA saves a large intermediate result during the forward pass so it can reuse it later, while FlashAttention throws it away and rebuilds it when it is needed [S1]. Three ideas explain why that choice matters.

**GPU memory has two levels.** In general, a GPU has a large but relatively slow main memory, which the paper calls HBM (high bandwidth memory), and a tiny but very fast scratch space on the chip itself, called SRAM. A useful analogy is a big warehouse and a small workbench. Every trip to the warehouse costs time, so fast code tries to keep work on the workbench.

**Recomputation trades extra arithmetic for less storage.** In general, training a model has two stages. The forward pass computes the answer. The backward pass then works out how to adjust the model, and it needs some of the forward pass's intermediate results. You can either save those results, which costs memory and warehouse trips, or recompute them later, which costs extra arithmetic.

**Kernel fusion means doing several steps in one go.** In general, a "kernel" is one job the GPU runs. Fusing several steps into a single kernel avoids carrying results to the warehouse and back between steps. FMHA already fuses the whole attention computation into one kernel [S1]. The FlashAttention authors used FMHA's code as their starting point [S1], so fusion is something the two share, not the source of this difference.

Here is the actual difference. In the forward pass, FMHA writes the attention matrix (the table of how much each word attends to every other word) to HBM so the backward pass can reuse it [S1]. FlashAttention skips that write, so its forward pass is a bit faster. It then has to recompute the matrix during the backward pass, which makes that pass a bit slower [S1].

Table 7 shows this pattern [S1]:

| Length | Forward (FMHA → Flash) | Backward (FMHA → Flash) | Total (FMHA → Flash) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 0.10 → 0.08 ms | 0.17 → 0.20 ms | 0.27 → 0.28 ms |
| 256 | 0.29 → 0.22 ms | 0.52 → 0.53 ms | 0.81 → 0.75 ms |
| 512 | 1.14 → 0.81 ms | 1.81 → 2.00 ms | 2.95 → 2.81 ms |

Adding both passes together, FlashAttention is about 4% slower at length 128, 8% faster at 256, and 5% faster at 512 [S1].

What FlashAttention gets in return is memory. Because FMHA stores the attention matrix, it doesn't save much memory and is limited to sequences of at most 512 [S1]. By not storing that matrix and by working in small pieces, FlashAttention can handle sequences up to length 64K [S1].

<question>
Why is FlashAttention slower than Apex FMHA on the backward pass but faster on the forward pass for short sequences?

answer:
Three background ideas explain the gap.

1. **GPU memory hierarchy.** In general, a GPU has large but relatively slow off-chip memory (HBM) and a small, fast on-chip memory (SRAM). Many attention kernels are limited by how many bytes they move to and from HBM, not by FLOPs. How much FlashAttention gains depends on HBM bandwidth and SRAM size [S2].
2. **Recomputation.** This is the same idea as gradient checkpointing. Instead of saving an intermediate tensor in the forward pass for use in backprop, you throw it away and compute it again during the backward pass. You spend extra compute and save memory and memory traffic.
3. **Kernel fusion.** Both FMHA and FlashAttention fuse $\text{dropout}(\text{softmax}(\text{mask}(QK^\top)))V$ into a single CUDA kernel [S1]. Fusion keeps intermediates on-chip instead of writing each step back to HBM, which is why both methods gain more when masking and dropout are used [S2].

The difference is what happens to the attention matrix $P = \text{softmax}(\text{mask}(QK^\top))$. FMHA writes $P$ to HBM in the forward pass so the gradient computation can reuse it [S1]. FlashAttention applies tiling and recomputation instead. It never stores $P$, and it rebuilds the blocks of $P$ from $Q$ and $K$ in the backward pass [S1].

Each pass gets one side of that tradeoff:

- **Forward:** FlashAttention skips writing an $N \times N$ matrix to HBM, so it is faster. At length 512 it takes 0.81 ms against 1.14 ms for FMHA [S1].
- **Backward:** FlashAttention must recompute $P$, while FMHA just reads it back. At length 512 FlashAttention takes 2.00 ms against 1.81 ms [S1].

Added together, FlashAttention's overall runtime is about 4% slower at sequence length 128, 8% faster at 256, and 5% faster at 512 [S1]. These were measured with masking and dropout at BERT-large size on an A100 [S1].

What FlashAttention buys with the extra backward compute is memory. Storing $P$ means FMHA "does not offer substantial memory saving," and FMHA only supports sequences up to 512. FlashAttention supports sequences up to 64K, more head dimensions, and more GPU types [S1]. For short sequences memory is rarely the bottleneck [S1], so the two end up close. The benefit of recomputation shows up as sequences get longer.

Since FMHA targets BERT models, it only supports head dimension 64, and only runs on A100 GPUs. FMHA fuses the attention computation dropout(softmax(mask(QK^{⊤})))V into one CUDA kernel. In the forward pass, it stores the attention matrix softmax(mask(QK^T)) to HBM to be used in gradient computation. As a result, it does not offer substantial memory saving (though for shorter sequences memory footprint is often not a primary concern).

We use FMHA code as a starting point, and apply two well-established techniques (tiling and recomputation) to deal with long sequences and to save memory as mentioned in Section 3. As a result, we can support much longer sequences (e.g., up to length 64K). We also support more head dimensions (16, 32, 64, 128) and broader GPU types (all Turing and Ampere GPUs at the time of writing).

In Table 7, we compare the performance of FlashAttention and Apex FMHA for short sequences (as FMHA only supports sequence length at most 512). Generally FlashAttention is slightly faster than FMHA in the forward pass and slightly slower than FMHA in the backward pass. This is because we do not store the attention matrix in the forward pass and recompute it in the backward pass. Compared to FMHA, the overall runtime of FlashAttention is about 4% slower for sequence length 128, 8% faster for sequence length 256, and 5% faster for sequence length 512.

<question>
Why is FlashAttention slower than Apex FMHA on the backward pass but faster on the forward pass for short sequences?
</question>

answer:
FMHA already fuses $\mathrm{dropout}(\mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{mask}(QK^\top)))V$ into a single CUDA kernel. In the forward pass it also writes the attention matrix $\mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{mask}(QK^\top))$ to HBM so the backward pass can reuse it [S1]. FlashAttention does not store that matrix. It recomputes it, tile by tile, in the backward pass [S1].

The asymmetry follows from where the extra work goes. In the forward pass, FlashAttention avoids the $O(N^2)$ HBM write of $P$, so it comes out slightly ahead. In the backward pass, FMHA just reads the stored $P$, while FlashAttention has to recompute $QK^\top$, the mask and the softmax from $Q$, $K$ and the saved softmax statistics. That extra FLOP cost makes its backward pass slightly slower [S1].

Table 7 (A100, batch 64, 16 heads, $d=64$, with masking and dropout) shows this [S1]:

| $N$ | Fwd FMHA / Flash | Bwd FMHA / Flash | Total FMHA / Flash |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 0.10 / 0.08 | 0.17 / 0.20 | 0.27 / 0.28 |
| 256 | 0.29 / 0.22 | 0.52 / 0.53 | 0.81 / 0.75 |
| 512 | 1.14 / 0.81 | 1.81 / 2.00 | 2.95 / 2.81 |

Overall, FlashAttention is about 4% slower at length 128, 8% faster at 256 and 5% faster at 512 [S1]. At length 128 the recomputation penalty in the backward pass outweighs the savings in the forward pass. At 256 and 512 the savings from skipping the HBM write win out.

The tradeoff is deliberate. Storing $P$ means FMHA offers no substantial memory saving and is limited to sequences of at most 512, head dimension 64 and A100 GPUs. Tiling plus recomputation gives FlashAttention linear memory in $N$ and support for sequences up to 64K, head dimensions 16/32/64/128, and Turing and Ampere GPUs [S1]. A slightly slower backward pass at short lengths is the cost of removing the $O(N^2)$ activation.

question: At long sequence lengths, is FlashAttention actually faster than approximate methods like Linformer in the forward pass, or does it lose out?
plan: Use Table 9 (forward pass, with dropout and masking). First note FlashAttention wins clearly at short lengths (e.g., 0.04 ms vs PyTorch 0.36 ms at 128) and stays competitive up to around 1K-2K. Then show that because exact attention scales quadratically, FlashAttention falls behind linear/sparse methods at long lengths (e.g., 670.76 ms vs Linformer 24.17 ms at 32K), though it still runs where PyTorch and Megatron run out of memory (dashes). Finally point out Block-Sparse FlashAttention is fastest across nearly all lengths (13.34 ms at 64K vs Linformer's 52.39 ms).

<question>
At long sequence lengths, is FlashAttention actually faster than approximate methods like Linformer in the forward pass, or does it lose out?
</question>

answer:
It loses at long lengths. In the forward pass, FlashAttention is the fastest method at short sequences, but past a few thousand tokens Linformer pulls far ahead. The version that stays fast everywhere is **Block-Sparse FlashAttention**, which combines both ideas.

Three pieces of general background (not from these passages) explain why:

1. **Quadratic cost.** In standard attention, every word in a sequence is compared with every other word. Doubling the length means four times as many comparisons, like a party where everyone shakes hands with everyone.
2. **Approximate attention.** Methods like Linformer, Longformer or BigBird skip or compress most of those comparisons. They no longer compute attention exactly, but their cost grows much more slowly with length. FlashAttention is *exact*: it still makes every comparison and only organizes the memory traffic more cleverly.
3. **Running out of memory.** A GPU has a fixed amount of memory. If a method needs more than that, it simply fails, which is called "out of memory".

Now the numbers from Table 9, which times the forward pass with dropout and masking:

- **Short sequences:** At length 128, FlashAttention takes 0.04 ms, compared with 0.36 ms for standard PyTorch attention and 0.67 ms for Linformer [S1]. At 2048 it is still close: 2.85 ms against Linformer's 1.65 ms, and ahead of Longformer (5.72 ms) and Local Attention (7.13 ms) [S1].
- **Long sequences:** Here the quadratic cost shows. At 32,768 tokens, FlashAttention needs 670.76 ms while Linformer needs 24.17 ms [S1]. At 65,536 the gap is 2682.35 ms against 52.39 ms [S1].
- **Still running:** FlashAttention does finish at those lengths. In the table, a dash marks a method that could not run at that length (the results it would need simply aren't there). Standard PyTorch attention has dashes beyond 4096 tokens and Megatron beyond 2048 [S1].

Block-Sparse FlashAttention skips comparisons the way approximate methods do, while keeping FlashAttention's careful memory handling. It is fastest at almost every length: 13.34 ms at 65,536 tokens, against Linformer's 52.39 ms [S1]. The backward and combined passes follow the same pattern. For example, in the combined pass at 32,768 tokens, plain FlashAttention takes 2339.11 ms, Linformer 61.47 ms, and Block-Sparse FlashAttention 32.73 ms [S2].

<question>
At long sequence lengths, is FlashAttention actually faster than approximate methods like Linformer in the forward pass, or does it lose out?
</question>

answer:
It loses. In the forward pass, FlashAttention beats Linformer at short sequence lengths, but from about 1K tokens on Linformer is faster, and by 32K Linformer is more than an order of magnitude faster [S1].

As general background, two ideas explain the pattern:

- **Exact attention cost grows quadratically.** Exact attention computes the full $N \times N$ score matrix $QK^\top$, so its compute grows as $O(N^2)$ in sequence length $N$. Doubling $N$ roughly quadruples the work. FlashAttention cuts memory traffic, but it still computes exact attention, so it cannot escape this quadratic compute.
- **GPU memory limits.** Standard implementations write the $N \times N$ matrix to GPU memory. At long lengths that matrix does not fit and the run fails with out-of-memory (OOM). Linformer and the other approximate methods avoid the full matrix and scale closer to linearly.

Table 9 (forward pass, with dropout and masking) shows three regimes:

- **Short sequences:** FlashAttention clearly wins. At length 128 it takes 0.04 ms, against 0.36 ms for PyTorch and 0.67 ms for Linformer. At 512 it still leads Linformer, 0.21 vs 0.69 ms [S1].
- **Crossover at 1K–2K:** Linformer edges ahead, 0.71 vs 0.82 ms at 1024 and 1.65 vs 2.85 ms at 2048. FlashAttention stays roughly competitive here [S1].
- **Long sequences:** the quadratic scaling dominates. FlashAttention's time goes 41.74 → 167.19 → 670.76 → 2682.35 ms from 8K to 64K, about 4× per doubling. Linformer reaches 24.17 ms at 32K and 52.39 ms at 64K [S1].

FlashAttention still does something the other exact implementations cannot at these lengths. It runs at every length tested, while PyTorch attention shows dashes (no result) beyond 4096 and Megatron beyond 2048 [S1]. Those gaps reflect the memory limit described above.

**Block-Sparse FlashAttention** combines IO-awareness with sparsity, and it is fastest at nearly every length. At 128 it takes 0.06 ms, just behind FlashAttention's 0.04 ms. At 64K it takes 13.34 ms, against Linformer's 52.39 ms [S1]. If you need long sequences and can accept approximation, the block-sparse variant beats Linformer outright. Plain FlashAttention is the right choice when you need exact attention.

<question>
At long sequence lengths, is FlashAttention actually faster than approximate methods like Linformer in the forward pass, or does it lose out?
</question>

answer:
It loses. In the forward pass, FlashAttention is fastest only at short lengths, and Linformer overtakes it at 1K tokens.

From Table 9 (forward pass, with dropout and masking) [S1]:

- **Short lengths:** FlashAttention is far ahead. It takes 0.04 ms at 128 versus 0.36 ms for PyTorch and 0.67 ms for Linformer, and it still beats Linformer at 512 (0.21 vs 0.69 ms) [S1].
- **Crossover:** At 1024, Linformer is slightly faster (0.71 vs 0.82 ms). By 2048 the gap has widened (1.65 vs 2.85 ms) [S1].
- **Long lengths:** FlashAttention is still exact, so its compute is $O(N^2)$. Its runtime roughly quadruples with each doubling of length: 167.19 ms at 16K, 670.76 ms at 32K and 2682.35 ms at 64K. Linformer's grows about linearly: 12.16, 24.17 and 52.39 ms [S1]. At 32K that makes FlashAttention about 28× slower. Local Attention (117.67 ms) and LSformer (179.66 ms) also beat it at 32K [S1].

What FlashAttention does have at long lengths is reach. It needs only linear memory, so it completes at every length tested, while PyTorch attention runs out of memory beyond 4K and Megatron beyond 2K (the dashes in the table) [S1]. Its advantage over standard attention comes from fewer memory reads and writes, not fewer FLOPs, and at long lengths the quadratic FLOP count dominates.

The method that is actually fastest at long lengths is Block-Sparse FlashAttention. It is the fastest or tied for fastest at every length from 256 up, taking 6.55 ms at 32K and 13.34 ms at 64K versus Linformer's 24.17 and 52.39 ms [S1]. The backward and combined passes (Tables 10 and 11) show the same pattern [S2].

<question>
At what sequence length does regular FlashAttention stop being the fastest option compared to approximate methods like Linformer, in the forward+backward masked benchmark?
</question>

answer:
Against Linformer, regular FlashAttention stops being the fastest at a sequence length of **1024**. There it takes 2.37 ms and Linformer takes 1.67 ms [S1]. Counting every method in the table, it loses first place even earlier, at 512, to its own sibling, Block-Sparse FlashAttention [S1].

Three general ideas, not taken from this table, explain why this happens:

- **Quadratic cost.** In standard attention, every word in a sequence is compared with every other word. Doubling the length doubles both the number of words and the number of comparisons each one makes, so the work grows about 4 times. FlashAttention computes this exact, full attention, so it keeps that growth pattern even though it runs each step faster.
- **Linear (approximate) attention.** Methods like Linformer skip most of those comparisons and use a compressed summary. Doubling the length then roughly doubles the work. The result is an approximation, but it grows much more slowly.
- **Sparse attention.** These methods compare each word with only a chosen subset of the others, which also cuts the work.

Table 14 shows these growth patterns. FlashAttention goes from 2.37 to 7.95 to 30.77 ms as the length doubles from 1024 to 2048 to 4096, roughly 4 times per step. Linformer goes from 1.67 to 3.67 to 6.99 ms, roughly 2 times per step [S1].

At short lengths, FlashAttention's speed advantage outweighs its faster growth. At 128 it takes 0.32 ms, compared with 0.80 ms for standard PyTorch attention and 1.51 ms for Linformer [S1]. At 512, FlashAttention is still clearly ahead of Linformer at 0.83 vs 1.56 ms [S1], so the two are not close to tied there. Somewhere between 512 and 1024 the lines cross, and by 1024 Linformer is faster. The gap then widens quickly: at 4096 Linformer takes 6.99 ms and FlashAttention takes 30.77 ms [S1]. This is like a sprinter racing a steady walker: the sprinter leads early, but if each lap gets four times longer for the sprinter and only twice as long for the walker, the walker eventually wins.

Two more points from the table:

- **FlashAttention keeps running where other exact methods stop.** PyTorch attention has no result past 4096, and Megatron has none past 2048. FlashAttention still finishes at 65536, in 7513.01 ms [S1].
- **Block-Sparse FlashAttention is the fastest or close to it at every length.** It combines FlashAttention's speed with sparse attention's reduced work. It is a hair behind plain FlashAttention at 128 and 256 (0.34 vs 0.32 and 0.30 ms). It is fastest from 512 onward, for example 0.69 ms at 1024 and 60.03 ms at 65536, where it also beats Linformer's 117.56 ms [S1].

<question>
At what sequence length does regular FlashAttention stop being the fastest option compared to approximate methods like Linformer, in the forward+backward masked benchmark?
</question>

answer:
In the masked forward+backward benchmark, regular FlashAttention loses to Linformer at **sequence length 1024**. At 512 it is still faster than every approximate method except its own block-sparse variant [S1].

Three ideas from general background (not from these tables) explain the pattern:

- **Quadratic complexity:** standard self-attention forms an $N \times N$ score matrix, so compute grows as $O(N^2)$. Each doubling of $N$ multiplies the work by about 4. FlashAttention is exact, so it still does all $O(N^2)$ work. It only reduces memory traffic.
- **Linear/approximate attention:** methods like Linformer project keys and values down to a fixed smaller size. This brings cost to roughly $O(N)$ but approximates the attention output.
- **Sparse attention:** methods like Longformer, BigBird and block-sparse attention compute only a subset of the $N^2$ query–key pairs. The cost grows with the number of nonzero entries, not $N^2$.

At short lengths FlashAttention's lower overhead wins. At 128 it takes 0.32 ms, compared with 0.80 for PyTorch and 1.51 for Linformer [S1]. Its runtime then grows close to quadratically: 0.83 → 2.37 → 7.95 → 30.77 → 119.98 ms from 512 to 8192, approaching 4× per doubling. Linformer grows much more slowly: 1.56 → 1.67 → 3.67 → 6.99 → 13.63 ms, about 2× per doubling once past 1024 [S1].

The crossover between the two:

| $N$ | FlashAttention | Linformer |
|---|---|---|
| 512 | 0.83 | 1.56 |
| 1024 | 2.37 | 1.67 |
| 2048 | 7.95 | 3.67 |

At 512 FlashAttention is still about twice as fast. By 1024 Linformer is ahead, and the gap widens from there [S1]. At 1024, Longformer (2.94) and BigBird (3.25) remain slower than FlashAttention [S1].

FlashAttention is not quite "the fastest option" all the way to 512. Block-Sparse FlashAttention already beats it there (0.36 vs 0.83 ms). <question>
At what sequence length does regular FlashAttention stop being the fastest option compared to approximate methods like Linformer, in the forward+backward masked benchmark?
</question>

answer:
Against Linformer, regular FlashAttention loses its lead at **sequence length 1024**: 2.37 ms vs 1.67 ms [S1]. At 512 it is still clearly ahead, 0.83 vs 1.56 ms [S1]. That is nearly 2× faster, not a near-tie.

**Why the crossover happens.** At short lengths FlashAttention wins outright (0.32 ms at 128 vs 0.80 for PyTorch and 1.51 for Linformer) [S1]. Its cost is still exact $O(N^2)$ compute, though. From 1024 onward its runtime grows about 4× per doubling: 2.37 → 7.95 → 30.77 → 119.98 ms [S1]. Linformer's low-rank projection makes it roughly linear, about 2× per doubling: 1.67 → 3.67 → 6.99 → 13.63 [S1]. The gap therefore widens steadily after 1024.

**Other approximate methods catch up later.** At 2048, Linformer (3.67) is the only approximate method faster than FlashAttention (7.95). Longformer (9.83) and BigBird (10.36) are still slower [S1]. At 4096 those two also pass it, at 21.35 and 22.57 vs 30.77 ms [S1].

**Two caveats on "fastest":**
- **Block-Sparse FlashAttention.** Strictly, regular FlashAttention is the fastest entry only at 128 and 256 (0.32/0.30 vs 0.34/0.34) [S1]. From 512 on, Block-Sparse FlashAttention is fastest in the table: 0.36 at 512, 0.69 at 1024, and 60.03 ms at 65536 vs Linformer's 117.56 [S1].
- **Exact methods.** Among exact methods, FlashAttention is the only one with numbers past 4096. Megatron has no entries from 4096 onward, and PyTorch has none past 4096. FlashAttention runs all the way to 65536 (7513.01 ms) [S1].

The dropout variant (Table 17) shows the same 1024 crossover against Linformer: 2.52 vs 1.39 ms, after 0.80 vs 1.30 at 512 [S2].

<source label="S1" section="Abstract" pages="1">
We present QLORA, an efficient finetuning approach that reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance. QLORA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters (LoRA). Our best model family, which we name Guanaco, outperforms all previous openly released models on the Vicuna benchmark, reaching 99.3% of the performance level of ChatGPT while only requiring 24 hours of finetuning on a single GPU. QLORA introduces a number of innovations to save memory without sacrificing performance: (a) 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a new data type that is information theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights (b) Double Quantization to reduce the average memory footprint by quantizing the quantization constants, and (c) Paged Optimizers to manage memory spikes. We use QLORA to finetune more than 1,000 models, providing a detailed analysis of instruction following and chatbot performance across 8 instruction datasets, multiple model types (LLaMA, T5), and model scales that would be infeasible to run with regular finetuning (e.g. 33B and 65B parameter models). Our results show that QLoRA finetuning on a small high-quality dataset leads to state-of-the-art results, even when using smaller models than the previous SoTA. We provide a detailed analysis of chatbot performance based on both human and GPT-4 evaluations showing that GPT-4 evaluations are a cheap and reasonable alternative to human evaluation. Furthermore, we find that current chatbot benchmarks are not trustworthy to accurately evaluate the performance levels of chatbots. A lemon-picked analysis demonstrates where Guanaco fails compared to ChatGPT. We release all of our models and code, including CUDA kernels for 4-bit training.^2

2 https://github.com/artidoro/qlora and https://github.com/TimDettmers/bitsandbytes

Preprint. Under review.
</source>
<source label="S2" section="§1 Introduction" pages="1-2">
Finetuning large language models (LLMs) is a highly effective way to improve their performance, [40, 62, 43, 61, 59, 37] and to add desirable or remove undesirable behaviors [43, 2, 4]. However, finetuning very large models is prohibitively expensive; regular 16-bit finetuning of a LLaMA 65B parameter model [57] requires more than 780 GB of GPU memory. While recent quantization methods can reduce the memory footprint of LLMs [14, 13, 18, 66], such techniques only work for inference and break down during training [65].

We demonstrate for the first time that it is possible to finetune a quantized 4-bit model without any performance degradation. Our method, QLORA, uses a novel high-precision technique to quantize a pretrained model to 4-bit, then adds a small set of learnable Low-rank Adapter weights [28] that are tuned by backpropagating gradients through the quantized weights.

QLORA reduces the average memory requirements of finetuning a 65B parameter model from >780GB of GPU memory to <48GB without degrading the runtime or predictive performance compared to a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline. This marks a significant shift in accessibility of LLM finetuning: now the largest publicly available models to date finetunable on a single GPU. Using QLORA, we train the Guanaco family of models, with the second best model reaching 97.8% of the performance level of ChatGPT on the Vicuna [10] benchmark, while being trainable in less than 12 hours on a single consumer GPU; using a single professional GPU over 24 hours we achieve 99.3% with our largest model, essentially closing the gap to ChatGPT on the Vicuna benchmark. When deployed, our smallest Guanaco model (7B parameters) requires just 5 GB of memory and outperforms a 26 GB Alpaca model by more than 20 percentage points on the Vicuna benchmark (Table 6).
</source>

<question>
If the base model is frozen and squashed down to 4 bits, how does QLoRA actually learn anything during finetuning?
</question>

answer:
The model's original weights never change. All the learning goes into a small set of new, adjustable weights attached to the frozen model, and those new weights are kept at full precision [S1][S2].

Three ideas show how this works.

**Low-rank adapters (LoRA)** are small extra pieces bolted onto a big model. Instead of rewriting millions of the model's existing numbers, you train a compact "correction" that gets added to their output. Think of a printed textbook you can't edit, with sticky notes in the margins that adjust what it says. In QLoRA, these adapters are the only parts that learn [S2].

**Quantization** means storing numbers with fewer digits of precision, much like rounding 3.14159 to 3.1 to save space. Here the pretrained model is stored in a 4-bit format, which uses far less memory than the usual 16 bits [S2]. The paper notes that earlier quantization methods worked only for using a model and broke down during training [S2]. QLoRA avoids that problem because the 4-bit weights themselves are never trained.

**Learning through frozen layers** works like this. In general, a model learns by measuring how wrong its answer was and then passing a "blame signal" (the **gradient**) backward through every layer, so each adjustable number knows which way to move. A frozen layer can still pass that signal along, even though the layer itself isn't updated. It acts like a pipe the signal flows through. QLoRA sends gradients through the frozen 4-bit model into the adapters [S1]. The squashed weights still shape the answer and carry the signal, but only the adapters change.

The authors add three tricks to save more memory without hurting quality [S1]:

1. **4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)** is a new 4-bit format. Model weights tend to follow a bell-curve pattern, and NF4 is designed to be "information theoretically optimal" for numbers spread that way, so rounding loses as little as possible [S1].
2. **Double Quantization** handles the small helper numbers that quantization needs to scale values back up. These helper numbers take memory too, so QLoRA rounds them down as well [S1].
3. **Paged Optimizers** deal with the sudden memory spikes that can happen during training [S1].

These pieces make a big difference together. Regular 16-bit finetuning of a 65-billion-parameter model needs more than 780 GB of GPU memory [S2]. QLoRA brings that under 48 GB, which fits on a single GPU, while matching the performance of full 16-bit finetuning [S1][S2].

<question>
If the base model is frozen and squashed down to 4 bits, how does QLoRA actually learn anything during finetuning?
</question>

answer:
The learning happens in a small set of extra weights added beside the frozen model. QLoRA keeps the pretrained model in 4-bit form and never updates it, and it backpropagates gradients *through* those frozen weights into Low Rank Adapters (LoRA), which are the only parameters that change [S1]. The authors describe it as adding "a small set of learnable Low-rank Adapter weights" tuned by backpropagating "through the quantized weights" [S2].

Three general ideas, which the paper takes as known, explain why this works:

1. **LoRA.** LoRA leaves a weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ fixed and learns a low-rank update $\Delta W = BA$, with $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$ and $r \ll \min(d,k)$. The layer computes $h = Wx + BAx$. Only $A$ and $B$ get gradients and optimizer state, which is a tiny fraction of the model, so the knowledge the model gains during finetuning lives in them.
2. **Weight quantization.** Quantization stores each weight with fewer bits (here 4) plus scaling constants. To compute with these weights, they are typically mapped back to a higher-precision value on the fly, so the forward pass still uses ordinary numbers.
3. **Backprop through frozen layers.** "Frozen" means a layer's parameters receive no update. It does not mean that gradients stop at that layer. The chain rule still needs $\partial L/\partial x = W^\top \partial L/\partial h$ to pass gradients to earlier layers, and this only requires reading $W$, never storing $\partial L/\partial W$. So adapters in early layers still get a learning signal through every frozen layer above them.

Together, the frozen 4-bit model supplies the pretrained features and routes gradients, and the adapters absorb the task-specific change.

The paper adds three components to make this cheap without losing accuracy [S1]:

- **4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)** is a data type that the authors call information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights. It targets accuracy at 4 bits.
- **Double Quantization** quantizes the quantization constants themselves, which lowers the average memory footprint.
- **Paged Optimizers** handle memory spikes during training.

As a result, finetuning a 65B model drops from more than 780 GB of GPU memory to less than 48 GB, which fits on a single 48GB GPU [S2]. The authors report this comes without degrading runtime or predictive performance compared with a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline [S2][S1].

We present QLORA, an efficient finetuning approach that reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance. Finetuning large language models (LLMs) is a highly effective way to improve their performance, [40, 62, 43, 61, 59, 37] and to add desirable or remove undesirable behaviors [43, 2, 4]. However, finetuning very large models is prohibitively expensive; regular 16-bit finetuning of a LLaMA 65B parameter model [57] requires more than 780 GB of GPU memory. While recent quantization methods can reduce the memory footprint of LLMs [14, 13, 18, 66], such techniques only work for inference and break down during training [65].

We demonstrate for the first time that it is possible to finetune a quantized 4-bit model without any performance degradation. Our method, QLORA, uses a novel high-precision technique to quantize a pretrained model to 4-bit, then adds a small set of learnable Low-rank Adapter weights [28] that are tuned by backpropagating gradients through the quantized weights.

QLORA reduces the average memory requirements of finetuning a 65B parameter model from >780GB of GPU memory to <48GB without degrading the runtime or predictive performance compared to a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline. This marks a significant shift in accessibility of LLM finetuning: now the largest publicly available models to date finetunable on a single GPU. Using QLORA, we train the Guanaco family of models, with the second best model reaching 97.8% of the performance level of ChatGPT on the Vicuna [10] benchmark, while being trainable in less than 12 hours on a single consumer GPU; using a single professional GPU over 24 hours we achieve 99.3% with our largest model, essentially closing the gap to ChatGPT on the Vicuna benchmark. <question>
If the base model is frozen and squashed down to 4 bits, how does QLoRA actually learn anything during finetuning?
</question>

answer:
The learning happens entirely in a small set of added parameters, not in the 4-bit weights. QLoRA keeps the pretrained model frozen and 4-bit quantized, and backpropagates gradients *through* it into Low Rank Adapters (LoRA), which are the only weights that get updated [S1]. The quantized weights still take part in the forward and backward passes, but they never receive updates themselves [S2].

These sources don't spell out the adapter mechanics, so the following is general background on LoRA. Each adapted layer computes $h = Wx + BAx$, where $W$ is frozen and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times k}$ with $r \ll \min(d,k)$. The gradient with respect to $B$ and $A$ only needs the activations and the upstream gradient flowing through $W$. So $W$ can sit in a low-precision storage format, as long as it is dequantized to compute precision for the matmuls. Optimizer state likewise exists only for $A$ and $B$.

The authors pair this with three memory-saving pieces [S1]:

- **4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)**: a data type that is information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights. It keeps quantization error in the frozen base small.
- **Double Quantization**: quantizes the quantization constants themselves to cut the average memory footprint.
- **Paged Optimizers**: handle memory spikes during training.

The claimed payoff is finetuning a 65B model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance [S1]. That is down from more than 780 GB for regular 16-bit finetuning of LLaMA 65B, with no loss in runtime or predictive performance against a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline [S2].

<question>
Why would you quantize the quantization constants themselves, and how much memory does that actually save?

answer:
**Quantization** means storing each number in a model with fewer bits, the way rounding prices to the nearest dollar saves space on a receipt. QLoRA squeezes the model's weights down to 4 bits each [S1]. This is general background: a 4-bit number can take only 16 possible values, so the original weights have to be mapped onto a small set of levels.

That mapping needs a "ruler" for each group of weights. In general, the weights are split into small blocks, and each block gets one extra number, a **quantization constant** (or scaling factor), that records how to stretch the 16 levels to fit that block's range. Without it, the 4-bit values can't be turned back into real weights. These constants are normally stored at higher precision. One sits beside every small block, so across billions of weights they add up to real memory.

The authors' answer is **Double Quantization**: compress those constants too, applying the same trick a second time to the rulers themselves. This saves an average of about 0.37 bits per parameter, which comes to approximately 3 GB for a 65B-parameter model [S1]. A third of a bit sounds tiny. Multiplied by 65 billion parameters, it frees gigabytes on a graphics card that may only have 48 GB to work with.

It helps to know where this memory is going. In general, LoRA (Low-Rank Adapters) leaves the big model frozen and trains only small add-on pieces. Because the frozen model is the bulk of the memory, shrinking it, and the bookkeeping that comes with it, matters most.

Double Quantization is one of three memory savers in QLoRA, all built around a LoRA setup with adapters at every layer [S1]:

1. **4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)** is a 4-bit format designed to fit how model weights are typically spread out, and it works better than plain 4-bit integers or floats [S1].
2. **Double Quantization** trims the overhead of the quantization constants [S1].
3. **Paged Optimizers** handle sudden memory spikes during training by using NVIDIA's unified memory [S1][S2].

NF4 does most of the shrinking. Double Quantization recovers the leftover overhead that would otherwise eat into the savings, and paged optimizers keep spikes from crashing training. Together, these let the authors finetune models as large as 65B parameters while recovering the quality of full 16-bit finetuning [S1].

<question>
Why did they compare QLoRA against 16-bit LoRA instead of full finetuning for the bigger LLaMA models, and did 4-bit actually hold up?
</question>

answer:
Three ideas from the paper need to be clear first. These definitions are general background, not taken from the passages shown here.

- **LoRA** (low-rank adaptation): Instead of adjusting every one of a model's billions of numbers during finetuning, you freeze them and train a small set of extra "adapter" numbers attached alongside. It is like adding sticky notes to a textbook instead of rewriting it, which saves a lot of memory.
- **NF4** (4-bit NormalFloat): A model's numbers are normally stored with 16 bits each. Squeezing them into 4 bits saves memory but loses detail, a bit like rounding prices to the nearest dollar. NF4 is the authors' way of choosing those rounded values so less detail is lost.
- **MMLU 5-shot**: MMLU is a large multiple-choice exam covering many school and professional subjects. "5-shot" means the model sees five solved example questions before answering, and the score is the percentage it gets right.

The paper gives a practical reason for the comparison. Fully finetuning models at 11 billion parameters and above "requires more than one server of high memory GPUs" [S1]. Running that baseline was out of reach, so the authors compared against the next-best standard: LoRA with the model kept at full 16-bit precision [S1]. The question became whether shrinking the frozen model to 4 bits costs anything compared with that.

For the test, they finetuned LLaMA models from 7 billion to 65 billion parameters on two instruction-following datasets, Alpaca and FLAN v2, and scored them on MMLU 5-shot [S1].

The 4-bit version did hold up. NF4 combined with double quantization (an extra trick that also compresses the small bookkeeping numbers used in the rounding) "fully recovers the 16-bit LoRA MMLU performance" [S1]. A plainer 4-bit format, FP4, came in about 1 percentage point behind [S1]. The choice of 4-bit format matters, and NF4 is the better one, which matches the authors' other experiments [S2]. Earlier tests on smaller models had already shown QLoRA matching both 16-bit LoRA and full finetuning, so this result extends the same pattern to bigger models [S1][S2].

The authors draw a practical lesson from this. If your memory budget is fixed, you get more out of a bigger model stored at lower precision than a smaller model at high precision [S1]. Because they saw no drop in quality at 4 bits, they also don't know where the breaking point is, meaning how low precision can go before performance suffers. They leave that question to future work [S1].

<question>
Why did they compare QLoRA against 16-bit LoRA instead of full finetuning for the bigger LLaMA models, and did 4-bit actually hold up?

answer:
Full finetuning was not feasible at that scale. Full finetuning at and beyond 11B parameters needs more than one server of high-memory GPUs, so for LLaMA 7B through 65B the authors used 16-bit LoRA as the reference point [S1]. Earlier experiments on smaller models had already shown that 16-bit LoRA matches full finetuning, provided LoRA is applied to all transformer layers [S2][S3 is not needed here]. That makes 16-bit LoRA a reasonable stand-in for the full-finetuning baseline.

Three pieces of background help in reading the result. These are general definitions; the paper takes them as known in this section.

- **LoRA** freezes the pretrained weight $W$ and learns a low-rank update $W + BA$, where $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times k}$ and $r \ll \min(d,k)$. Only $A$ and $B$ are trained. QLoRA keeps this setup but stores the frozen $W$ in 4 bits instead of 16.
- **NF4** is a 4-bit data type whose 16 levels are placed at quantiles of a normal distribution. This suits pretrained weights, which are roughly normally distributed. FP4 is the ordinary 4-bit float it is compared against.
- **5-shot MMLU** measures multiple-choice accuracy across many academic subjects. The model sees 5 solved examples in its prompt before each question and is not trained on the task.

The comparison itself finetunes LLaMA 7B–65B on two instruction datasets, Alpaca and FLAN v2, and scores each model with 5-shot MMLU accuracy (Table 4) [S1]. The paper also reports that double quantization, which quantizes the quantization constants themselves, does not degrade performance [S1].

QLoRA with FP4 trails the 16-bit BrainFloat baseline by about 1 percentage point [S1]. This matches the earlier smaller-scale results, where NF4 beat FP4 and other 4-bit types, for example on perplexity: 27.41 for NF4+DQ versus 29.48–31.07 for the Float4 variants [S2].

The authors draw a practical lesson. For a fixed finetuning and inference budget, it is better to use a larger base model at lower precision than a smaller one at higher precision [S1]. Because they saw no degradation at 4 bits, they leave open where the precision–performance trade-off actually starts to bite for QLoRA [S1].

More specifically, Double Quantization treats quantization constants c^FP32 of the first quantization 2 as inputs to a second quantization. This second step yields the quantized quantization constants c^FP8 and the second level of quantization constants c^FP32. We use 8-bit Floats with a blocksize of 2 1 256 for the second quantization as no performance degradation is observed for 8-bit quantization, in line with results from Dettmers and Zettlemoyer [13]. Since the c^FP32 are positive, we subtract 2 the mean from c_2 before quantization to center the values around zero and make use of symmetric quantization. On average, for a blocksize of 64, this quantization reduces the memory footprint per parameter from 32/64 = 0.5 bits, to 8/64 + 32/(64 · 256) = 0.127 bits, a reduction of 0.373 bits per parameter.

Paged Optimizers use the NVIDIA unified memory^3 feature wich does automatic page-to-page transfers between the CPU and GPU for error-free GPU processing in the scenario where the GPU occasionally runs out-of-memory. The feature works like regular memory paging between CPU RAM and the disk. We use this feature to allocate paged memory for the optimizer states which are then automatically evicted to CPU RAM when the GPU runs out-of-memory and paged back into GPU memory when the memory is needed in the optimizer update step.

<question>
If the base model weights are frozen in 4-bit, why does QLoRA still need to dequantize them during the backward pass?
</question>

answer:
Being frozen means the 4-bit weights are never *changed*, not that they drop out of the calculation. To train the small add-on weights, the learning signal still has to flow *through* the frozen layer, and that step needs the weights as ordinary numbers.

Three ideas make this clear:

1. **LoRA** (general background). LoRA bolts a pair of small, trainable matrices onto each big layer of the model. The big original weights stay fixed, and only these small add-ons, called adapters, learn. In the paper's layer formula, the output is the frozen weights' contribution plus the adapters' contribution [S1].

2. **Backpropagation** (general background). After the model makes a prediction, training measures the error and passes a "who's to blame" signal backward, layer by layer, from the output toward the input. Each layer tells the layer before it how much it contributed to the mistake. Doing this requires multiplying by that layer's weights, much like retracing a route on a map: you need the actual map, not just a note that it exists.

3. **Block-wise quantization** (general background). To save memory, weights are chopped into small groups, or blocks, and each block is squeezed into a few bits along with one scaling number that restores its range. Squeezed numbers are compact for storage but can't be used directly in ordinary arithmetic. They first have to be expanded back, which is called **dequantization**.

The authors state that updates only need gradients for the adapter weights, not for the 4-bit weights [S1]. A gradient is the "how should this weight change" signal. However, adapters sit in many layers. For an adapter in an early layer to get its signal, that signal must first pass backward through all the frozen layers after it. Passing through a frozen layer means using its weights, so the 4-bit weights are expanded into 16-bit "BrainFloat" numbers (BF16) to do that calculation [S1]. Nothing is computed or stored to change the frozen weights themselves. They only serve as the route the signal travels along.

The authors summarize this as two data types. NF4, a 4-bit format, is used for storage, and BF16 is used for computation. Weights are expanded from storage to computation form for both the forward pass and the backward pass, but only the LoRA parameters ever get updated [S1].

Equations 5 and 6 describe how the expansion happens, in two steps because of "double quantization." Even the per-block scaling numbers are themselves compressed, to 8 bits, to save extra memory [S1]. So the layer first unpacks those scaling numbers, then uses them to unpack the 4-bit weights into BF16 [S1]. The weights use blocks of 64 for precision, and the scaling numbers use blocks of 256 to save memory [S1].

The compressed copy is what lives in memory. A temporary full-precision copy is made whenever arithmetic needs it, going forward or backward.

Describe the storage vs. computation data type split: NF4 for storage, double-dequantized to BF16 for forward and backward matmuls. Tie to Eq. 5-6 (doubleDequant: first recover the block constants from FP8, then the weights).

<question>
If the base model weights are frozen in 4-bit, why does QLoRA still need to dequantize them during the backward pass?
</question>

answer:
Only the adapters are updated, but the gradient that reaches each adapter has to pass through the frozen weights of every layer above it. That pass needs $W$ in a number format the matmul hardware can use.

**LoRA** keeps a pretrained weight matrix $W$ frozen and learns a low-rank correction $L_1 L_2$ beside it, so a layer computes $XW + XL_1L_2$. Only the small $L_1, L_2$ are trained. This is general background; §2 of the paper introduces LoRA, but that passage isn't among these sources.

**Block-wise quantization** splits a tensor into small blocks and stores each block in low precision together with one scaling constant per block. Recovering a usable value means multiplying the stored code by its block's constant. This is also general background.

QLoRA stores $W$ in 4-bit NF4 with a blocksize of 64, and it quantizes the per-block constants as well, to FP8 with a blocksize of 256 [S1]. A layer is then computed as

$$Y^{\text{BF16}} = X^{\text{BF16}}\,\text{doubleDequant}(c_1^{\text{FP32}}, c_2^{k\text{-bit}}, W^{\text{NF4}}) + X^{\text{BF16}}L_1^{\text{BF16}}L_2^{\text{BF16}}$$

where doubleDequant first recovers the block constants from $c_2$ and then uses them to recover $W^{\text{BF16}}$ (Eqs. 5–6) [S1].

The paper says that parameter updates need only $\partial E/\partial L_i$, not $\partial E/\partial W$ [S1]. Computing $\partial E/\partial L_i$, however, still involves derivatives through the base layer computed via Eq. 5, which requires dequantizing $W^{\text{NF4}}$ to $W^{\text{BF16}}$ [S1].

Concretely, in general terms: in a layer $Y = XW + XL_1L_2$, the gradient sent down to the layer below is $\partial E/\partial X = (\partial E/\partial Y)\,(W + L_1L_2)^\top$. Every adapter beneath that layer receives its gradient through this product, so the frozen $W$ must take part in the backward matmul. Freezing $W$ only means skipping $\partial E/\partial W$. It does not remove $W$ from the chain rule.

The authors summarize this as a split between data types. NF4 is the storage type and BF16 is the computation type. Weights are dequantized for both the forward and backward passes, but weight gradients are computed only for the BF16 LoRA parameters [S1]. Memory therefore stays at roughly 4 bits per base parameter, and each dequantized $W^{\text{BF16}}$ is only needed while its layer's matmul runs.

<question>
If the base model weights are frozen in 4-bit, why does QLoRA still need to dequantize them during the backward pass?
</question>

answer:
Freezing the base weights removes the need for $\partial E/\partial W$, but not the need to use $W$ during the backward pass. Only the adapter gradients $\partial E/\partial L_i$ are used for updates [S1]. To get them, though, the error still has to flow back through every frozen layer [S1].

Consider one layer from Eq. 5 [S1]:

$$
Y = X\,\mathrm{doubleDequant}(c_1^{\text{FP32}}, c_2^{k\text{-bit}}, W^{\text{NF4}}) + X L_1 L_2
$$

The adapter gradients for this layer need only $X$, $L_1$, $L_2$ and the upstream gradient $\partial E/\partial Y$. The problem is the adapters in earlier layers, which need $\partial E/\partial X$. That term is

$$
\partial E/\partial X = (\partial E/\partial Y)\,(W + L_1L_2)^\top,
$$

so the backward pass has to multiply by $W^\top$ at every layer. The paper describes this as computing the derivative through Eq. 5, with $W$ dequantized from storage to compute precision [S1]. Its notation "$\partial X/\partial W$" refers to this input-gradient path, not to a weight gradient.

The 4-bit codes can't go directly into the matmul. QLoRA therefore splits data types into a storage type, usually NF4, and a computation type, BF16. It dequantizes from one to the other in both the forward and the backward pass, and computes weight gradients only for the BF16 LoRA parameters [S1].

Eq. 6 defines the dequantization as two steps [S1]:

1. Recover the per-block FP32 constants $c_1$ from their FP8 quantization $c_2$ (blocksize 256), using the second-level constants $c_1^{\text{FP32}}$.
2. Use those constants to dequantize the NF4 weights (blocksize 64) to $W^{\text{BF16}}$ [S1].

So $W$ is materialized in BF16 only transiently for each matmul. Memory still scales with 4-bit storage, while the arithmetic, including the gradient propagation that the adapters depend on, runs in BF16 [S1].

question: If LoRA is supposed to save memory, why don't they try to shrink the number of LoRA parameters even further? Where is the memory actually going during finetuning?
plan: Explain that the memory cost of LoRA finetuning is dominated by activation/input gradients and the base model, not the adapter weights. Walk through the 7B LLaMA numbers: 26 MB for LoRA params vs 567 MB input gradients, dropping to ~18 MB per sequence with gradient checkpointing, against 5,048 MB for the 4-bit base model. Conclude that cutting LoRA parameters yields negligible savings, so one can afford more adapters, which the authors say matters for matching 16-bit performance.

Memory Requirement of Parameter-Efficient Finetuning One important point of discussion is the memory requirement of LoRA during training both in terms of the number and size of adapters used. Since the memory footprint of LoRA is so minimal, we can use more adapters to improve performance without significantly increasing the total memory used. While LoRA was designed as a Parameter Efficient Finetuning (PEFT) method, most of the memory footprint for LLM finetuning comes from activation gradients and not from the learned LoRA parameters. For a 7B LLaMA model trained on FLAN v2 with a batch size of 1, with LoRA weights equivalent to commonly used 0.2% of the original model weights[28, 37], the LoRA input gradients have a memory footprint of 567 MB while the LoRA parameters take up only 26 MB. With gradient checkpointing [9], the input gradients reduce to an average of 18 MB per sequence making them more memory intensive than all LoRA weights combined. In comparison, the 4-bit base model consumes 5,048 MB of memory. This highlights that gradient checkpointing is important but also that aggressively reducing the amount of LoRA parameter yields only minor memory benefits. This means we can use more adapters without significantly increasing the overall training memory footprint (see Appendix G for a detailed breakdown). As discussed later, this is crucial for recovering full 16-bit precision performance.

<source label="S2" section="§3 QLORA Finetuning" pages="4">
QLORA achieves high-fidelity 4-bit finetuning via two techniques we propose—4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantization and Double Quantization. Additionally, we introduce Paged Optimizers, to prevent memory spikes during gradient checkpointing from causing out-of-memory errors that have traditionally made finetuning on a single machine difficult for large models.

QLORA has one low-precision storage data type, in our case usually 4-bit, and one computation data type that is usually BFloat16. In practice, this means whenever a QLORA weight tensor is used, we dequantize the tensor to BFloat16, and then perform a matrix multiplication in 16-bit.

We now discuss the components of QLORA followed by a formal definition of QLORA.

4-bit NormalFloat Quantization The NormalFloat (NF) data type builds on Quantile Quantization [15] which is an information-theoretically optimal data type that ensures each quantization bin has an equal number of values assigned from the input tensor. Quantile quantization works by estimating the quantile of the input tensor through the empirical cumulative distribution function.

<question>
If LoRA is supposed to save memory, why don't they try to shrink the number of LoRA parameters even further? Where is the memory actually going during finetuning?
</question>

answer:
Shrinking LoRA further would barely help, because the LoRA parameters were never the big memory cost. Most of the memory goes to the base model itself and to bookkeeping that training needs along the way [S1].

The paper uses two terms here without defining them, so first some general background. **Gradient checkpointing** is a memory-saving trick: instead of keeping every intermediate result the model produces, training keeps only a few "checkpoints" and recomputes the rest when needed. It trades extra computation for less memory.

The intermediate results it saves on are **activations**, also general background. Training works in two passes. The forward pass runs the text through the model and produces many intermediate numbers. The backward pass then works out how to adjust each weight. That backward pass needs those intermediate numbers, so they must be stored, or recomputed, until it finishes. These stored numbers, and the gradients (adjustment signals) computed from them, take up memory that grows with the length of the text being processed. Think of a long math problem: the final answer is small, but the scratch paper can fill a notebook.

Here are the paper's numbers for a 7-billion-parameter LLaMA model trained on the FLAN v2 dataset, one example at a time, with LoRA weights at 0.2% of the original model's size [S1]:

- **LoRA parameters (the trainable add-ons):** only 26 MB [S1].
- **Input gradients for the LoRA layers:** 567 MB, more than 20 times the adapters themselves [S1].
- **Those gradients with gradient checkpointing:** about 18 MB per sequence on average. That is still comparable to all the LoRA weights combined [S1].
- **The base model, compressed to 4 bits:** 5,048 MB, which dwarfs everything above [S1].

So the adapters are a rounding error. Cutting them in half would save roughly 13 MB out of several gigabytes. The authors conclude that gradient checkpointing matters, but "aggressively reducing the amount of LoRA parameter yields only minor memory benefits" [S1]. The base model's size is the cost worth attacking, and that is why QLoRA's main effort goes into storing it in 4 bits [S2].

The authors take the opposite approach. Because adapters are so cheap, they add *more* of them without noticeably raising total memory. They say this is crucial for matching the quality of full 16-bit finetuning [S1].

We now describe an overview of the experimental setup with full details in Appendix B.

Data As, to our knowledge, there is no comprehensive study of recent instruction-following datasets, we select eight recent datasets. We include datasets obtained through crowd-sourcing (OASST1 [31], HH-RLHF [4]), distillation from instruction-tuned models (Alpaca [55], self-instruct [59], unnaturalinstructions [26]), corpora aggregations (FLAN v2 [12]), as well as hybrids (Chip2 [32], Longform [30]). These datasets cover different languages, data sizes, and licenses.

Training Setup To avoid confounding effects from different training objectives, we perform QLoRA finetuning with cross-entropy loss (supervised learning) without reinforcement learning, even for datasets that include human judgments of different responses. For datasets that have a clear distinction between instruction and response, we finetune only on the response (see ablations in Appendix B). For OASST1 and HH-RLHF, multiple responses are available. We then select the top response at every level of the conversation tree and finetune on the full selected conversation, including the instructions. In all of our experiments, we use NF4 QLORA with double quantization and paged optimizers to prevent memory spikes during gradient checkpointing. We do small hyperparameter searches for the 13B and 33B LLaMA models and we find that all hyperparameter settings found at 7B generalize (including number of epochs) except learning rate and batch size. We halve the learning rate for 33B and 65B while doubling the batch size.

Baselines We compare our models to both research (Vicuna [10] and Open Assistant [31]) and commercial (GPT-4 [42], GPT-3.5-turbo and Bard) chatbot systems. The Open Assistant model is a LLaMA 33B model finetuned with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) on the same OASST1 dataset that we experiment with. Vicuna does full fine-tuning of LLaMA 13B on proprietary user-shared conversations from ShareGPT and is thus the result of distillation from OpenAI GPT models.
</source>
<source label="S2" section="§5.2 Evaluation" pages="8-9">
Following common practice, we use the MMLU (Massively Multitask Language Understanding) benchmark [24] to measure performance on a range of language understanding tasks. This is a multiple-choice benchmark covering 57 tasks including elementary mathematics, US history, computer science, law, and more. We report 5-shot test accuracy.

We also test generative language capabilities through both automated and human evaluations. This second set of evaluations relies on queries curated by humans and aims at measuring the quality of model responses.

While this is a more realistic testbed for chatbot model performance and is growing in popularity, there is no commonly accepted protocol in the literature. We describe below our proposed setup, using nucleus sampling with p = 0.9 and temperature 0.7 in all cases.

Benchmark Data We evaluate on two curated datasets of queries (questions): the Vicuna prompts [10] and the OASST1 validation dataset [31]. We use the Vicuna prompts, a set of 80 prompts from a diverse set of categories, without modifications. The OASST1 dataset is a multilingual collection of crowd-sourced multiturn dialogs between a user and an assistant. We select all user messages in the validation dataset as queries and include previous turns in the prompt. This procedure leads to 953 unique user queries. We term these two datasets the Vicuna and OA benchmarks.

Automated Evaluation First, based on the evaluation protocol introduced by Chiang et al. [10], we use GPT-4 to rate the performance of different systems against ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 Turbo) on the Vicuna benchmark. Given a query along with ChatGPT’s and a model’s responses, GPT-4 is prompted to assign a score out of ten to both responses and provide an explanation. The overall performance of a model is calculated as a percentage of the score that ChatGPT achieved. Note this relative score can be higher than 100% if the model achieves a higher absolute score than ChatGPT. We find a significant ordering effect with GPT-4 increasing the score of the response occurring earlier in the prompt. To control for such effects, we recommend reporting the mean score over both orders.

<question>
Why didn't they use RLHF on datasets like HH-RLHF that already have human preference rankings, and what did they do with those multiple responses instead?
</question>

answer:
The authors wanted a fair comparison. They finetuned on eight different datasets, and if some had been trained one way and others another way, they couldn't tell whether a difference in results came from the data or from the training method. So they trained every dataset the same simple way, using "cross-entropy loss (supervised learning) without reinforcement learning, even for datasets that include human judgments of different responses" [S1].

The paper takes these two terms as known, so here is some general background. **Supervised finetuning** means showing the model example conversations and having it learn to copy them, like a student studying worked answers. **Cross-entropy loss** is the score used during that copying. At each word, the model guesses what comes next, and it is penalised more the less likely it thought the correct word was. Training adjusts the model to shrink that penalty. RLHF is a different, more involved process. It uses the rankings to reward the model for preferred answers, instead of having it copy one fixed answer.

In OASST1 and HH-RLHF, a conversation can branch like a tree: at each turn, people wrote several possible replies and ranked them [S1]. Instead of feeding those rankings into RLHF, the authors used them as a filter. At every level of the tree they kept only the top-ranked reply, which left one single best conversation path [S1]. That path became an ordinary example for supervised finetuning. The rankings still mattered, because they decided which examples the model learned from.

There is one more difference. For most other datasets, the model learns only from the response part, not the instruction that came before it [S1]. For OASST1 and HH-RLHF, it learns from the full selected conversation, including the user's messages [S1].

This choice also sets up an interesting comparison. The Open Assistant baseline is a 33B LLaMA model trained with RLHF on the same OASST1 data [S1]. Comparing against it shows how far plain copying of the best-ranked conversations can go without the extra RLHF machinery.

Optionally note the contrast with the Open Assistant baseline, which used RLHF on the same OASST1 data.

<question>
Why didn't they use RLHF on datasets like HH-RLHF that already have human preference rankings, and what did they do with those multiple responses instead?
</question>

answer:
The authors deliberately used one training objective for all eight datasets: QLoRA finetuning with cross-entropy loss, with no reinforcement learning, "even for datasets that include human judgments of different responses" [S1]. Their stated reason is to avoid confounding effects from different training objectives [S1]. The study compares instruction datasets, so if HH-RLHF had been trained with RLHF and Alpaca with plain supervised learning, a difference in results could come from the objective rather than the data.

Here, **supervised finetuning** means treating each target text as ground truth and minimizing token-level cross-entropy:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_t \log p_\theta(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x)$$

RLHF instead fits a reward model to the preference rankings and optimizes the policy against it. Supervised finetuning can only learn from a single "correct" target, so the multiple ranked responses have to be reduced to one.

OASST1 and HH-RLHF provide multiple responses organized as a conversation tree. The authors kept the top-ranked response at every level of the tree and finetuned on the full selected conversation, including the instructions [S1]. The rankings therefore act as a filter for choosing training targets rather than as a reward signal.

This differs from how they handled the other datasets. For datasets with a clear instruction/response split, they trained only on the response tokens, so the loss is masked on the instruction [S1]. They justify this choice with ablations in Appendix B [S1].

The choice also shapes one comparison in the paper. The Open Assistant baseline is LLaMA 33B finetuned with RLHF on the same OASST1 dataset [S1]. Guanaco trained on OASST1 therefore sets supervised learning on top-ranked paths against RLHF on the full preference data.

question: Why didn't they use RLHF on datasets like HH-RLHF that already have human preference rankings, and what did they do with those multiple responses instead?
plan: Explain that the authors used plain supervised cross-entropy finetuning across all datasets to avoid confounding from different training objectives, even when preference data existed. Then describe how, for OASST1 and HH-RLHF, they picked the top-ranked response at each level of the conversation tree and trained on the full selected conversation including instructions, contrasting this with other datasets where only the response is trained on. Optionally note the contrast with the Open Assistant baseline, which used RLHF on the same OASST1 data.

<question>
Why didn't they use RLHF on datasets like HH-RLHF that already have human preference rankings, and what did they do with those multiple responses instead?
</question>

answer:
The authors chose this on purpose. They wanted one training objective across all eight datasets so that differences between datasets would not be confounded with differences between objectives. Every model was QLoRA-finetuned with a plain cross-entropy (supervised) loss and no reinforcement learning, "even for datasets that include human judgments of different responses" [S1]. RLHF on HH-RLHF and OASST1 but SFT on Alpaca, FLAN v2 and the others would have mixed a dataset effect with an objective effect.

They handled the preference data in two steps [S1]:

- **Top-ranked path selection.** At every level of the conversation tree they kept only the top-ranked response. This collapses the tree into a single best conversation, so the rankings act as a filter rather than as a reward signal.
- **Loss on the full conversation.** They finetuned on that whole conversation, including the instructions. Datasets with a clean instruction/response split were trained on the response tokens only, with the instruction tokens masked; Appendix B has ablations on this choice.

So the human judgments are reduced to a hard argmax at each turn. Margins between responses and the lower-ranked alternatives are thrown away instead of being used to fit a reward model or a pairwise objective.

This sets up a natural comparison in the paper's baselines. The Open Assistant model is LLaMA 33B finetuned with RLHF on the same OASST1 data [S1]. Guanaco, trained on OASST1 with this supervised top-response recipe, can therefore be read against an RLHF model trained on identical source data.

The retrieved passages give no result that isolates the effect of SFT versus RLHF while holding everything else fixed. The paper's stated reason for avoiding RLHF is experimental control, not a claim that SFT is better.
